A painful lesson for Nvidia NVDA -4.11% on the way to becoming a $100 billion
company: sometimes it’s the little things that count.
Take, for instance, Nvidia’s business selling chips for data centers. It is small,
accounting for just 16% of the company’s trailing 12-month revenue. It is also growing
quickly, more than doubling on a year-over-year basis for the last five quarters. That
success is central to the belief that Nvidia’s chips will be the key components in
artificial intelligence systems of the future. This thesis has taken the company’s
market value from $32 billion a year ago to just above $100 billion earlier this week.
The breathtaking rise has left some investors gasping, which explains why Nvidia’s
stock price slipped 7% Friday in the wake of quarterly results that were excellent by
almost any measure. Overall revenue jumped 56% year-over-year to $2.2 billion,
driven by growth in all of the company’s segments. Operating income more than
doubled to $688 million. The growth exceeded the company’s already optimistic
forecast, and the revenue outlook issued for the current quarter was also well above
Wall Street’s forecasts.

chips to large cloud-service operators like Google and Amazon. Revenue here nearly
tripled year over year to $416 million—a notable accomplishment given that Nvidia’s

market for artificial intelligence chips. It has also made Nvidia one of the most
expensive stocks on the chip market at more than 50 times forward earnings, which

wsj.summary_analysis: Two WSJ pieces cover this event from opposite sides of the report. A same-morning preview, published before the after-market release, set expectations of $1.16 in per-share earnings (up 17% year over year) and $2.68 billion in revenue (up 23%), and flagged three things to watch: data-center momentum (growth had slowed to 2% in one recent quarter before rebounding to 20% in the next, with RBC's Mitch Steves looking for mid-single to double-digit sequential growth); cryptocurrency mining, described as a "double-edged sword" since crypto-related demand embedded in the gaming and OEM segments could disappear if the mining vogue faded, with Stifel's Kevin Cassidy quoted saying Nvidia "played down importance of crypto because they know it can be fickle"; and the unannounced launch timing of next-generation Volta gaming cards, which Barclays analyst Blayne Curtis expected to be unveiled around spring. A second piece, a "Heard on the Street" column published three days later, reports what actually happened: fiscal-year gaming revenue jumped 33% to a record $5.5 billion, full-year sales rose 41% to a record $9.7 billion, operating income surged 66% to a record $3.2 billion, and the operating margin hit a record 33% (versus 28% the prior year), with data-center sales more than doubling for the year. CEO Jensen Huang told analysts on the Thursday earnings call that the company was working with manufacturing partners to keep up with demand from data centers, gamers, and cryptocurrency miners all competing for the same GPUs. The column also notes Nvidia's market value had just passed IBM's, with shares trading at 37 times forward earnings after surging nearly 90% over the prior 12 months.
wsj.why_moved: The reaction piece states directly that Nvidia's stock "defied Friday's turbulence to pick up 7%" the trading day immediately after the Thursday earnings call. As detailed above, the article ties that gain to results that beat the preview's own expectations framework across the board -- record revenue, record operating income, and a record operating margin, plus explicit management commentary about strong demand from all three of the preview's watch items (data centers, gaming, and crypto) simultaneously, rather than any one of them disappointing as the "double-edged sword" framing had worried. Neither article characterizes the announcement day itself: the preview predates the results entirely, and the reaction piece only describes the Friday session that followed. The column also flags a valuation caveat -- at 37 times forward earnings after a 90% rally, "high expectations can set up disappointments down the road" -- which is forward-looking commentary rather than an explanation of this specific reaction.

Nvidia’s Cryptic Road Ahead
Chip maker’s record fiscal year creates high hopes for a repeat
By Dan Gallagher
Feb. 11, 2018 at 10:30 am ET
Nvidia Corp. GeForce GTX 1070 graphic processing units sit stacked inside a ‘mining rig’ computer, which is used to
mine the Ethereum cryptocurrency. AKOS STILLER/BLOOMBERG NEWS
Nvidia NVDA -4.24% may have only high-quality problems these days, but it still
needs to solve them.
One problem the chip maker has is that it seems to be selling all the chips it can make.
Nvidia’s graphics processors, also called GPUs, are in hot demand by everyone from
giant tech companies building data centers to videogamers to cryptocurrency
enthusiasts. The latter two in particular are competing for the type of GPU cards used
in supercharged PCs, causing a shortage that began last summer but seemed to have
https://www.wsj.com/articles/nvidias-cryptic-road-ahead-1518363000 Page 1 of 3
Nvidia’s Cryptic Road Ahead - WSJ 2026-08-28, 2:29 PM
worsened later in the year as the value of cryptocurrencies continued to soar.
That gave a boost to what was already a strong year for Nvidia. Revenue from the
company’s gaming segment jumped 33% to a record $5.5 billion for the fiscal year
ended Jan. 28. This included an unspecified contribution from crypto demand, as well
as the chips the company sells to Nintendo that are used in its popular Switch console.
Nvidia is a “fabless” chip company that outsources the actual manufacturing of its
chips to others. CEO Jensen Huang said on the company’s earnings call Thursday that
it is working with its partners to “catch up to that demand.”
The recently ended fiscal year was the company’s best ever. Sales jumped 41% to a
record $9.7 billion, while operating income surged 66% to $3.2 billion—another
record. The company’s operating margin for the year was also at a record high 33%,
compared with 28% the previous year. Data center sales, representing chips sold to
companies such as Google, Amazon and Microsoft to establish artificial intelligence
capabilities in their networks, more than doubled during the year.
That means Nvidia’s main “problem” for the year ahead is how to improve on
perfection. Chances are that it can. Capital spending on data centers is expected to
continue growing in the double-digit range this year. Gaming demand will remain
strong as well, particularly with Nintendo boosting production of the Switch. Crypto
is a wild card, with the value of those currencies swinging wildly of late, but Nvidia is
wisely cautious about those customers, maintaining its focus on its gamer base and
the burgeoning data center opportunity.
Still, the company has a lot to live up to. Its stock defied Friday’s turbulence to pick up
7% after already having surged nearly 90% in the previous 12 months. Nvidia’s market
value is now ahead of that of IBM’s, with the shares fetching 37 times forward
earnings. High expectations can set up disappointments down the road. Still, there are
worse problems to have.

The Heard on the Street piece and the main earnings story both report that crypto-specific product sales collapsed to just $18 million in the fiscal second quarter ended July 29, down from $289 million the prior quarter, as specialized mining chips reached the market just as cryptocurrency values crashed; CFO Colette Kress is quoted saying "whereas we had previously anticipated cryptocurrency to be meaningful for the year, we are now projecting no contributions going forward," after the company had previously expected roughly $100 million in crypto-related revenue for the quarter. TECH
Apple Pins Hopes on iPhone 7 as Profit, Revenue
Decline
Full-year top and bottom lines decline for the first time since 2001, but the tech giant’s
forecast for current-quarter revenue is bullish
By Robert McMillan
Updated Oct. 25, 2016 at 7:10 pm ET
Apple Inc. posted its first annual revenue decline in 15 years, but projected a return to
growth in the current quarter behind strong sales of its new iPhone 7.
Apple has grown to be the most valuable company in the world over the past decade
on the tremendous success of the iPhone. But that formula proved less effective in the
past year amid lukewarm sales of the iPhone 6S models and slowing growth in
smartphone sales world-wide, especially in China, Apple’s biggest growth market in
recent years.
For its fiscal fourth quarter, ended Sept. 24, Apple reported its third consecutive
decline in revenue and profit. Net income fell 19% to $9 billion, or $1.67 a share, from
$11.1 billion, or $1.96 a share, in the same period a year earlier. Analysts polled by
Thomson Reuters had expected earnings of $1.65 a share.
Revenue fell 9%, to $46.9 billion, mostly ahead of the launch of the iPhone 7, which
went on sale a week before the end of the quarter.
The iPhone accounted for 63% of Apple’s revenue in the just-completed fiscal year, but
growth in the smartphone market has slowed recently and consumer buying habits
are changing. In the fourth quarter, Apple said it sold 45.5 million iPhones, 2.5 million
https://www.wsj.com/articles/apple-profit-and-revenue-slide-as-it-copes-with-dwindling-iphone-sales-1477427419 Page 1 of 4
Apple Pins Hopes on iPhone 7 as Profit, Revenue Decline - WSJ 2026-08-28, 1:04 PM
fewer than a year earlier.
But Apple projected revenue of $76 billion to $78 billion in the current quarter, which
includes the holiday-shopping season and sales of the new phone. That would be an
increase from $75.9 billion in the same period a year earlier. Before Apple’s
announcement, analysts had been expecting revenue in the current quarter of $74.9
billion, according to FactSet.
Apple also projected gross margin, a closely watched measure of profitability, of 38%
to 38.5%, ever so slightly up from 38% in the just-completed quarter.
“We return to growth in the quarter despite the supply shortages that we’ve currently
got,” said Apple Chief Executive Tim Cook.
Mr. Cook said the response to the iPhone 7, released in September “has really been off
the charts.” He said there are waits for some models, particularly the high-end iPhone
7 Plus. Neil Cybart, an independent analyst who follows Apple, said there is an eight-
week wait for some models.
Mr. Cook also touted improvements in the company’s services business, which
includes Apple Music, iTunes and the App Store, where revenue grew 24% from a year
earlier. Apple Music revenue rose 22%, Mr. Cook said, calling services “our huge
highlight in the quarter.”
Apple faces multiple challenges as it looks to augment the success of the iPhone. Sales
of Macintosh computers, for which Apple is expected to introduce new models later
this week, fell 17% from a year earlier. IPad sales, which have fallen in recent years,
were flat. Sales of Apple’s “other products” category, which include the Apple Watch,
fell 22% from a year earlier. And Apple’s secretive automotive project has yet to
produce results.
Still, Apple remains the most profitable U.S. company, with net income of $45.7 billion
for the fiscal year it just ended. The company reported holding $237.6 billion in cash

and investments, up from $231.5 billion three months earlier.
It also may be benefiting from rival Samsung Electronics Co.’s decision to cancel its
Galaxy Note 7 smartphone after a series of battery fires and overheating incidents.
Asked in an interview how Samsung’s problems influenced Apple’s outlook, Mr. Cook
said, “We’ve had a large number of Android switchers that are looking for better
experiences. We want to offer anybody who would like to come over a great
experience.”
In after-hours trading, Apple shares fell 2.8%, after rallying more than 20% over the
past three months amid growing optimism about the iPhone 7 and Samsung’s travails.
Toni Sacconaghi, an analyst at Sanford C. Bernstein & Co., said investors may have
been disappointed that Apple’s projections for the current quarter weren’t even more

Mr. Cybart, the independent analyst, said the revenue projection for the current
quarter implies that Apple expects iPhone unit sales to increase more than 5% from a
year earlier, when the iPhone 6S was its newest model.
Apple is running out of large untapped markets where it could reproduce its
breakneck success in China in recent years. Sales in greater China, which includes

Mr. Cook hopes India, where iPhone sales grew by more than 50% during the most

results on Tuesday. RICHARD B. LEVINE/ZUMA PRESS
Apple Inc. snapped out of three straight quarters of falling revenue as strong demand
for the iPhone 7 raised investors’ hopes that the technology giant is emerging from its
roughest period since it reinvented the market for mobile devices.
Sales of the new smartphone model, which Apple unveiled in September, propelled
total iPhone shipments 5% higher to a record during the three months through
December. iPhones, which account for two-thirds of Apple’s sales, helped boost total

Apple’s services business—which includes its App Store sales and its music and
payments services—continued to boom. Revenue in that segment jumped 18% from a
year ago to $7.2 billion, making it bigger than many large companies. It had nearly
three times the sales of Netflix Inc. during the same period.
Apple Chief Executive Tim Cook said in an interview he expects services revenue to
double over the next four years.
“There’s a lot to feel great about,” Mr. Cook said.
Apple’s shares rose more than 3% after normal trading hours Tuesday to more than

Still, the results overall showed that Apple continues to struggle to regain the type of
momentum that made it the world’s most valuable company. The iPhone 7, while it
helped results, didn’t spark the double-digit increase in overall sales of iPhones that
previous new models did in their first full quarter on the market. Unit shipments of
the iPhone jumped 46% in the October-December quarter of 2014 after the launch of
the iPhone 6, for example.
Apple’s China business remains a soft spot, though it showed signs of stabilizing.
Competition in that market, long a growth driver, has intensified and Apple lost
market share to less expensive smartphones from local rivals like Oppo Electronics

Revenue and profit increase by double digits amid sales rise in China, and the company

By Tripp Mickle
Updated Nov. 2, 2017 at 4:48 pm ET
The Apple logo at a store in Miami Beach, Fla. Apple posted double-digit increases in revenue and profit in the latest
quarter. ALAN DIAZ/ASSOCIATED PRESS
Apple Inc. delivered its best quarterly growth in two years with strong sales in all of
its key products and a rebound in the critical China market as it prepares to start
shipping its most important new iPhone model in a decade.
Demand for the iPhone, which accounts for about two-thirds of total sales, along with
an upturn in sales of Mac computers and iPad tablets helped Apple deliver its fourth-
consecutive quarterly increase in revenue and third quarterly increase in profit, which
rose 19% to $10.71 billion. Shipments of the iPhone rose 2.6% from a year earlier to 46.7

Consistent revenue gains, combined with anticipation for a jump in iPhone sales in
2018, have helped send Apple’s stock up about 50% over the past year through
Thursday’s close and pushed its market value to over $860 billion, after a steep
decline in 2016 because of weak China revenue and iPhone 6s sales.
Shares rose about 3% in after-hours trading.
Questions remain about Apple’s immediate future. The iPhone 8 and 8 Plus, which
started shipping to customers Sept. 22, had the weakest initial sales of any new
iPhone in years, according to estimates by market-research firms.
The iPhone X, which ships Friday and features facial recognition and an edge-to-edge
display, has been dogged by production challenges that delayed manufacturing at
least one month and hounded by questions about its $999 price tag. Customers who
ordered iPhone Xs online in advance of Friday were told there would be long shipping
delays.
Apple Chief Executive Tim Cook said the two iPhone 8s have outsold other models
since shipping but added that he never expected sales to exceed initial sales of last
year’s iPhone 7 and 7 Plus because it is releasing three phones this year. He said that
Apple had earlier planned to release the iPhone X even later than Nov. 2, but decided
to “be very bold and do it sooner.” He declined to offer specifics.
Mr. Cook acknowledged that Apple’s approach this year has brought challenges.
“Having three models is new,” he said in an interview. “The staggered launch is new.
There’s a lot of firsts here. So yes, it is complex [to forecast] and we don’t profess to be
able to do it perfectly.”
Still, he said orders for the iPhone X are “very strong” and that Apple is making
headway on production.

China has posed the biggest test for Apple. The iPhone, which surged in sales in 2015

its market share for products including the iPhone, which he said increased unit
shipments by a double-digit percentage.
Tarun Pathak, Counterpoint’s associate director, said he expects demand for the X
model among China’s 100 million iPhone users to be strong enough to lift volumes and
sales in the quarters ahead.
Supply-chain issues have caused analysts to slash iPhone X sales projections for the
critical holiday sales period this year. Market-research firm Strategy Analytics cut its

The price tag for the iPhone X, though, has counteracted that.

wsj.summary_analysis: The article reports Apple delivered its best-ever revenue for its typically weakest fiscal quarter, with iPhone demand holding up despite a contracting global smartphone market and app-store/services revenue reaching a record. iPhone revenue rose 20% to $29.91 billion even as unit shipments rose less than 1% to 41.3 million, reflecting an average selling price up roughly 20% to about $724, which the article attributes partly to the $999 iPhone X making up an estimated one-quarter of iPhones sold. Total revenue rose 17% for a seventh straight quarter of accelerating growth, to $53.27 billion, above Wall Street expectations and near the high end of Apple's own guidance, while profit rose 32% to $11.52 billion ($2.34 a share), also above analysts' consensus. Cook is quoted saying "we're expanding our reach into emerging markets and seeing strong double-digit growth in revenue," and CFO Luca Maestri noted demand had remained consistent for the iPhone X, 8 and 8 Plus even in a seasonally weak period. Services revenue hit a record $9.55 billion, up 31%, and the article notes Apple's market value was approaching $950 billion, putting it "on the cusp of becoming the first $1 trillion U.S. company." It also flags real risks: escalating U.S.-China trade tensions that could expose Apple's roughly one-fifth China revenue exposure to tariffs, criticism from Chinese state media (including Xinhua and CCTV) over iMessage spam and App Store gambling apps, and Huawei having overtaken Apple as the world's second-largest smartphone vendor by shipments, according to Strategy Analytics.
wsj.why_moved: The article states shares rose 3.7% to $197.33 in after-hours trading. Building on the detail above, the article ties the reaction to revenue and profit both beating expectations — profit up 32%, revenue near the high end of guidance — combined with resilient iPhone demand in a contracting global market and record 31% services growth, with the ASP-driven iPhone revenue growth on essentially flat unit shipments underscoring the pricing-power narrative the piece repeatedly emphasizes. The trade-war and Chinese-regulatory risks the article also details are presented as separate overhangs rather than something explicitly tied to tempering the immediate stock reaction.

wsj.summary_analysis: The WSJ framed Alphabet's first-quarter 2016 report around the idea that "even a small miss can have big consequences": revenue of $20.26 billion, up 17% year over year, came in just below the average analyst estimate of $20.37 billion (Thomson Reuters), and non-GAAP earnings of $7.50 a share missed the $7.97 analysts expected. Net income itself rose to $4.21 billion ($6.02 a share) from $3.52 billion ($5.10) a year earlier, so the underlying business was healthy; the article says there was "no single reason" for the miss, pointing instead to a combination of slightly lower revenue and slightly higher expenses, particularly rising personnel costs and growing payments to advertising partners as more ad revenue shifted to mobile and flowed through middlemen. CFO Ruth Porat told analysts the results "underscored the great momentum of our businesses globally," attributing it primarily to increased mobile search use, while Macquarie's Ben Schachter noted Google was "showing more ads in a smaller space" on phones, driving higher click-through but lower revenue per click (cost per click fell 9% year over year). The article also detailed Alphabet's "Other Bets" segment, the second quarter it reported those figures separately: operating losses widened to $802 million from $633 million even as segment revenue more than doubled to $166 million, and Porat cautioned investors to expect "lumpiness" in that unit's results quarter to quarter. Total costs and expenses grew 16.4%, slower than revenue, which the piece attributed to expense discipline under Porat alongside continued hiring (2,300 net new employees). The report also noted that the day before earnings, EU regulators had filed formal antitrust charges against Google over Android, adding a fresh regulatory overhang on top of an existing EU shopping-service case.
wsj.why_moved: The article states Alphabet shares fell 6% in after-hours trading, and ties that reaction directly to the modest revenue and EPS misses detailed above ($20.26 billion versus $20.37 billion expected, $7.50 versus $7.97 a share) rather than to any single identifiable cause, explicitly noting there was "no single reason." The framing device the article opens with — that a small miss can have outsized consequences — reflects that this was a business still growing at double-digit rates, but doing so after a 46% rally in Alphabet shares over the prior year had raised the bar for what would satisfy investors. The widening Other Bets losses ($802 million from $633 million) and the fresh EU antitrust charges reported the day before add to a mildly negative backdrop but are not framed by the article as primary drivers of the stock reaction; the piece keeps the emphasis on the expectations miss itself.

wsj.summary_analysis: Alphabet's second-quarter 2016 report was described as part of a two-day pattern of "blockbuster earnings" from internet giants riding the mobile shift, with Facebook having reported its own strong quarter the day before. Revenue rose 21% to $21.5 billion, beating the average analyst estimate of $20.76 billion (Thomson Reuters), while profit surged 24% to $4.88 billion ($7 a share, up from $3.93 billion/$4.93 a year earlier); non-GAAP EPS of $8.42 beat the $8.04 consensus. CEO Sundar Pichai told analysts "the strength of the quarter is about mobile," and RBC's Mark Mahaney offered pointed comparative framing, saying the results countered a persistent Wall Street narrative that "Google's best days are behind it and that search is a dramatically maturing business" — a notable rebuttal given that Alphabet had missed analyst estimates in eight of the prior twelve quarters. The article detailed the click/price dynamic underlying the beat: paid clicks rose 29% (a fourth straight quarter above 22% growth) while average cost per click fell only modestly, with analysts noting early signs that mobile ad bidding was strengthening. It also flagged competitive context, noting Google and Facebook together captured roughly 77%-to-99%-type dominance of ad-market growth (specifically that the two firms captured 99% of the online ad industry's revenue growth in 2016 per Pivotal Research's Brian Wieser, with Facebook's ad market share rising to 12% from 8.6% in 2014 even as Google held about 31% of the broader digital-ad market). Nonadvertising revenue, primarily cloud, accelerated to 33% growth to $2.17 billion, while Other Bets revenue jumped to $185 million from $74 million even as its operating loss widened to $859 million from $660 million; total expenses grew 20%, a touch slower than revenue, continuing the cost discipline theme under CFO Ruth Porat.
wsj.why_moved: The article reports Alphabet shares jumped 4% in after-hours trading, and links that reaction explicitly to the revenue and EPS beats described above ($21.5 billion versus $20.76 billion expected, $8.42 versus $8.04 a share) alongside Mahaney's framing that the results rebutted the "Google is maturing" bear case that had built up after eight quarters of misses in the prior twelve. The 29% growth in paid clicks and the deceleration in mobile Facebook comparisons together painted a picture of Google's mobile transition succeeding rather than cannibalizing growth, which is consistent with the reported rally. Given that Alphabet stock had actually been down 1.6% for the year heading into the print, the beat represented a meaningful reset of sentiment. The accelerating cloud/nonadvertising growth (33%, up from prior quarters) also supported the diversification narrative the article highlights as a secondary driver of investor enthusiasm beyond the core ad beat.

Google Profits Surge on Strong Ad Demand
Internet giant continues to capture users and advertisers as they shift to mobile
By Jack Nicas
Updated July 28, 2016 at 7:19 pm ET
Search ads remain Google’s main moneymaker, but there are signs of a slight deceleration in spending on those ads.
BLOOMBERG NEWS
Google parent Alphabet Inc. said quarterly profit soared 24%, the second internet
giant in two days to report blockbuster earnings driven by consumers’ rapid shift to
mobile devices.
Alphabet said growth continued as companies bought more ads on its search engine
and other products, while users increasingly clicked on those ads. Revenue, fueled by
Google’s advertising business, rose 21% to $21.5 billion in the second quarter from a
year ago, beating analysts’ average estimate of $20.76 billion.
https://www.wsj.com/articles/google-profits-surge-on-strong-ad-demand-1469736762 Page 1 of 5
Google Profits Surge on Strong Ad Demand - WSJ 2026-08-28, 2:43 PM
The rise of smartphones has put internet-connected computers in the pockets of more
than a billion people world-wide, leading to a surge in internet use—and a major boost
to the bottom lines of tech giants such as Google and Facebook Inc. As consumers use
the companies’ wildly popular free services more, Google and Facebook can sell more
ads to companies trying to reach those users.
“The strength of the quarter is about mobile,” Google Chief Executive Sundar Pichai
said Thursday. “Our investment in mobile now underlines everything that we do
today, from search and YouTube to Android and advertising.”
Alphabet stock, which had slid 1.6% in 2016 through Thursday’s close, jumped 4% in
after-hours trading. The company had recently struggled to meet investor
expectations, with earnings missing analysts’ estimates in eight of the past 12
quarters.
“The big overhang of concern on Wall Street was that Google’s best days are behind it
and that search is a dramatically maturing business. I think they just proved that’s not
the case,” said Mark Mahaney, an analyst with RBC Capital Markets. The shift to
mobile phones has revitalized Google’s business, he said. “More smartphones means
more use of Google, and YouTube, too.”
Facebook, Google’s chief rival, also is gaining strength from mobile. Facebook said
Wednesday that its second-quarter profit nearly tripled from a year earlier to $2.1
billion, easily beating Wall Street estimates. Mobile accounted for 84% of its $6.2
billion in second-quarter advertising sales.
While Google still controls about 31% of the roughly $187 billion world-wide digital-ad
market, Facebook’s market share has risen to 12% from 8.6% in 2014, according to
research firm eMarketer.
Google’s success capturing advertisers and users as they shift to mobile devices from
traditional personal computers is helped by its Android smartphone software, which
https://www.wsj.com/articles/google-profits-surge-on-strong-ad-demand-1469736762 Page 2 of 5

gives its search engine and other services top billing on more than a billion devices.
Google also pays Apple Inc. to make Google the default search engine on iPhones.
Google said last year that more than half of its searches now come on mobile devices,
and some analysts estimate more than half of its revenue comes from mobile.
Advertisers’ spending on mobile search ads increased 63% in the second quarter over
a year prior, while overall search-ad spending rose just 10% over the period, according
to marketing-technology firm Kenshoo Ltd.
Alphabet on Thursday said net profit in the quarter that ended June 30 rose to $4.88
billion, or $7 a share, from $3.93 billion, or $4.93 a share, a year earlier. Excluding
certain items, Alphabet earned $8.42 a share, beating analysts’ estimates of $8.04 a
share.
Clicks on ads that Google shows users increased 29% in the second quarter over a year
prior, the fourth consecutive quarter with growth above 22% after a year of slower
growth.
Google said it is now reaping the rewards from the shift to mobile because companies
are increasingly willing to advertise on smartphones. That is in part because Google is
adding new mobile ad formats and better measuring the efficacy of such ads,
including tracking users’ locations to see if they visit a physical store after seeing an
ad for the store on their phones, Google said.
One downside to mobile’s rise for Google has been a simultaneous decline in the
average amount that advertisers pay Google per ad click. Mobile ads are generally less
expensive than desktop ads, so as the number of mobile ads has increased,
advertisers’ overall cost per click has declined.
But analysts say there are some signs ad buyers are bidding more for mobile ads, and
on Thursday Google said advertisers’ cost per click decreased 7% in the second
quarter over a year prior, compared with a 9% decline in the first quarter and steeper

declines before that.
Google’s 19% growth in advertising revenues was outpaced by nonadvertising sales,
which grew 33% to $2.17 billion over a year prior. That jump was an acceleration for
Google’s nonadvertising business, which executives said was primarily driven by its
cloud business of hosting other companies’ data and processing on its servers.
Google is betting the cloud can become a major revenue driver over the next several
years and is investing hundreds of millions of dollars in building new data centers.
Other nonadvertising businesses include hardware sales and Google’s share of app
sales in its Play Store.
Thursday’s results are the third time the firm reported as Alphabet, a parent company
created in October to house Google and a series of “other bets,” from home-
automation firm Nest to the research lab X, which is working on long-term projects
such as self-driving cars, internet-beaming balloons and delivery drones.
While the Google unit accounts for virtually all of Alphabet’s revenue, analysts and
investors have closely watched financial results of the other initiatives for a sense of
how much money they are losing. Revenue for those other bets increased to $185
million from $74 million a year ago, and the operating loss widened to $859 million
from $660 million.
Cost controls have also been a recent focus since the arrival of former Morgan Stanley
executive Ruth Porat as finance chief last year. Investors cheered Ms. Porat’s hire,
hoping she would step up scrutiny of Alphabet’s costs. Second-quarter total expenses

The piece highlighted the widening divergence between ad volume and ad pricing as a specific point of concern: ad clicks rose 36% year over year while advertisers' prices for those ads fell 15%, with the article noting both figures were the highest in at least three years, and attributing the pricing decline specifically to the growing share of YouTube ads, which generally earn less than ads shown above Google search results. CFO Ruth Porat told analysts that newer ad formats — mobile search, YouTube, and automated ad buying — had "only begun to scratch the surface," citing "sizable opportunities that have not yet been tapped," while JMP Securities analyst Ron Josey called YouTube the "heir apparent to search." The article detailed Alphabet's diversification progress in concrete terms: advertising fell to 85.9% of revenue from 89.4% a year prior, with nonadvertising sales surging 62% to $3.4 billion, boosted by the fourth-quarter launch of three new hardware products (Pixel smartphones, Google Home, and VR headsets). Capital expenditures jumped nearly $1 billion to $3.08 billion, partly to build data centers to compete with Amazon and Microsoft in cloud. Other Bets revenue rose 75% to $262 million with the operating loss narrowing 10% to $1.09 billion, mostly from Nest, Google Fiber, and Verily (which separately disclosed an $800 million investment from Temasek). RBC's Mark Mahaney provided historical framing, noting Google's advertising business had posted 20%-plus annual growth (ex-currency) for 20 consecutive quarters, calling it "the strongest it's ever been."

Even though Alphabet attributed the shortfall to a one-time tax item rather than operating weakness, and even though Mahaney's 20-consecutive-quarter growth framing underscored the durability of the core ad business, the market's initial reaction still registered as a miss on the headline profit number. The widening gap between the 36% rise in ad clicks and the 15% decline in ad prices — attributed to the YouTube mix shift discussed above — may have compounded concerns about margin durability even as volume growth stayed strong.

The article's key contextual detail is that this beat came despite an active advertiser boycott: major brands including Coca-Cola and Wal-Mart had pulled spending from non-search Google advertising (i.e., YouTube and display) after their ads appeared alongside offensive content, and analysts had expected this to weigh on the quarter's ad revenue. YouTube responded by giving advertisers more control over ad placement, and the strong results suggest the boycott's financial impact was limited, at least in this reporting period — the headline is explicitly framed as growth continuing "seemingly unscathed" by the boycotts. Paid clicks rose 44% year over year, though average cost per click fell 19%, which the article attributes to the continued mix shift toward lower-priced mobile and YouTube inventory. The piece also supplied useful competitive-market framing: Google and Facebook together captured an estimated 77% of gross global ad spending in 2016 (up from 72% the year before) and 99% of the online ad industry's entire revenue growth that year, according to Pivotal Research's Brian Wieser, effectively squeezing out the rest of the industry. On diversification, the "other revenues" segment that includes cloud grew 49% to $3.1 billion, while Other Bets revenue rose to $244 million from $165 million even as its operating loss grew to $855 million from $774 million.

The framing that growth continued despite the Coca-Cola/Wal-Mart boycotts appears central to the positive reaction: investors had gone into the print bracing for a possible hit to YouTube-adjacent ad revenue from that controversy, and the fact that paid clicks still grew 44% and overall revenue still beat estimates likely removed a specific overhang rather than just delivering a generic beat. The 49% growth in the cloud-inclusive "other revenues" segment reinforced the diversification narrative that had been a recurring theme in prior quarters' coverage, adding a secondary positive alongside the core ad beat.

wsj.summary_analysis: This Heard on the Street column on Alphabet's second-quarter 2017 results emphasized a specific historical marker: traffic acquisition costs (TAC) — what Google pays partners like Apple to route search traffic to it — rose 28% year over year to a record $5.1 billion, and for the first time in five years, TAC growth outpaced revenue growth. The column contrasted this against otherwise strong headline metrics: paid clicks surged 52% year over year, the biggest jump in at least seven years, which the piece called notable given the company's ad revenue base had grown nearly fourfold over that same period. The article also isolated the effect of a one-time item on profitability: operating income would have hit a record $6.9 billion were it not for a $2.7 billion fine levied by the European Union, and even accounting for that framing, underlying operating income growth of 15% year over year was described as the company's slowest pace in two years. The piece's central argument is that click growth of this magnitude is not costless — Google's ability to generate "an unprecedented ability to generate economic activity" from search comes bundled with rising distribution costs that increasingly eat into margin expansion, a dynamic the headline explicitly calls "traffic costs jam up Google." The column closes by noting Alphabet stock had run up 26% year to date heading into the report, providing valuation context for how investors might react even to solid underlying growth.
wsj.why_moved: The column reports Alphabet shares slipped 3% on the Monday following the results, and explicitly attributes that decline to two specific factors laid out above: the earnings deceleration (15% underlying operating income growth, the slowest in two years, driven by TAC growth outpacing revenue for the first time in five years) and the stock's already-large 26% run-up for the year, which had left less room for a merely solid quarter to satisfy expectations. In other words, the piece frames this less as a reaction to a "miss" in the traditional sense — paid clicks actually grew at the fastest rate in seven years — and more as a valuation-driven pullback once investors focused on the rising traffic-cost dynamic described above. The column's closing framing, that "growth has its price," directly describes the TAC-versus-revenue dynamic as the mechanism connecting the underlying business results to the stock's decline.

Google generates a lot of clicks. But they aren’t free—nor always cheap.

Separately, the piece noted Alphabet's $101 billion overseas cash pile, the appointment of new chairman John Hennessy (former Stanford president, replacing Eric Schmidt), a fresh $2.71 billion EU fine over shopping-comparison bias, and marketer backlash over YouTube ad placement next to objectionable content. wsj.summary_analysis: Alphabet's first-quarter 2018 report showed net profit surging 73% to $9.4 billion, which the article describes as the company's strongest earnings growth since the fourth quarter of 2009 — a striking historical comparison. Advertising revenue, still nearly all of the company's top line, rose 24% to $26.6 billion. Critically, the article details that roughly $3 billion of the profit increase came not from operations but from a change in accounting rules requiring Alphabet to report the current fair value of nonmarketable securities, most notably its stake in Uber; the company did not disclose how much of that $3 billion was Uber specifically, but the article notes Uber's implied valuation was itself uncertain, having last priced at a $48 billion valuation in a December share sale led by SoftBank — a roughly 30% discount to the $68 billion valuation from Uber's last primary funding round. The piece also detailed rising cost pressure: traffic acquisition costs rose 35% to $6.3 billion, representing about one-fifth of revenue for five consecutive quarters, with Pivotal Research's Brian Wieser noting that Google's partner-driven ad revenue "is growing faster, which helps their top line, but is lower margin." Capital expenditures nearly tripled to $7.3 billion, including a $2.4 billion purchase of a building in Manhattan's Chelsea Market, which CFO Ruth Porat said "reflects the demand we are seeing" rather than one-off spending. The article also gave a rare look at Nest's standalone financials — $726 million in revenue across all of 2017, about 60% of total Other Bets revenue that year — while noting Nest had been moved back into the core Google unit and had been "upstaged" by smart speakers like Amazon Echo and Google Home. It also flagged that YouTube's revenue remains undisclosed, with analysts estimating $11 billion to $20 billion, and noted a backdrop of intensifying privacy scrutiny (GDPR taking effect May 25) that CEO Sundar Pichai said Google was prepared for.
wsj.why_moved: The article explicitly states that "Alphabet's shares were little changed in after-hours trading" following the report, framing the results as a solid but not surprising beat given the unusual accounting boost from the Uber stake revaluation described above, which investors may have partly discounted as non-operational. The tripled capital expenditures and 35% rise in traffic acquisition costs discussed above raised questions about margin pressure even amid the headline profit beat, though the article characterizes the immediate market response to the results as muted rather than as a reaction to those cost pressures specifically.

wsj.summary_analysis: Microsoft's fiscal third-quarter 2016 report centered on a specific deceleration story: Intelligent Cloud segment revenue grew 3% (8% in constant currency) with Azure up 120% in constant currency, but the article emphasizes this was a slowdown from the immediately prior quarter, when the same segment had grown 5% (11% constant currency) and Azure had grown 140%. Pacific Crest analyst Brendan Barnicle called it "deceleration, for sure," though he tempered that by noting Azure was still a small, early-stage business. Adjusted per-share profit was flat at 62 cents, 2 cents below the Thomson Reuters analyst consensus; CFO Amy Hood attributed the miss to a "catch up" tax adjustment reflecting an expected higher full-year tax rate, saying earnings were "closer to 66 cents when you take out the tax." The article detailed several bright spots that offset the cloud slowdown narrative: the More Personal Computing segment (including Windows) posted operating profit growth of 57% despite revenue up just 0.9%, and Surface revenue rose 61% in constant currency, topping $1 billion for a second consecutive quarter — notably the first time that had happened outside of a holiday quarter. Windows revenue from PC makers still declined 2% in constant currency despite rapid adoption of Windows 10 (270 million active devices, though many were free, non-revenue-generating upgrades). Office 365 showed strong subscriber growth (consumer users up 79%, commercial up 57%), which Hood said "helps pull along new usage of Azure," and the article included an anecdote about Fruit of the Loom's CIO praising Azure's security features as the company began migrating disaster-recovery workloads there. Guidance for the following quarter across all three segments came in below analyst expectations.
wsj.why_moved: The article states shares fell about 5.5% in after-hours trading to $52.70, and ties that decline directly to the combination of factors detailed above: the cloud-growth deceleration (Azure slowing from 140% to 120% constant-currency growth, and the Intelligent Cloud segment slowing from 5% to 3% headline growth) landing alongside a 2-cent EPS miss, even though Hood attributed the miss to a one-time tax item rather than an operating shortfall. The article explicitly says "the slowing growth in cloud computing coupled with the earnings miss spooked investors," making clear that it was the combination of both factors, not either alone, that the piece identifies as the trigger for the selloff. The below-consensus guidance for the following quarter across Productivity and Business Processes, Intelligent Cloud, and More Personal Computing likely compounded the reaction by signaling the deceleration was expected to continue rather than being a one-quarter blip.

TECH
Microsoft’s Cloud Business Slows
Per-share earnings fall short of Wall Street expectations
By Jay Greene
Updated April 21, 2016 at 9:46 pm ET
Microsoft’s own Surface line of computers remains a bright spot. DAN HIMBRECHTS/EUROPEAN PRESSPHOTO AGENCY
Microsoft Corp., MSFT 1.76% a rare tech stalwart that has appeared to be making a
deft transition to the new world of Web-based, on-demand computing, faltered in the
most recent quarter as the growth of its cloud business slowed.
Revenue from Microsoft’s Intelligent Cloud segment, which includes its Azure on-
demand computing services as well as its older server software sales, grew 3% to $6.1
billion. The gain was 8% in constant currency, and the company said that Azure grew
120% in constant currency.
But just one quarter earlier, the same segment grew 5%, or 11% in constant currency,
https://www.wsj.com/articles/microsofts-profit-slides-25-1461270478 Page 1 of 5
Microsoft’s Cloud Business Slows - WSJ 2026-08-28, 3:15 PM
and Azure was up 140%.
“That’s deceleration, for sure,” said Brendan Barnicle, an analyst at Pacific Crest
Securities. However, Mr. Barnicle noted that Azure represents only a fraction of
overall revenue and is relatively new. “Those numbers are still so small, and it’s still so
early,” he said.
Microsoft also missed analyst forecasts for profit in its third quarter. Adjusted per-
share profit was flat at 62 cents, 2 cents below what analysts surveyed by Thomson
Reuters expected.
Microsoft Chief Financial Officer Amy Hood attributed the miss to a “catch up” tax
adjustment to account for an expected increase in the full-year tax rate. Earnings per
share are “closer to 66 cents when you take out the tax,” Ms. Hood said in an interview.
The slowing growth in cloud computing coupled with the earnings miss spooked
investors. Shares traded after hours fell about 5.5% to $52.70.
Sales of Windows have tracked the declining PC industry, though the company’s More
Personal Computing segment, which includes the flagship operating system, has been
a bit more resilient. Revenue in the segment edged up 0.9% to $9.46 billion, while
operating profit jumped 57%.
Uptake of Windows 10, the latest version, has been more rapid than any previous
version. Still, Windows revenue from computer makers declined 2% in constant
currency. Microsoft last month said 270 million active devices run the new version,
though many of those are free upgrades that bring no revenue.
Microsoft’s own Surface line of computers remains a bright spot. Surface revenue
increased 61% in constant currency and topped $1 billion for the second straight
quarter for the first time outside of a holiday period, the company said.
In the segment that includes Microsoft’s popular Office productivity software
https://www.wsj.com/articles/microsofts-profit-slides-25-1461270478 Page 2 of 5
Microsoft’s Cloud Business Slows - WSJ 2026-08-28, 3:15 PM
franchise, sales rose 1% to $6.52 billion—but profit declined 6.6%.
One of the big growth engines for Microsoft has been its Office 365, the cloud version
of its productivity software suite. (Revenue from Office 365 is lumped with the on-
premises version of Office, not with other cloud businesses.)
Consumer users of Office 365 grew 79% year-over-year, while the number of
commercial users climbed 57%, the company said.
Office 365’s growth is an important metric because Microsoft is working hard to upsell
those customers to other cloud services. Ms. Hood said Office 365 “helps pull along
new usage of Azure.”
One of those customers, Fruit of the Loom Inc., moved its email to Office 365 two years
ago and started tinkering with Azure, using it for external websites and software
development and testing.
The Bowling Green, Ky., apparel company was impressed with Azure’s security and
management features, enough that it began moving the disaster-and-recovery service
for its business-management software to Azure in January, said Chris Krebs, Fruit of
the Loom’s chief information officer.
“Microsoft understands enterprise customer needs,” he said.
For its fourth quarter, Microsoft projected its Productivity and Business Processes
revenue at $6.5 billion to $6.7 billion “with continued annuity shift to the cloud,
offsetting the impact of a weaker PC market,” Ms. Hood said during a conference call
with analysts.
Revenue for the Intelligent Cloud segment should come in between $6.5 billion and
$6.7 billion. And Microsoft expects revenue in the More Personal Computing segment
of $8.7 billion to $9 billion. All of those estimates are below analyst expectations.

Overall, Microsoft said its third-quarter net income fell to $3.76 billion, or 47 cents a
share, down from $4.99 billion, or 61 cents a share, a year earlier. Revenue slid 5.5% to
$20.5 billion, and on an adjusted basis rose 1.6% to $22.08 billion.

wsj.summary_analysis: Microsoft's fiscal fourth-quarter 2016 report contained a notable historical marker buried within otherwise positive results: full-year fiscal 2016 revenue fell 8.8% to $85.32 billion, the company's first annual revenue decline since 2009, driven by Microsoft's continued retreat from its mobile-phone bet (a further $1.1 billion charge tied to unwinding the Nokia handset acquisition, which CFO Amy Hood said "reflects all of our judgments today") and the ongoing decline in Windows/PC sales. The article frames this decline as not troubling investors, quoting Stifel's Brad Reback saying "it's really important to focus on what's growing and what's falling... Everything that matters grew and grew at a good clip." Azure revenue alone grew 102% (108% in constant currency) year over year, part of an Intelligent Cloud segment that grew 6.6% (9.6% constant currency) to $6.71 billion, while the Office/Dynamics segment grew 4.6% (7.6% constant currency) to $6.97 billion, including 54% growth in commercial Office 365 revenue. The article also flagged a specific margin cost tied to the cloud transition: gross margins fell 14% to $12.64 billion, reflecting that cloud subscription revenue carries thinner margins than the legacy software-license model, with Hood indicating margins would likely decline further over the next year even as she said Microsoft expected to begin "reaping the rewards" of scale from its prior infrastructure investment. Net income of $3.12 billion (39 cents a share) compared favorably against a prior-year loss of $3.2 billion, though that comparison was skewed by $8.4 billion in mobile-related charges taken a year earlier; adjusted EPS of 69 cents and revenue of $22.64 billion (adjusted) beat the Thomson Reuters consensus of 58 cents and $22.1 billion.
wsj.why_moved: The article reports Microsoft shares rose 4% in after-hours trading, and attributes that reaction to the beat on both adjusted EPS and revenue detailed above (69 cents versus 58 cents expected, $22.64 billion versus $22.1 billion expected), with the strength concentrated specifically in Azure's 102% growth, which Stifel's Reback framed as evidence that "they are effectively getting their customers to transition to the cloud." Despite the historically notable first annual revenue decline since 2009 discussed above, the article makes clear investors were not troubled by that headline figure because the underlying growth drivers — cloud and Office 365 — were performing strongly, consistent with Reback's framing that what mattered was "what's growing," not the aggregate top line. The gross-margin compression flagged in the article (down 14% to $12.64 billion) does not appear to have weighed on the reaction, suggesting investors were willing to accept lower near-term margins as the cost of the cloud transition given the growth being delivered.

Software giant’s Azure service offsets decline in Windows segment and struggling
mobile-phone business
By Jay Greene
Updated July 19, 2016 at 7:13 pm ET
The strength of Microsoft’s cloud business surprised investors. Shares rose 4% in after-hours trading. REUTERS
Microsoft Corp. remains a distant second to Amazon.com Inc. in cloud computing, but
the software giant’s latest quarterly results suggest that it is effectively managing the
transition from selling software licenses to selling on-demand computing services.
In its fiscal fourth quarter, sales of the Redmond, Wash., company’s Azure cloud
computing service more than doubled, offsetting a decline in the segment that
includes its flagship Windows operating system and its struggling mobile-phone
business.

The strength of Microsoft’s cloud business surprised investors. The company beat
expectations for both sales and profit, which spurred a 4% rise in Microsoft’s shares in
after-hours trading.
Microsoft has proved especially adept at selling its cloud services to existing
customers, taking advantage of longstanding relationships with companies that have
run its software in their own data centers.
“They are effectively getting their customers to transition to the cloud,” Stifel
Nicolaus & Co. analyst Brad Reback said.
Microsoft’s transition to the cloud comes with an important cost: eroded margins.
When the company relied on software licenses sold to companies every few years, it
registered fat profits. But margins on cloud services, which are sold by subscription,
are slimmer.
For the quarter, gross margins slid 14% to $12.64 billion.
Microsoft Chief Financial Officer Amy Hood expected margins to decline slightly in the
next year as well, she said in an interview.
Chief Executive Satya Nadella in his two years on the job has orchestrated the shift. In
the process, he has pulled Microsoft back from its mobile-phone investments
championed by his predecessor Steve Ballmer.
In May, Microsoft further dismantled the acquisition of Nokia Corp.’s handset
business, contributing to a $1.1 billion charge in the quarter. Ms. Hood said the charge
“reflects all of our judgments today” about the business.
Microsoft’s decision to roll back the phone business—along with a continuing decline
in sales of personal computers that run its Windows operating system—led the
company to post its first decline in annual revenue since 2009. Sales fell 8.8% to $85.32
billion in fiscal 2016.

The decline in annual revenue didn’t trouble investors.

The biggest gains came in the segment that includes the Azure cloud computing

The software giant’s results beat expectations, with strong gains in selling web-based
services to corporate customers
By Jay Greene
Updated July 20, 2017 at 7:20 pm ET
A Microsoft retail store in San Diego. The company released earnings Thursday that beat market expectations. MIKE
BLAKE/REUTERS
Microsoft Corp. continued its rebirth as a force in cloud-computing, posting stronger-
than-expected gains in its business of selling web-based services to corporate
customers.
The software giant has been working to expand the business selling web-based
services to corporate customers, and now has solidified its spot as the No. 2 provider
of on-demand computing processing and storage behind market pioneer Amazon.com
Inc. In its fiscal fourth quarter, Microsoft notched gains in its Azure cloud-computing
https://www.wsj.com/articles/cloud-computing-helps-power-microsoft-earnings-1500583095 Page 1 of 5

business and Office 365, the online version of its widely used productivity software.
The Redmond, Wash., company said Thursday that its Intelligent Cloud segment,
which includes Azure, rose 11% to $7.4 billion. In the Productivity and Business
Processes segment, which includes the Office franchise, revenue climbed 21% to $8.4
billion.
Microsoft doesn’t disclose revenue figures for its Azure and Office 365 businesses, but
it said Azure revenue jumped 97% and Office 365 revenue rose 43%.
“Azure was the primary source of our outperformance in the quarter,” Microsoft
finance chief Amy Hood said in an interview. “It’s higher than I was expecting.”
Overall, Microsoft posted $6.51 billion in fourth-quarter net income, or 83 cents a
share, compared with a profit of $3.12 billion, or 39 cents a share, a year ago. Excluding
the impact of revenue deferrals and other items, adjusted earnings climbed to 98
cents from 69 cents a year earlier. Per-share earnings in the most recent quarter
included a 23-cent tax benefit related to Microsoft winding down its mobile-phone
business.
Revenue rose 13% to $23.32 billion and was $24.7 billion when adjusted to reflect
Windows 10 revenue deferrals.
Analysts surveyed by S&P Global Market Intelligence expected Microsoft to report
adjusted per-share earnings of 71 cents, a figure that didn’t include the 23-cent tax
benefit, on $24.29 billion in adjusted revenue.
Shares rose 3.1% to $76.50 in after-hours trading after results beat expectations. The
software giant’s shares closed at a record on Thursday, after setting its previous high
a day earlier.
Microsoft’s growth in the so-called hyperscale public cloud market was faster in the
quarter than investors anticipated. The cloud unit is still smaller than Amazon in the

said Stifel Nicolaus & Co. analyst Brad Reback.
“They are the undisputed No. 2 in the hyperscale public cloud market, and it will be
extraordinarily difficult for anyone to catch them,” Mr. Reback said.
Two years ago, Microsoft forecast its commercial-cloud run-rate—the last month of
sales of its Azure and Office 365 products, multiplied by 12—would top $20 billion in
the 2018 fiscal year that began July 1. At the end of the fourth quarter, the run-rate
stood at $18.9 billion.
“Obviously, we’re feeling pretty confident about hitting” the target, Ms. Hood said.
The strides Microsoft has made in the cloud come as its legacy Windows operating-
system business shrinks. Revenue in its More Personal Computing segment, which
includes Windows as well as the mobile-phone and gaming businesses, slid 2% to $8.8
billion. Last week, International Data Corp. reported world-wide PC shipments fell
3.3% in the second quarter, while Gartner Inc. estimated the drop at 4.3%.
Revenue for Microsoft’s Surface line of computers also fell 2%. Three months ago, that
business was hit hard, registering a 26% revenue decline, which the company
attributed to older Surface computers in the market, as well as increased price
competition.
Since then, Microsoft has introduced a new Surface laptop for the education market
and an update to its Surface Pro tablet-laptop hybrid device, though those products
made their debut with just a few weeks left in the quarter.
LinkedIn Corp., the professional social network Microsoft acquired last December for
$27 billion, added $1.07 billion in revenue and posted a $361 million operating loss.
Microsoft is working to connect its business products to LinkedIn, giving sales
representatives using its Dynamics software, for example, tools to easily mine the
professional social network to prospect for leads.

Microsoft Reports Gains in Cloud-Computing
Business
Company recorded a $13.8 billion charge related to changes in U.S. tax law
By Jay Greene
Updated Jan. 31, 2018 at 6:42 pm ET
Cloud computing was a source of strength in Microsoft’s latest earnings report. ALTAF QADRI/ASSOCIATED PRESS
Microsoft Corp. MSFT 1.63% took a $13.8 billion charge related to the new U.S. tax
law but reported significant growth in its cloud operations, the business fueling the
company’s resurgence.
Microsoft keeps overseas the vast majority of its cash, which rose to $142.8 billion in
the quarter. In an interview, Chief Financial Officer Amy Hood declined to say when
the company might bring home some of that money.
Ms. Hood said Microsoft has been “one of the leading returners of capital to
https://www.wsj.com/articles/microsoft-reports-gains-in-cloud-computing-business-1517434433 Page 1 of 4
Microsoft Reports Gains in Cloud-Computing Business - WSJ 2026-08-28, 3:27 PM
shareholders” in recent years, using debt to finance much of that. She said the cash
would mitigate the need to turn to debt markets to pay for stock repurchases.
Microsoft already has carved a spot for itself as the No. 2 company behind
Amazon.com Inc. in renting computing power and storage over the web. For its fiscal
second quarter, the company reported strong gains in the two biggest pieces of its
cloud-computing business: its Azure infrastructure services and Office 365 online-
productivity business.
Though Microsoft doesn’t disclose revenue for those businesses, it said Azure jumped
98% and Office 365 grew 41%. In the previous quarter, Azure gained 90% and Office 365
grew 42%.
Its Intelligent Cloud segment, which includes Azure, climbed 15% to $7.8 billion. Its
Productivity and Business Processes segment, which includes Office, gained 25% to
$8.95 billion.
Overall, Microsoft posted a loss of $6.3 billion, or 82 cents a share, compared with a
profit of $6.27 billion, or 80 cents a share, a year earlier. Revenue grew 12% to $28.92
billion.
Excluding the impact of the tax law, Microsoft reported a profit of $7.5 billion, or 96
cents a share.
Analysts surveyed by S&P Global Market Intelligence expected Microsoft to report
per-share earnings of 86 cents on revenue of $28.41 billion.
Shares, which have climbed nearly 50% in the past year to set records, fell a penny to
$95 in after-hours trading.
The company’s adjusted tax rate, which doesn’t count the big charge, was 18%, up
slightly from a year ago. Looking ahead, Ms. Hood said it expects a 16% tax rate for the
second half of the fiscal year, plus or minus 2 percentage points. For fiscal 2019, the
https://www.wsj.com/articles/microsoft-reports-gains-in-cloud-computing-business-1517434433 Page 2 of 4
Microsoft Reports Gains in Cloud-Computing Business - WSJ 2026-08-28, 3:27 PM
company expects the tax rate to be slightly below the new U.S. corporate rate of 21%.
Microsoft rose to its former tech dominance on the strength of Windows, its PC
operating system. And while the More Personal Computing segment that includes
Windows is Microsoft’s largest, it is also the company’s slowest growing.
That is in part because growth in world-wide PC sales remains sluggish, inching up
only 0.7% in the last quarter, according to International Data Corp. More Personal
Computing, though, gained 2% to $12.17 billion in the latest period.
In a conference call with Wall Street analysts, Chief Executive Satya Nadella said
investments in security technology helped Microsoft quickly address the recent
threats from the Spectre and Meltdown processor vulnerabilities.
“Our investments to make Windows 10 the most secure, always up-to-date operating
system enabled us to move quickly to protect customers in the face of these threats,”
Mr. Nadella said.
The More Personal Computing segment also includes Microsoft’s Xbox videogame
business. The holiday quarter is particularly important for gaming at Microsoft, even
more so after the company released its new Xbox One X console in November. In the
period, gaming revenue—which includes sales of the Xbox console, Xbox Live
subscriptions and transactions, and game and accessory sales—rose 8%.
It has been a year since Microsoft purchased LinkedIn Corp., the professional social
network, for $27 billion. In the quarter, LinkedIn added $1.31 billion in revenue.

djnw.summary_analysis: Microsoft reported fiscal second-quarter total revenue of $28.92 billion, up 12% year over year, with Azure infrastructure services growing 98% and Office 365 up 41%. The Intelligent Cloud segment, which houses Azure, rose 15% to $7.8 billion, while the Productivity and Business Processes division, containing Office products, gained 25% to $8.95 billion, reinforcing the company's position as the second-largest cloud provider behind Amazon. However, Microsoft recorded a $13.8 billion charge tied to U.S. tax-law changes, which pushed the company to a net loss of $6.3 billion, or $0.82 per share, on a GAAP basis. Excluding that tax impact, adjusted earnings were $0.96 per share, above the $0.86 analysts had projected on expected revenue of $28.41 billion.
djnw.why_moved: The article states that Microsoft shares declined 2% to $93.30 in after-hours trading following the earnings release, despite the stock having climbed nearly 50% over the preceding year. It presents this decline alongside the $13.8 billion tax-law charge that drove the company to a GAAP net loss, even though adjusted earnings of $0.96 per share beat the $0.86 analysts had expected. The juxtaposition in the article -- strong adjusted results and continued cloud growth on one hand, a large tax-related GAAP loss on the other -- is the explanation the piece offers for the after-hours share decline, without further elaboration on which factor investors weighted more heavily.

wsj.summary_analysis: Microsoft's fiscal third-quarter 2018 report highlighted a specific historical consistency marker for Azure: the article notes Azure "has never grown slower than 90%" since Microsoft began reporting the metric in October 2015, and this quarter's 93% growth extended that streak. Combined, Azure and commercial Office 365 (up 42%) generated about $6 billion in revenue, up 58%, which CFO Amy Hood attributed to "better-than-expected demand," while also citing 20% growth in server-products and cloud-services revenue as evidence of Microsoft's hybrid-cloud strategy resonating with customers who mix on-premises and cloud infrastructure. The article provided sharp competitive market-share context: in the cloud-infrastructure market, Amazon held 31.7% share in early 2018 versus Microsoft's 16% and Google's 7.4% (Canalys research), prompting Stifel's Brad Reback to observe that "two years ago, there was a clear No. 1 with no clear No. 2," but that Microsoft had since "put significant distance between themselves and all of the other" Amazon rivals. Profit rose 35% to $7.42 billion (95 cents a share) and revenue rose 16% to $26.82 billion, beating the S&P Global consensus of 85 cents and $25.78 billion. The article's key forward-looking detail is that the stock's after-hours move was driven specifically by guidance rather than the quarter itself: Hood projected roughly 13% growth for Productivity and Business Processes, about 16% growth for Intelligent Cloud, and about 13% growth for More Personal Computing in the coming quarter — all strong figures that the article frames as the proximate driver of the reaction. It also noted Windows had been organizationally split into two engineering divisions the prior month, described as "a recognition" that Windows now plays "a supporting role" to Microsoft's cloud efforts, while Surface revenue jumped 32% to $1.10 billion and LinkedIn revenue grew 37% to $1.34 billion, with Nadella saying LinkedIn's results were "ahead of expectations across all lines."
wsj.why_moved: The article states the stock climbed 3.2% in after-hours trading to $97.41, and is explicit that this move came specifically "after the company provided strong guidance for the current fiscal fourth quarter" — distinguishing the driver from the already-solid but perhaps more expected quarterly beat itself (95 cents versus 85 cents adjusted EPS expected, as detailed above). This is a useful distinction the article draws directly: strong current-quarter results plus market-share momentum against Amazon (as Reback's comments underscore) established the baseline positive sentiment, but it was the forward guidance across all three segments — Intelligent Cloud in particular, guided to roughly 16% growth — that the article credits with pushing shares higher after hours specifically. The extension of the "never grown slower than 90%" Azure streak reinforced that the guidance was credible given the pattern of consistent execution the article had tracked over prior quarters.

Server-products and cloud-services revenue, the article's proxy for hybrid-cloud performance, rose 26%; Stifel's Brad Reback estimated the category at roughly $7.9 billion in revenue, calling the growth "massive" and saying Microsoft was "playing from their strength" by using its server-software legacy to pull existing customers toward the cloud. The report also contained a specific deceleration data point worth noting: Azure revenue grew 89%, down from 93% the prior quarter — the first time Azure's growth rate had dipped below 90% since Microsoft began disclosing the metric in October 2015, an inflection point after several quarters in this batch where the article coverage had emphasized that streak's persistence. Overall revenue rose 17% to $30.09 billion and net income was $8.87 billion ($1.14 a share), beating the S&P Global consensus of $1.08 and $29.23 billion. wsj.why_moved: The article is explicit that the stock's reaction split into two distinct phases: shares "moved little" in response to the quarterly results themselves — consistent with the deceleration in both Azure (down to 89% growth, first time below 90%) and Office 365 (down to 38% growth) detailed above, which likely tempered enthusiasm for the headline numbers despite the milestone $100 billion revenue figure — but then "jumped more than 3% during after-hours trading" specifically when Hood delivered a strong outlook for the current quarter, with those forward projections beating Wall Street's expectations. This pattern, where the guidance rather than the reported quarter itself drove the stock reaction, mirrors the dynamic the article describes in the immediately preceding quarter's coverage, reinforcing that investors had come to treat Microsoft's in-line cloud growth as expected and were instead trading on the trajectory implied by management's forward commentary. The Walmart cloud deal and the "massive" server-and-cloud-services growth Reback highlighted likely supported confidence in that guidance being achievable rather than aspirational.

wsj.summary_analysis: This Heard on the Street column by Dan Gallagher frames Amazon's first-quarter 2016 results around the growing importance of Amazon Web Services to the company's overall profitability. AWS revenue jumped 64% year over year to about $2.6 billion, and while the cloud unit still represented just 9% of Amazon's total revenue base, it accounted for a striking 56% of the company's operating profits for the period. Overall company revenue climbed 28% to $29 billion, and net income totaled $513 million versus a loss of $57 million in the same quarter a year earlier — results the article says beat Wall Street's projections and fueled an after-hours surge in the stock. The article frames AWS's current strength against its own history of volatility, noting that two years earlier a series of sharp price cuts and heavy capital spending had slashed the unit's operating margin to 8% from 23% within a single quarter, a reminder that today's profitability isn't guaranteed to persist. The column cites RBC Capital analyst Jonathan Atkin's assessment that AWS had avoided major price cuts over the past year while still carrying some of the lowest prices in the cloud segment, which the article argues may reduce the near-term risk of another margin-eroding price war. The piece also grounds the results in valuation context: Amazon's market value had doubled in the year since it began disclosing AWS results separately, and the stock traded around 100 times forward earnings, meaning Wall Street's expectation of continued rapid profit growth left the company, in the column's words, unable to 'let its cloud burst.'
wsj.why_moved: The stock's roughly 10% two-day rally reflects that both the AWS growth rate (64%) and overall company profitability (a swing to $513 million in net income from a year-earlier loss) beat Wall Street's projections, as the article states directly. Because, as the piece emphasizes, AWS supplied 56% of operating profit from just 9% of revenue, the segment's strength did outsized work in flipping the whole company profitable and validating the profit assumptions embedded in Amazon's rich valuation. The article's framing that Amazon 'can't afford to let its cloud burst' underscores why AWS's continued momentum, rather than the retail business, was the key swing factor investors were watching, and its acceleration removed a source of uncertainty around the multiple the market was already paying. The historical margin-collapse example the article cites — AWS's operating margin falling from 23% to 8% two years prior — suggests the market may have been pricing in some risk of a repeat, and this quarter's results, with prices held steady per RBC's Atkin, appear to have alleviated that concern for the moment.

By Dan Gallagher

Amazon Web Services recorded a 64% jump in first-quarter revenue. KRISTOFFER TRIPPLAAR/SIPA USA
Amazon.com’s AMZN 3.72% cloud continues to swell. That is helpful to investors who
have based a rather large bet on that continuing for the long haul.
First-quarter revenue for the company’s Amazon Web Services segment jumped 64%
year over year to about $2.6 billion. The cloud still represents just 9% of Amazon’s
total revenue base, but it accounted for 56% of the company’s operating profits for the
period.
Amazon’s overall revenue climbed 28% to $29 billion in the quarter, and net income

Second-quarter earnings reached $857 million, or $1.78 a share, well above the $1.11 a share analysts had expected, on sales of $30.4 billion versus $23.19 billion a year earlier. Revenue rose 31%, including a 58% jump at AWS to $2.89 billion from $1.82 billion, keeping the cloud unit on track to exceed CEO Jeff Bezos's goal of $10 billion in AWS sales for the year. Operating margin more than doubled to 4.2% from 2% a year earlier. Robert W. Baird analyst Colin Sebastian is quoted calling the 'accelerating revenue growth...a pleasant surprise,' while cautioning that 'people may be expecting quarters like this now' — that is, that consistent beats were starting to reset the bar. CFO Brian Olsavsky stressed the company's investment philosophy hadn't changed, noting Amazon planned to add 18 new warehouses in the third quarter versus six a year earlier, even as shipping costs jumped 44% to $3.36 billion. The article also details Amazon's broader strategic moves: it had recently overtaken Walmart by market value, was opening physical bookstores, extending Prime to India with a $5 billion investment pledge, and rolling out monthly (rather than only annual) Prime and video subscriptions. For the coming quarter, Amazon guided to $31 billion-$33.5 billion in sales, above analysts' $31.63 billion consensus.
wsj.why_moved: The roughly 2-3% share gain reflects a straightforward beat-and-raise: EPS of $1.78 crushed the $1.11 analysts expected, as noted above, while the third-quarter revenue guidance of up to $33.5 billion also topped the $31.63 billion Wall Street was modeling. Sebastian's quoted caution that expectations may now reset higher hints at why the reaction, while positive, was more measured rather than explosive — investors were already primed for strong results after two prior blowout quarters. The 58% AWS growth cited above continued to do heavy lifting on the profit side, reinforcing the margin-expansion story that had already been rewarded in the prior quarter's stock reaction. Olsavsky's comments defending continued heavy warehouse investment, including 18 new facilities and rising shipping costs, suggest the market was, for now, comfortable trading near-term margin pressure for the sales and profit beat actually delivered.

A UPS driver delivers packages from Amazon.com in Palo Alto, Calif. ASSOCIATED PRESS
Amazon.com Inc. AMZN 3.77% on Thursday reported in its third consecutive record
profit, nearly doubling its prior high-water mark, and its fifth straight quarter in the
black.
Amazon’s revenue jumped 31% including a 58% gain at its Amazon Web Services cloud
computing unit. The company also more than doubled its operating margin, which
historically has been razor thin, and issued a cheery outlook for the coming quarter.
Shares of the company rose another 2% in after-hours trading after finishing up $15.94

wsj.summary_analysis: A preview piece published the afternoon before the report set the stage: with Amazon's stock trading above $800 after surging roughly 70% since February, about 90% of covering analysts rated it a "buy" -- the most bullish Wall Street had been on the stock since the dot-com boom, with at least four analysts carrying price targets of $1,000 or higher. The preview's framing was that a simple beat-or-miss on the quarter wouldn't be enough; investors needed evidence the core retail business could eventually be highly profitable in its own right, not just AWS, given that cloud computing (already facing rising competition from Google, IBM and Microsoft) was the source of more than half of Amazon's pretax operating income. The reaction piece, published the day of the report, shows the results falling short of that bar: Amazon posted its lowest quarterly profit in a year, with heavy investment in new warehouses and faster delivery sharply increasing costs. The company opened 23 new warehouses since July (versus just three in the first half of the year), and CFO Brian Olsavsky called the expansion "a big undertaking" for the holiday season. Reported earnings were $252 million, or 52 cents a share -- well below the 78 cents analysts surveyed by Thomson Reuters had expected -- even as sales rose to $32.7 billion. Operating expenses climbed 29% to $32.1 billion, nearly eclipsing revenue and pushing operating margin down to 1.8% from 4.2% the prior quarter. Shipping costs rose 43% to $3.9 billion as Prime's faster delivery options expanded; Olsavsky acknowledged "that's expensive," but added "customers love it." The international segment posted a steeper loss of $541 million (versus $208 million a year earlier), which Olsavsky attributed to expansion spending including in India. AWS remained a bright spot, growing sales 55% to $3.23 billion, still tracking toward Bezos's $10 billion target. Robert W. Baird's Colin Sebastian warned that "Amazon is still in investment mode, and the Street should not necessarily expect linear growth in profitability." For the holiday quarter, Amazon guided to $42-45.5 billion in revenue, below the $44.6 billion analysts had expected.
wsj.why_moved: Shares fell more than 6% in after-hours trading, as the reaction article states, on the combination of the profit miss (52 cents versus 78 cents expected) and a fourth-quarter revenue outlook below the $44.6 billion Wall Street had modeled. As detailed above, the preview piece had explicitly set a high bar -- near-unanimous bullish analyst sentiment, a stock already up 70% for the year, and a specific ask that Amazon show its retail business (not just AWS) could become durably profitable -- which this quarter's results directly disappointed, with operating margin falling to 1.8% from 4.2% on a 29% surge in operating expenses concentrated in new-warehouse and shipping costs. Sebastian's quoted warning that investors "should not necessarily expect linear growth in profitability" captures the market repricing away from the profitability narrative the preview piece said investors were specifically looking to confirm. The steeper-than-expected international loss, tied by Olsavsky to India expansion spending, adds another concrete cost pressure layered on top of the warehouse and shipping buildout the preview had flagged as the key swing factor to watch.
