Amazon Takes Hit as Costs Surge
Results disappoint as retail giant invests heavily on warehouses, trimming delivery times
By Laura Stevens
Updated Oct. 27, 2016 at 7:28 pm ET
Amazon is targeting new growth markets like fashion and beauty, where analysts expect quick gains due to its
relatively small market share. ROSS D. FRANKLIN/ASSOCIATED PRESS
Amazon.com Inc. posted its lowest quarterly profit in a year as it invested heavily to
meet consumer demand for more orders delivered faster.
The online retail giant said Thursday that opening new warehouses and shipping
items with shorter delivery times caused its costs to soar in the third quarter. The
company predicts heavy investments will continue through the rest of the year.
Amazon opened 23 warehouses world-wide to fill orders since July, after opening just
three in the first half of the year.

The company’s shares fell more than 6% in after-hours trading on concerns about the
higher spending, as well as a holiday outlook that fell short of expectations.
The results show “Amazon is still in investment mode, and the Street should not
necessarily expect linear growth in profitability,” said Robert W. Baird & Co. analyst
Colin Sebastian.
The company has been pushing its $99-a-year Prime membership program to broaden
its base of loyal shoppers who often spend double their non-Prime counterparts on
the site, analysts estimate. Prime promises free, fast shipping on millions of items on

shipping costs 43% in the third quarter to $3.9 billion.
“We acknowledge that’s expensive,” Mr. Olsavsky said. But “customers love it.”
The retail giant has started laying the groundwork for its own shipping business to

people familiar with the matter.
It is leasing 40 planes to carry goods and buying branded truck trailers, but the
investments it is making to build its own logistics operations generally break even or

Amazon accelerated its investments in its own transportation capabilities after the

wsj.summary_analysis: Laura Stevens reports Amazon's first-quarter 2017 profit rose 41% to $724 million, or $1.48 a share, comfortably beating the $1.12 a share analysts surveyed by Thomson Reuters had expected. Sales of $35.71 billion landed within Amazon's own guidance range of $33.25 billion-$35.75 billion and above the $35.3 billion analyst consensus. The stock rose 4.1% in after-hours trading following a session in which shares had already finished up 1%, extending a roughly 22% year-to-date gain. The article documents a new phase of 'heightened investment' that analysts expected to run at least through mid-2018, tied to Amazon's pledge to hire 130,000 U.S. workers in that window, international expansion into markets like Mexico and India (where Flipkart, backed partly by eBay, had just raised $1.4 billion), and a newly announced push into Australia. The international segment's operating loss widened slightly to $481 million on sales of $11.06 billion, up from $9.57 billion. The piece also details Amazon's buildout of its own logistics network — a first air cargo hub in Kentucky, 40 leased planes, more than 4,000 dedicated truck trailer hitches, and one-hour delivery now available in over 40 cities — which contributed to a 34% rise in shipping costs to $4.38 billion. AWS revenue grew 43% to $3.66 billion, though the article notes the unit 'is facing tougher competition from both Microsoft Corp. and Alphabet Inc.'s Google...amid price wars.' For the second quarter, Amazon guided to $35.25 billion-$37.75 billion in revenue, above the $36.87 billion analysts expected at the low end, with operating income guidance of $425 million-$1.08 billion.
wsj.why_moved: The roughly 2-4% gain across the reaction window reflects the straightforward beat on both lines described above — EPS of $1.48 versus $1.12 expected, and sales above the $35.3 billion consensus — plus second-quarter revenue guidance that cleared the $36.87 billion analysts were modeling. That the stock rose despite the article's extensive documentation of 'heightened investment,' including international losses, the 34% jump in shipping costs, the new Kentucky air hub, and the multiyear hiring pledge, suggests investors were, at this point, willing to look past elevated spending as long as both current results and the growth trajectory continued to beat expectations. The article's closing note about AWS facing 'tougher competition' and cloud 'price wars' reads as a forward risk the piece flags rather than something that weighed on this particular reaction, since AWS's 43% growth this quarter still came in strong.

wsj.summary_analysis: Laura Stevens's article centers on Amazon's second-quarter 2017 profit falling 77% to $197 million — its smallest quarterly profit in nearly two years — even as sales jumped 25% to $38 billion. CFO Brian Olsavsky frames the spending as strategic, quoted saying the company invests in businesses where 'customers love them, they can grow to be large, they have strong financial returns and they are durable and can last for decades.' The piece explicitly states Amazon 'missed profit and guidance expectations,' and notes the stock's 2.3% after-hours decline was 'a tempered reaction given that other retail stocks often drop in the double digits when Amazon makes a move to compete in the same market' — framing this as relatively muted by Amazon's own standards. The article situates the results against Amazon's broader disruption of traditional retail: Gullane Capital's Trip Miller is quoted saying 'I would hate to be the competition in anything they get involved in,' and the piece cites Amazon's roughly 40-cents-of-every-online-dollar share (Slice Intelligence) versus Walmart's 1.7%, and 55% of product searches starting on Amazon versus 28% on search engines (BloomReach). It highlights the freshly announced $13.7 billion Whole Foods acquisition, noting Whole Foods' own comparable sales had fallen again, and reports Amazon becoming an official seller for Nike and Sears' Kenmore brand. On a symbolic note, the article records that Amazon's morning stock spike briefly made Jeff Bezos the world's richest person, with a net worth of $90.6 billion, before shares retreated by the close. AWS operating income of $916 million topped the entire company's $628 million operating income, even as the unit logged its fifth consecutive quarter of decelerating operating income growth (28%). Amazon guided to a potential operating loss in the third quarter, citing heavier holiday-season warehouse and hiring costs tied to its 130,000-worker pledge.
wsj.why_moved: The roughly 2-3% pullback reflects the profit and guidance miss the article states directly, compounding the 77% profit decline described above with a warning that operating income 'could swing to a loss in the next quarter.' Yet the piece is explicit that the market's reaction was unusually restrained for Amazon — down only 2.3% after-hours — compared with the 'double digits' hit that rival retailers typically take when Amazon expands into their markets, suggesting investors were already conditioned to accept lower near-term profitability from Amazon in exchange for the dominant market-share gains and disruption narrative documented throughout the article, including the 40-cents-per-dollar online share and the 55% search-origination figure. The fifth consecutive quarter of decelerating AWS operating income growth cited above is a detail the article surfaces but does not explicitly connect to the share reaction, leaving it as a data point rather than an established driver.

wsj.summary_analysis: Three WSJ pieces published the same day, April 26, 2018, cover Amazon's first-quarter 2018 results from different angles. The main earnings article by Laura Stevens reports Amazon 'delivered a double punch': its best revenue growth in more than six years (43%, to about $51 billion, the strongest mark since Q3 2011) while topping $1 billion in profit for a second straight quarter, with net profit more than doubling to $1.6 billion — just under the prior quarter's $1.9 billion record. The piece explicitly states this beat expectations: investors 'were already expecting Amazon to post strong numbers,' but 'this quarter, Amazon was expected to post a more modest profit as it refocused on longer-term investments after a blowout holiday period' — meaning the magnitude of the profit beat was itself the surprise. CFO Brian Olsavsky guided operating income could 'potentially more than double to as high as $1.9 billion' in Q2, while cautioning 'we certainly will always have periods of higher investment.' The Dan Gallagher Heard on the Street column adds granular detail: operating income surged 93% to $1.9 billion, more than double the 43% sales growth rate, with AWS revenue up 49% to $5.4 billion and AWS operating profit up 57% to $1.4 billion — AWS now represented about 11% of revenue but generated 22% more profit than the North American retail arm despite that unit's nearly six-times-larger revenue base. The third article details Amazon's announced 20% Prime price increase to $119, its second increase in Prime's 13-year history, with Olsavsky explaining on the earnings call that 'the value of Prime to customers has never been greater' while costs — shipping and streaming content — have also risen; he contrasted today's more than 100 million Prime-eligible items against the roughly 20 million eligible for two-day shipping when the price last rose to $99 in 2014. The earnings piece also directly compares Amazon's $1.6 billion profit against much larger profits from peers reporting the same week: Facebook's nearly $5 billion (up 50% revenue, sending its stock up 9.1%), Microsoft's $7.42 billion (up 35%), and Alphabet's $9.4 billion (up 73%) — underscoring that Amazon's profit, while a record for the company, remained modest by mega-cap tech standards.
wsj.why_moved: The roughly 7% after-hours pop (shares rose 7.2% to $1,627 per the main article) and the ~6.7% two-day return reflect the scale of the profit beat detailed above — operating income up 93% against 43% sales growth, as the Heard column emphasizes, delivering the 'double punch' of both record revenue growth and doubled profit that Stevens's piece frames as exceeding the 'more modest' profit investors had been bracing for post-holiday. The AWS figures cited above (49% revenue growth, 57% profit growth, generating outsized returns relative to its revenue share) reinforced the same margin-expansion story that has driven prior AMZN rallies, giving investors confidence the profit surge wasn't a one-off. Notably, the market's reaction came despite the same-day Prime price increase to $119 — a move that could have been read as a signal of rising internal cost pressure, since Olsavsky cited shipping and content costs — suggesting investors treated the fee hike as a positive incremental-revenue lever rather than a red flag, especially with over 100 million Prime members already in the base. The explicit comparison to Facebook, Microsoft, and Alphabet's larger absolute profits in the same article suggests the market's enthusiasm was less about closing that gap than about the trajectory, with Olsavsky's own guidance pointing to further growth in Q2 operating income.

wsj.summary_analysis: Laura Stevens reports Amazon's second-quarter 2018 profit topped $2 billion for the first time ($2.53 billion, up from $197 million a year earlier), marking three straight quarters above $1 billion and extending a three-year profitability streak. The article attributes the jump to 'newer services businesses' — cloud computing, advertising, and third-party seller services — helping offset the traditionally lower-margin core retail business. CFO Brian Olsavsky credited 'a greater-than-expected efficiency in a lot of our spend, in warehouses, in data centers and also in things like marketing,' alongside reduced headcount growth. Operating margin reached 5.6%, the highest in more than a decade. However, the piece is explicit that 'quarterly revenue of $52.89 billion did underwhelm Wall Street, coming in a bit below estimates even if up 39%,' and that guided third-quarter revenue of $54 billion-$57.5 billion was 'also below analysts' consensus estimates' — a genuine top-line miss alongside the profit beat. The article notes online-store revenue growth was slowing, up 12% to $27.17 billion, 'a smaller lift than in the past several quarters,' with third-party sellers now accounting for about 53% of units sold at roughly a 15% take rate for Amazon — a structural shift toward higher-margin marketplace revenue. AWS revenue grew 49% to $6.1 billion, its third straight quarter of accelerating growth despite competition from Microsoft and Google, driven by machine-learning and analytics demand per Olsavsky. The 'other' (mostly advertising) category more than doubled to $2.19 billion, with Olsavsky calling it 'now a multibillion-dollar business for us.' The piece contrasts Amazon's quarter favorably against Facebook's report a day earlier, when Facebook signaled slowing growth and its stock plunged 19% — a reminder, the article says, 'that growth from tech's titans isn't always guaranteed.'
wsj.why_moved: Despite the after-hours pop described in the article, with shares rising 3.2% to $1,866 immediately following the report, the stock's actual multi-day reaction was negative, down roughly 1.6% over two days, which aligns with the revenue miss the article flags directly — both current-quarter sales and forward guidance came in 'below' Wall Street's estimates, as noted above, even as profit dramatically beat. This is consistent with a pattern seen elsewhere in Amazon's WSJ coverage where the market weighs top-line growth, a proxy for the durability of Amazon's expansion story, more heavily than a single quarter's profit outperformance. The slowing 12% growth in the core online-store segment, explicitly flagged in the article as smaller than 'in the past several quarters,' may have compounded concern about deceleration in Amazon's largest reporting segment even as AWS and advertising continued to accelerate. The article's own juxtaposition with Facebook's growth-scare selloff the day before suggests investors entered Amazon's report already sensitized to growth-deceleration risk across large tech platforms, which likely sharpened the reaction to Amazon's revenue shortfall even though the headline profit number was a record.

wsj.summary_analysis: A preview published the morning of the report confirmed the exact consensus figures the reaction piece would later cite: analysts expected revenue of about $3.6 billion and earnings of $2.38 a share for the quarter ended May 1, versus $1.6 billion in revenue and $1.21 a share a year earlier for standalone Avago. The preview flagged two things to watch: progress toward the merged company's stated goal of $750 million in annual cost savings, and debt paydown following the $9 billion borrowed to fund the deal, set against an unprecedented slowdown in Apple's iPhone -- a major outlet for Broadcom's signal-filtering chips, representing about 15% of the combined company's revenue per RBC Capital's Amit Daryanani. The preview's counterargument was that the merger itself was a hedge against that smartphone risk: analysts expected the wireless segment to fall to about 25% of combined revenue this fiscal year, down from 37% for standalone Avago the year before, with the added communications and data-center business carrying a better growth outlook, and the stock trading at a relative-bargain 13 times forward earnings, down from 16 times a year earlier. Tess Stynes's reaction piece, covering Broadcom Ltd.'s first quarterly report as the combined company, shows results landing ahead of that framework: adjusted per-share earnings from continuing operations rose to $2.53 from $2.13 a year earlier, beating the $2.38 consensus the preview had cited, even as the company posted a GAAP loss of $3.02 a share on acquisition- and restructuring-related charges. Revenue more than doubled to $3.54 billion, with continuing-operations revenue of $3.56 billion landing "on the higher end of Broadcom's projections." Gross margin from continuing operations slipped to 60% from 61%. CEO Hock Tan attributed resilience to the deal's added scale and diversity, with strong wired-infrastructure product cycles offsetting weaker enterprise-storage and wireless demand -- directly validating the preview's diversification thesis. The company raised its quarterly dividend a penny to 50 cents and guided next-quarter revenue to $3.75 billion, plus or minus $75 million, above the $3.71 billion analysts polled by Thomson Reuters expected.
wsj.why_moved: The roughly 5% share gain reflects the adjusted-earnings beat detailed above ($2.53 versus the $2.38 consensus the preview had already flagged), combined with revenue landing at the high end of guidance and a next-quarter outlook of $3.75 billion that itself topped the $3.71 billion consensus -- the reaction article states directly that shares rose "as the company offered a rosy outlook for the current quarter." As detailed above, the preview piece had specifically framed this report as a test of whether the Avago-Broadcom merger's diversification thesis could offset the iPhone slowdown it was designed to hedge against; Tan's commentary on wired infrastructure offsetting wireless and storage softness reads as a direct confirmation of that pre-earnings thesis, not just a generic beat. The dividend increase, though modest at a penny per share, reinforced a message of financial confidence alongside the earnings beat, and the stock's cheap starting valuation (13 times forward earnings per the preview) may have left more room for a positive re-rating than a richly valued stock would have had on the same results -- a plausible inference from the preview's own framing, though neither article states that valuation cushion explicitly as a driver of the reaction.

Broadcom: It’s Better to Branch Out
Diversifying from smartphones helps as the chip maker digests a huge merger
By Dan Gallagher
June 1, 2016 at 2:53 pm ET
Broadcom is scheduled to report quarterly results Thursday. MIKE BLAKE/REUTERS
The company now known as Broadcom owes much of its fortune to its ability to
separate signal from noise. That will come in handy in the months ahead.
The company, formerly known as Avago, is in the early days of integrating the largest
merger ever in the chip industry. The $37 billion combination between Avago and
Broadcom, announced a year ago, was completed in February. Fiscal second-quarter
results due Thursday will be the first to reflect the combined business.
Analysts expect revenue of about $3.6 billion with earnings of $2.38 a share for the
quarter ended May 1. Avago, which assumed Broadcom’s corporate identity with the
https://www.wsj.com/articles/broadcom-its-better-to-branch-out-1464807225 Page 1 of 3
Broadcom: It’s Better to Branch Out - WSJ 2026-08-28, 4:14 PM
deal, posted revenue of $1.6 billion with per-share earnings of $1.21 from continuing
operations in the same period last year as a stand-alone business.
Of key interest will be Broadcom’s progress on its stated goal of achieving $750
million in annual cost savings. It also has promised to rapidly pay down debt, of which
$9 billion was incurred to get the deal done.
That is challenging at the best of times. But it also comes during an unprecedented
slowdown for Apple’s iPhone, a major outlet for Broadcom’s chips that filter signal
interference common in phones that operate on several different spectrum bands.
Apple represents about 15% of the combined company’s revenue, Amit Daryanani of
RBC Capital estimates.
Avago brings a strong operating history that suggests it is up to the tasks ahead. It
helps that the combination makes the company much less reliant on the cyclical
smartphone business.
Analysts expect the wireless segment to account for about 25% of the combined
company’s revenue this fiscal year compared with 37% for stand-alone Avago last year.
The addition of Broadcom’s business also beefs up the segment the sells chips used in
communications and data-center equipment, which has a better growth outlook.
It also helps that Broadcom shares are a relative bargain at 13 times forward earnings,
down from 16 times a year ago. Its discount to peers gives the stock breathing room as
the company hustles to work through the merger and stay ahead of rivals.
That signal should resonate.

wsj.summary_analysis: Tess Stynes's article reports Broadcom's second quarter as a merged company: adjusted per-share earnings of $2.89 beat both the year-earlier $2.24 figure and the $2.77 analysts polled by Thomson Reuters expected, while revenue more than doubled to $3.79 billion, with net revenue from continuing operations of $3.8 billion landing 'in line with Broadcom's projections.' The company nonetheless reported a GAAP loss of $298 million, or 75 cents a share, versus a year-earlier profit of $240 million, or 91 cents a share — again a standalone-Avago comparison, since the combined entity didn't exist a year prior. The piece notes shares had hit an all-time high just two days before the report. Guidance for the current quarter called for net revenue of $4.09 billion, plus or minus $75 million, above the $4.06 billion analysts expected. The article repeats the strategic framing from the prior quarter: the $37 billion Avago-Broadcom merger reduced reliance on smartphone chips, a segment IDC cut its 2016 shipment forecast for again that same day, citing expected sales declines in developed markets including the U.S. and Western Europe. Broadcom also raised its quarterly dividend a penny to 51 cents a share.
wsj.why_moved: This is a case where the article's reported figures — an adjusted EPS beat of $2.89 versus $2.77 expected, and forward guidance above consensus at $4.09 billion versus $4.06 billion expected — do not obviously explain the stock's decline. The article itself states shares fell 2.1% to $173.40 in after-hours trading 'though the chip maker's revenue outlook for the current quarter topped Wall Street estimates,' explicitly flagging the disconnect between the beat-and-raise result and the negative price reaction without offering a specific explanation for it. Possible contributing factors the article does mention — the stock having just hit an all-time high two days earlier, raising the bar for what would be read as good news, and IDC's same-day cut to its 2016 global smartphone shipment outlook — are plausible context, but the piece does not draw an explicit causal line from either to the share-price drop. The GAAP net loss, while expected given ongoing acquisition and restructuring charges, is also not identified in the article as a driver of the decline. In short, the article documents a fundamentally positive quarter accompanied by a negative stock reaction, and does not itself supply the bridge between the two.

wsj.summary_analysis: Imani Moise and Ted Greenwald's article covers Broadcom's fiscal fourth-quarter 2017 results against the backdrop of its hostile $105 billion takeover bid for Qualcomm, which had turned confrontational just days earlier when Broadcom nominated a slate of candidates to overhaul Qualcomm's board after Qualcomm rejected the unsolicited offer. On the earnings call, Broadcom offered little detail on the bid beyond saying it aimed to 'engage in a constructive dialogue,' had received positive shareholder and customer reactions, and believed it could close a deal, including regulatory approvals, within 12 months, while declining to answer questions about the bid or its planned relocation from Singapore to the U.S. On the operating results, profit swung to $636 million, or $1.50 a share, from a year-earlier loss of $632 million, or $1.59 a share; adjusted earnings rose to $4.59 a share from $3.47, beating the $4.52 analysts had projected. Revenue rose 8.5% to $4.84 billion, roughly in line with the $4.83 billion analysts expected. The article attributes the earnings strength specifically to smartphone-parts sales to 'a large North American smartphone customer,' implicitly Apple, which offset weakness in the core wired-infrastructure business; CEO Hock Tan said he expected wireless growth to continue into the current quarter because that customer's new products 'had been ‘pushed out’ compared with prior years,' referencing the October iPhone X preorders following September's iPhone 8 launch. Wireless communications, over a third of revenue, grew 33%, while wired infrastructure, 45% of sales, rose just 3%. Guidance for the current quarter, which for the first time included contributions from the newly acquired Brocade Communications Systems, called for revenue of $5.22 billion-$5.37 billion, well above the $4.83 billion analysts had forecast. The board also raised the quarterly dividend to $1.75 a share from $1.02.
wsj.why_moved: The article reports shares rose 4.2% to $274.92 in after-hours trading, adding to a 0.9% gain during the regular session, driven by the adjusted-EPS beat and the guidance jump described above — a forecast of $5.22 billion-$5.37 billion in revenue that towered over the $4.83 billion analysts had penciled in, aided by the newly consolidated Brocade contribution and continued wireless strength tied to the delayed iPhone X cycle. However, the recorded returns show that initial pop largely faded: the one-day return was a modest +0.99%, and the five-day return actually turned negative at -2.02%, meaning the after-hours enthusiasm the article captured did not persist through the following days. The article does not explain this fade, since it reports only the immediate post-earnings reaction; it does note the company's studied silence on the increasingly contentious Qualcomm bid, which was actively evolving with board nominations and a rejected offer in the same news cycle, and it is plausible that renewed uncertainty around that unresolved, high-stakes takeover fight — rather than anything in the earnings themselves — weighed on the stock in the days that followed, though this is not something the article itself states.

wsj.summary_analysis: A "Heard on the Street" preview published the afternoon before the report -- itself dominated by the fresh news that Broadcom had been ordered by President Trump the prior Monday to abandon its unsolicited takeover bid for Qualcomm on national-security grounds, which the company agreed to on Wednesday morning -- framed the earnings release mainly as a test of Broadcom's standalone financial strength now that the roughly $105 billion Qualcomm deal was off the table. Notably, the preview reveals that Broadcom had already pre-disclosed preliminary results in January: revenue in the range of $5.3-5.35 billion (29% year-over-year growth at the midpoint) and free cash flow expected to surge 81% to nearly $1.9 billion. The preview also noted the stock traded at only 13 times forward earnings, a then-record 21% discount to the PHLX Semiconductor Index, and that CEO Hock Tan -- with the Qualcomm deal dead -- was left considering smaller alternative targets such as Mellanox, Marvell or Xilinx, none of which would add more than 13% to Broadcom's revenue. The reaction piece, published the day of the report, shows results landing within that already-disclosed range: net revenue rose 28% to $5.33 billion, within the $5.3-5.35 billion range and above the $5.32 billion analyst consensus. Quarterly profit surged to $6.23 billion ($14.62 a share) from $239 million a year earlier, driven substantially by a one-time $6 billion tax benefit from the U.S. tax overhaul; excluding that and other items, adjusted profit of $5.12 a share modestly beat both Broadcom's own guidance of $5.10 and the $5.04 consensus. Wireless communications, boosted by an extra week in the quarter and the Brocade acquisition, surged 88% to overtake wired infrastructure as the largest segment for the first time. Tan said the company expects to "sustain top-line momentum" via data-center and storage demand offsetting a seasonal wireless decline. The article also flags cash falling to $7.08 billion from $11.2 billion the prior quarter, while long-term debt of $17.48 billion ticked up slightly.
wsj.why_moved: The reaction article states shares closed up on the reporting day at $267.76, up 19% over the trailing 12 months, consistent with the recorded one-day return of +2.97%, reflecting the modest beats on adjusted EPS and revenue described above alongside Tan's upbeat commentary on data-center and storage momentum. However, that initial gain did not hold: the two-day return turned negative at -2.24% and the five-day return fell further to -5.71%, a reversal that neither article explains directly. As detailed above, the preview piece adds a relevant fact worth weighing: Broadcom had already pre-announced this quarter's approximate revenue and free-cash-flow figures back in January, meaning the actual results carried comparatively little new information relative to a typical earnings report -- a plausible contributing factor to why an initial modest pop failed to hold over the following sessions, though this is an inference from combining the two articles' facts, not something either piece states as an explanation for the multi-day decline. The preview's framing of the report as fundamentally about the Qualcomm bid's collapse and Broadcom's next strategic move, rather than about the quarter's numbers themselves, similarly suggests investors may have been more focused on reassessing capital-allocation plans than on the incremental, largely pre-telegraphed earnings beat -- again a plausible bridge between the two articles' content rather than a stated causal claim in either one.

Broadcom Lives Well to Fight Another Day
Chipmaker’s strong earnings and cash flow—and cheap stock—give it time to plot its next
move
By Dan Gallagher
Updated March 14, 2018 at 2:20 pm ET
Hock Tan isn’t easily dissuaded. It is a quality that has served the Broadcom CEO very
well over the last few years as he has cobbled together one of the largest and most
successful chip companies in the world.
But there is a time to stand down or, in the case of Mr. Tan, to live to fight another day.
His dogged pursuit of Qualcomm—a notably larger company in both employees and
revenue—was a bold gambit that would have made Broadcom the world’s third largest
chip maker, trailing only Samsung and Intel Corp. But Broadcom was ordered Monday
by President Trump to desist in the name of national security, which the company
begrudgingly agreed to do on Wednesday morning.
That leaves Broadcom with the problem of what to do with itself now. Mr. Tan has
spent the last several years building up a chip empire that now owns strong positions
in several key markets such as smartphones, data centers and networking gear. Mr.
Tan’s deft management of these entities has allowed the company to grow revenue,
earnings and cash flow consistently. But M&A always has been a key part of that plan.
The company, once known as Avago, has swallowed up several large chip businesses in
the last five years, including LSI Corp. in 2014 and its $37 billion takeover of Broadcom
that wrapped up two years ago and gave the company its new identity.
https://www.wsj.com/articles/broadcom-lives-well-to-fight-another-day-1521043362 Page 1 of 3
Broadcom Lives Well to Fight Another Day - WSJ 2026-08-28, 4:26 PM
Qualcomm would have been the most ambitious move to date. The loss of that deal
frees up Mr. Tan to consider others, with the obvious drawback being that almost
anything else at this point will seem small by comparison. Analysts have pointed to
companies such as Mellanox, Marvell and Xilinx as potential targets, but even the
largest of those only would add 13% to Broadcom’s current revenue. Qualcomm’s
chipset business alone would have nearly doubled the company’s top line.
But Broadcom’s next move may not be apparent for a while. The company is currently
in the process of re-domiciling to the U.S., a process it expects to complete by May 6.
That should help with the heightened government scrutiny that now accompanies
tech deal making in the U.S.
In the meantime, Broadcom’s strong financial performance should give it a strong line
of credit with investors as it plots its next move. Broadcom’s fiscal first quarter results
due Thursday afternoon will show revenue in the range of $5.3 to $5.35 billion,
according to a preliminary results reported by the company in January. That
represents growth of 29% year over year at the midpoint. Free cash flow for the
quarter is expected to have surged 81% to nearly $1.9 billion. With Broadcom’s stock
price now fetching only 13 times forward earnings—a record discount of 21% to the
PHLX Semiconductor Index—investors shouldn’t need audacious deals to make this
bet pay off.

wsj.summary_analysis: This Dan Gallagher Heard on the Street column is an opinion/analysis piece rather than a straight news report, and frames Broadcom's fiscal second-quarter 2018 results against the aftermath of President Trump formally blocking its roughly $117 billion bid to acquire Qualcomm in March. The column opens with the line 'Sometimes saving $117 billion can be costly,' noting Broadcom's stock was up only 3% for the year at the time of writing, making it 'among the worst performers' in the PHLX Semiconductor Index, which had risen 14%, though the column notes 'that Qualcomm's shares have done even worse is some consolation.' On the actual results, revenue rose 20% year-over-year to $5 billion, which the column says was 'in line with the chipmaker's pre-announcement a month ago,' meaning the company had already signaled the top-line figure in advance, while operating income more than doubled to $1.2 billion. Notably, the column states this was achieved 'despite a sharp reduction in shipments to the ‘large North America customer’,' understood to be Apple, which analyst Stacy Rasgon of Bernstein estimated at about 20% of Broadcom's business, meaning operating income growth outpaced revenue growth even with a headwind from a major customer. Free cash flow surged 58% year-over-year to a record $2.1 billion, and the column notes the failed Qualcomm deal 'freed up more cash to distribute': Broadcom announced a $12 billion buyback in mid-April and had already executed $1.5 billion of it, alongside a dividend yield of 2.6%, among the highest of chip-sector peers. The column concludes that Broadcom shares, at under 14 times forward earnings, were 'the cheapest among large-capitalization chipmakers' for 'a company whose solo act is going strong.'
wsj.why_moved: Because the second-quarter revenue figure was 'in line with the chipmaker's pre-announcement a month ago,' as the column states, this was not really a surprise data point capable of moving the stock on its own — the market had already had a month to price in the top-line number, which helps explain why a fundamentally solid quarter, with operating income more than doubling despite the Apple shipment headwind, record free cash flow, and an active buyback, did not translate into a share-price gain; the two-day return was actually negative. The column's own framing, that the stock has 'languished' and remains one of the worst performers in its semiconductor peer group even as 'performance remains solid,' is itself an acknowledgment that the fundamentals described are not fully explaining the price action, which the piece attributes more to lingering investor uncertainty about Broadcom's acquisition strategy after the Qualcomm deal's collapse than to anything specific in this quarter's numbers, quoting that 'investors still seem to be wondering what to do with the hyper-acquisitive Broadcom in an environment in which huge global deals have become much harder to pull off.' As an opinion column rather than a news report, the piece is explicitly making the bullish case that the stock's cheap valuation is unwarranted given the results, but it does not claim, and the return data does not support, that this particular earnings report itself lifted the shares; if anything the disconnect between 'solid' results and a 'languished' stock is the column's central thesis.

wsj.summary_analysis: Maria Armental's article covers Broadcom's fiscal third-quarter 2018 results, marking a sixth consecutive quarter of more-than-doubled profit, alongside plans to substantially raise shareholder payouts. The dominant storyline is the company's first earnings call since announcing its proposed $19 billion acquisition of software company CA Inc., a deal that 'had hit Broadcom's stock hard,' with CEO Hock Tan defending the move, calling CA a 'big doorway' and a 'new and huge opportunity,' saying 'we're buying CA because of their customers and [CA's] importance to these customers... CA sells mission-critical software to virtually all of the world's largest enterprises.' The article frames this as roughly tripling Broadcom's addressable opportunity in the estimated $200 billion infrastructure-technology market, per comments finance chief Tom Krause had previously given the Journal, and notes the deal came only months after Broadcom's $117 billion-plus hostile Qualcomm bid was blocked by President Trump. On operating performance, profit surged to $1.2 billion, or $2.71 a share, from $481 million, or $1.14 a share, a year earlier; profit from continuing operations rose to $4.98 a share, or $4.83 adjusted, from $4.10, beating the $2.70 GAAP / $4.83 adjusted consensus analysts expected on $5.07 billion in revenue, up 13%, which itself matched estimates. Gross margin improved to 51.7% from 48.2%. The article details segment dynamics: enterprise storage revenue rose 70%, boosted heavily by the prior year's Brocade acquisition, though Tan said storage was 'robust year-over-year' even stripping that out, with growth expected to accelerate in the fourth quarter, while wireless communications remained a drag, with Tan and Krause saying that segment wouldn't return to double-digit growth until fiscal 2020 after 'a temporary dip in fiscal 2019.' Guidance called for about $5.4 billion in current-quarter revenue, above the $5.35 billion analysts projected. Krause said the strong free cash flow performance, over $2.13 billion as of early August, would support 'another substantial increase' in the dividend, following December's raise to $1.75 a share from $1.02. The article notes shares had lagged the market with a 16% decline for the year heading into the report.
wsj.why_moved: The roughly 5.7% two-day gain reflects the combination of the adjusted-EPS and revenue beats detailed above, plus above-consensus fourth-quarter guidance of $5.4 billion versus $5.35 billion expected, and the signal of 'another substantial increase' in the dividend, as Krause indicated — concrete, forward-looking capital-return language on top of an already-strong quarter. Given that the CA acquisition announcement 'had hit Broadcom's stock hard' in the weeks before this report, as the article states, Tan's extended on-call defense of the deal's strategic logic, tripling the addressable infrastructure-software market, appears to have helped address the specific overhang the article identifies, alongside Krause's reassurance that the company saw 'no fundamental changes in its long-term growth rate.' The 70% enterprise-storage growth and Tan's comment that underlying, ex-Brocade, storage growth was expected to 'accelerate in the fourth quarter' offered a concrete offset to the wireless segment's acknowledged weakness, which the article notes wouldn't meaningfully recover until fiscal 2020, giving investors a specific, dated growth narrative to weigh against the near-term wireless drag. That the stock still gained despite entering the report down 16% for the year suggests this combination of beat, raise, dividend signal, and CA-deal reassurance was enough to reverse at least part of the year's underperformance, even though the one-day return itself was slightly negative at -2.06%, pointing to some initial digestion before the gain solidified over the following day.

wsj.summary_analysis: Facebook's first-quarter 2016 report, covered in both a news story and a Heard on the Street column, described a blowout quarter that stood in sharp contrast to weak results from Silicon Valley peers. Revenue rose 52% year over year to $5.38 billion, ahead of the $5.26 billion analysts polled by Thomson Reuters expected, while adjusted earnings of 77 cents a share beat the 62-cent consensus; GAAP net profit of $1.51 billion nearly tripled the $512 million earned a year earlier. Advertising revenue jumped 57% to $5.2 billion, with mobile ads making up roughly four-fifths of that total, and average revenue per user climbed 33% to $3.32 as monthly active users grew 15% to 1.65 billion. COO Sheryl Sandberg said growth was 'broad-based' but singled out video ads as a strong spot, while CFO David Wehner cautioned that growth rates could slow later in the year as the company faces tougher year-over-year comparisons against 2015's accelerating ad revenue. The article explicitly frames Facebook's results as bucking a broader industry trend: Apple had just reported its first quarterly revenue decline in 13 years, Twitter's revenue fell short of expectations, and Alphabet had missed analysts' targets the week before. Facebook also announced a new nonvoting Class C share structure, mirroring a similar 2014 move by Google, that would let CEO Mark Zuckerberg sell or give away shares without diluting his majority voting control, a move he tied to his and his wife's pledge to give away 99% of their shares over their lifetimes.
wsj.why_moved: Shares jumped 8.8% in after-hours trading, and the coverage ties that reaction directly to the scale of the beat described above: revenue and adjusted earnings both topped Wall Street's consensus figures at a moment when comparable tech giants were disappointing investors across the board. The Heard on the Street piece frames the governance news about the new nonvoting share class -- a move that could be read as entrenching Zuckerberg's control at shareholders' expense -- as unlikely to trouble investors specifically because the underlying business results were so strong, concluding that 'with Facebook's business hurtling forward, investors may not even notice a share-class speed bump.' In other words, the article explicitly subordinates the governance story to the earnings beat as the driver of the stock's reaction, even as it flags Zuckerberg's plan to sell up to $1 billion of stock annually as a longer-term overhang worth watching.

Shares climb as both the top and bottom lines beat Wall Street’s estimates
By Deepa Seetharaman
Updated July 27, 2016 at 10:21 pm ET
Facebook Inc.’s mobile bet has shrunk the time it takes the social network to leap from
one milestone to the next: On Wednesday, Facebook topped $2 billion in quarterly
profit, six months after crossing the billion dollar mark for the first time.
The number of new users—and the ad dollars that follow them—surged in the second
quarter.
Facebook added 220 million monthly active users in the past year, bringing the total
audience to 1.71 billion users. More than 90% of Facebook’s users are on mobile
devices, where Facebook rakes in the bulk of its ad dollars.
Advertising on mobile devices accounted for 84% of Facebook’s $6.2 billion in
advertising sales in the latest quarter.
Revenue generated from mobile ads jumped 80% in the second quarter, faster than
Facebook’s overall 59% advertising growth rate.
“Mobile continues to be the strength,” Facebook Chief Financial Officer Dave Wehner
said in an interview.
The banner results drove Facebook’s shares to a new high, crowning it the fourth most
valuable listed company in the U.S. In Thursday trading, the stock price rose 3% to
$127.06, giving the company a market capitalization of around $370 billion.

Executives said they expect growth to slow over the rest of the year, as the company
laps the second half of 2015, when revenue growth began to accelerate. But it has its
next growth move planned: video.
For now, mobile is enabling an acceleration of growth. Facebook and Google—now
known as Alphabet Inc.—each hit $2 billion in quarterly profit 12 years after their
founding. But it took Google 3 ½ years to go from $1 billion to $2 billion—something
Facebook accomplished in a half a year.
The social network said net income in the second quarter totaled $2.06 billion, or 71
cents a share, nearly tripling the $719 million in profit a year ago.
Facebook is outpacing its competitors in advertising and user growth.
On Tuesday, Twitter Inc. said it has added nine million users in the past year, as it
reported its smallest quarterly gain in revenue. Yahoo Inc. generated $504 million in
sales last quarter from its mobile, video, native and social ads.
Facebook’s market share in mobile advertising, where it is the second-biggest player
after Google, is expected to jump to 12% this year from 8.6% two years ago, according
to research firm eMarketer. Twitter and Yahoo both trail, with less than a 2% market
share this year.
“There’s a common misconception that the law of large numbers will prevent
Facebook from growing further,” said Rahul Shah, chief executive of Ideal Asset
Management, who says Facebook accounts for about 40% of his allocation. “But I
think what they’re missing is that they’re stealing ad dollars from every other source
there is. Pricing will continue to rise and they’ll continue to beat estimates.”
Facebook generated $3.82 in revenue per user in the second quarter, up from $2.76 a
year ago. Its average price per ad rose 9% as users spent more time on their mobile
app, where Facebook only shows higher-priced news feed ads, Mr. Wehner said.

On desktop, Facebook shows a mix of news feed ads as well as lower-priced ads on the

and said he kicked out anybody who proposed features tailored for desktop.
Wednesday, Mr. Zuckerberg said Facebook would apply that same focus to becoming

wsj.summary_analysis: Facebook's third-quarter 2016 report combined a striking beat with an explicit warning about the durability of its growth engine. Revenue soared 56% to $7 billion and profit nearly tripled to $2.38 billion, putting the company on pace for $27 billion in annual revenue; the article cites Standard & Poor's Capital IQ data showing Facebook's top-line growth rate was double that of any other U.S. company with revenue of $20 billion or more that wasn't growing through acquisitions. Pivotal Research analyst Brian Wieser is quoted calling this inevitable given the 'law of large numbers,' adding that 'nobody was expecting the company to grow at the same rate.' The piece also frames Facebook's dominance within a broader duopoly narrative: together with Google, Facebook captured 68% of U.S. online ad spending growth in the second quarter, and Digital Content Next's Jason Kint is quoted warning that 'no one is able to collect data on the scale they can,' a concern about two companies capturing nearly all ad-market growth. Mobile made up 84% of the quarter's ad revenue, monthly active users reached 1.79 billion (93% mobile), and executives again pointed to video -- and Zuckerberg's ambition to make Facebook 'video-first' -- as the next growth lever, aimed partly at the roughly $70 billion U.S. television ad market.

The explicit warning that the primary driver of ad revenue growth over the prior two years was being phased out starting mid-2017, combined with CFO Wehner's statement that growth would 'come down meaningfully,' gave investors a concrete reason to discount the backward-looking beat in favor of a more conservative forward growth outlook -- reinforced by analyst Brian Wieser's comment that slower growth was structurally inevitable given the company's size. The article also notes Facebook's plans to increase spending on data centers and engineering hiring next year, adding a margin concern on top of the revenue-growth deceleration flagged by management, both factors the piece connects to the stock's decline despite otherwise blowout underlying numbers.

wsj.summary_analysis: Facebook's first-quarter 2017 results, as described in the article, 'allayed concerns' that had built up around two specific issues: questions about video-ad performance measurement and criticism over the spread of violent and graphic content on the platform. Profit surged 76% to $3.06 billion and revenue jumped 49% to $8.03 billion, a result the piece frames as echoing Alphabet's own 29% profit growth despite a brand-safety backlash affecting YouTube. Ad prices rose 14% during the quarter while ad impressions grew about a third, with CFO David Wehner attributing the strength to continued mobile usage growth; monthly active users reached 1.94 billion. Even so, Wehner reiterated a warning first raised the prior quarter that ad revenue growth would 'come down meaningfully over the course of 2017' as ad load -- the number of ads shown per user in the news feed -- plays a smaller role in driving growth after mid-2017, pushing the company toward newer, less-proven formats: mid-roll 'ad breaks' in videos, ads on Messenger, and eventually WhatsApp monetization. The article details specific skepticism around this pivot, citing a GroupM/WPP report finding that for every 20 video ads served in the news feed, only one was watched for 10 seconds or longer and just three were watched for at least three seconds -- with some of that skepticism explicitly traced back to Facebook's disclosure the previous fall that it had vastly overestimated average video-ad viewing time for two years. Concerns about violent content on Facebook Live, including a cited case of a Cleveland man's fatal shooting being broadcast, are also described as a factor that could give advertisers pause, prompting Zuckerberg's same-day pledge to hire 3,000 more content reviewers over the next year.
wsj.why_moved: Facebook's share price 'slipped in after-hours trading' despite the strong headline beat described above, and the article ties this specifically to unresolved doubt about whether the newer ad formats can replace the news-feed ad-load growth that Wehner again cautioned would 'come down meaningfully' through the rest of 2017 -- the same warning issued the prior quarter, now repeated with the deceleration presumably closer at hand. The GroupM findings that so few video ads are actually watched for a meaningful duration, combined with the lingering credibility hit from Facebook's earlier video-metrics overstatement, gave investors concrete reasons to question the video and messaging pivot even as current-quarter numbers beat expectations. The article suggests advertiser sentiment remained more cautious than the headline growth implied, noting that marketing executives were 'concerned about fake news and the problems Facebook has had with live video' even though that concern had not yet visibly affected ad spending, a dynamic consistent with a stock that slipped modestly on strong results accompanied by a familiar growth-deceleration warning.

By Deepa Seetharaman
Updated May 3, 2017 at 7:33 pm ET
Facebook posted a sharp increase in revenue on Wednesday as more advertisers flocked to platform. PHILIPPE
WOJAZER/REUTERS
Facebook Inc. continues to sweep digital advertising, alongside rival Google, despite
unrest among marketers about how their advertising is handled.
Facebook on Wednesday said first-quarter profit surged 76% to $3.06 billion, allaying
concerns that questions over video-ad performance and the spread of violent and
graphic content would mar growth. The social network’s soaring results echoed
strength at Google parent Alphabet Inc., which last week reported 29% growth in net
profit despite a backlash that began late in the quarter from companies upset about
their brands being advertised against objectionable videos on its YouTube video

Facebook and its photo-sharing app, Instagram, are the “two most important mobile-
ad platforms,” Chief Financial Officer David Wehner said in an interview.
Facebook and Google dominate the online advertising market. The two tech giants
snatched 99% of the online-ad industry’s revenue growth last year, estimated Pivotal
Research analyst Brian Wieser using data published by the Interactive Advertising
Bureau. Facebook holds 16% of the global digital-ad market, behind Google’s 33%
share, says forecasting firm eMarketer.
Marketing executives “acknowledge they’re concerned about fake news and the
problems Facebook has had with live video,” said eMarketer principal analyst Debra
Aho Williamson. “They’re concerned that at some point this will affect users—but
they haven’t seen that yet. So that’s why spending keeps going up.”
Facebook’s growing market share in digital advertising has helped drive its stock up
29% over the past year. Other metrics were also strong: the number of users who
check into Facebook at least once a month rose to 1.94 billion, for example. However,
its share price slipped in after-hours trading on concerns about whether new ad
formats will be able to replace the booming growth it has experienced with its news
feed ads.
The 49% jump in quarterly revenue to $8.03 billion was a sign of how marketers are
increasingly embracing Facebook and Instagram. Marketing-technology company
Kenshoo, which manages about $6 billion in marketing spending a year, said its clients
were spending 41% more on social-media ads, largely Facebook.
Years ago, Chief Executive Mark Zuckerberg put mobile at the heart of the company, a
focus that has fueled Facebook’s growth for years. Facebook’s ad prices jumped 14%
during the first quarter, while the number of ad impressions increased by about a
third, as users spent more time on their mobile apps. “Mobile continues to be the

driver of our business,” Mr. Wehner said.
Now Mr. Zuckerberg is weaving more video throughout Facebook’s products, adding
more opportunities for Facebook to show more-expensive video ads—but also
creating new uncertainties.
Video and Instagram could pick up the slack from an anticipated slowdown in
advertising in the news feed. On Wednesday, Mr. Wehner reiterated his warning from
last year that Facebook’s ad revenue growth will “come down meaningfully over the
course of 2017.” Facebook also expects the ad load—the number of ads it can jam into
its main news feed—will play a smaller role in driving revenue growth after mid-2017.
Facebook is fielding pitches for TV-like original programming, in the hopes that
weekly shows on Facebook will change the way people currently use the platform and
eventually draw marketing dollars that have traditionally gone to television.
Facebook is now testing a way to profit from those longer videos through “ad breaks”
—ads that appear in the middle of a video—in both live broadcasts and on-demand
videos. It also tweaked a setting so sound is on by default in some videos, a move
designed to appease advertisers.
If successful, these “ad breaks” will help Facebook convince publishers to create
longer videos without the platform paying them outright, executives said. Advertisers
are concerned that users will drop off a video once they see an ad in the middle of a
video. In addition, Facebook users aren’t accustomed to watching longer videos on the
site.
But advertisers aren’t entirely sold on Facebook’s nascent video-ad products.
Facebook’s video product remains “uncertain ground,” according to a new report by
GroupM, the ad-buying unit of WPP PLC. For every 20 video ads served in the news
feed, just one was watched for 10 seconds or longer and three watched for at least

wsj.summary_analysis: Facebook's second-quarter 2017 report showed profit spiking 71% and net income of $3.9 billion actually surpassing larger rival Alphabet's bottom line, which had been hit by a European Union fine; revenue jumped 45% to $9.3 billion, boosted by a 24% increase in the average ad price. But the article's framing is less about the beat than about a structural constraint: Facebook's news feed, its primary and most profitable source of ad revenue, is 'hitting a ceiling' on how many ads it can show without alienating users, with analyst Jan Dawson of Jackdaw Research noting that already one of every seven to ten posts in the feed is an ad. In response, Zuckerberg told analysts he expects video to become the largest driver of Facebook's business over the next two to three years and messaging (Messenger and WhatsApp, the latter now used by 1 billion people daily) to yield returns within five years, while artificial intelligence could improve ad targeting. Executives acknowledged on the call that these newer formats -- mid-roll video ads and the newly launched Messenger ads -- carry lower margins than news feed ads, partly because Facebook shares ad revenue with video creators, prompting Zuckerberg's own admission that 'there are real questions there that we need to manage well' regarding the video pivot, tempered by his statement that 'I want to see us move a little faster here, but I'm confident that we're going to get this right over the long term.' COO Sheryl Sandberg told analysts that television ads simply 'do not work as well as ads that are natively mobile,' comparing advertisers' current adjustment to the early, awkward days of television advertising itself, and noted many marketers were still repurposing TV creative rather than building mobile-native ads.
wsj.why_moved: Facebook's stock rose 3.7% in after-hours trading, building on a 44% year-to-date gain, a reaction the article frames as more measured than the size of the underlying beat (profit up 71%, revenue up 45%, average ad prices up 24%) might otherwise suggest. Consistent with the 'ceiling' framing established above, the more modest post-earnings pop appears tied to the article's emphasis that Facebook's most lucrative ad inventory is running out of room to expand, forcing a shift toward video and messaging formats that management itself acknowledged carry structurally lower margins and, in Zuckerberg's own words, 'real questions' still to be resolved. The article does not attribute the stock's reaction to a single explicit cause, but the juxtaposition of the strong current-quarter numbers against management's candid acknowledgment of margin pressure and execution risk in the pivot to video and messaging is the clearest throughline it offers for a gain that, while positive, was smaller than the magnitude of the earnings beat itself.

The article's real focus, however, is the collision between those results and the political scrutiny Facebook faced the same day: the earnings release coincided with congressional hearings in which lawmakers grilled Facebook, Twitter and Google executives over Russian propagandists' use of their platforms during the 2016 election, with Facebook disclosing that 146 million users had seen posts from accounts linked to the Internet Research Agency, a pro-Kremlin outfit. In direct response, Zuckerberg announced Facebook would double its safety and security staff to 20,000 people by the end of 2018, warning investors that 2018 expenses could rise by as much as 60% and that this would 'significantly impact our profitability going forward,' adding, 'I am dead serious about this.' The article also notes that advertisers were separately wary of Facebook's video ad products following prior measurement missteps, and details several of the company's remediation efforts, including a commitment to hire a total of 4,000 content and ad reviewers, testing a feature to disclose more about who is behind an ad, and building new AI systems to detect what Zuckerberg called 'bad content and bad actors.'

Still, company remains under scrutiny over Russian activity
By Deepa Seetharaman
Updated Nov. 1, 2017 at 7:52 pm ET
Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg ERIC RISBERG/ASSOCIATED PRESS
Facebook Inc. extended its dominance in online advertising in the third quarter but
said it would sacrifice some future growth to invest more heavily in its safety and
security operations to address the growing scrutiny of its power and influence.
The social-media giant reported a 79% jump in third-quarter profit on Wednesday, the
same day lawmakers grilled executives from Facebook, Twitter Inc. and Alphabet
Inc.’s Google during congressional hearings that focused on alleged Russian
propagandists’ activity during the election. Facebook and Google together capture the
bulk of the growth in digital advertising.

Facebook plans to double the number of employees and contractors who handle safety
and security issues to 20,000 by the end of 2018. It is also redoubling security-focused
engineering efforts in some areas and building new artificial-intelligence systems to
detect what Chief Executive Mark Zuckerberg described as “bad content and bad
actors.” Facebook’s 2018 expenses could rise as much as 60% compared with 2017.
“I am dead serious about this,” Mr. Zuckerberg told investors. “I’ve directed our teams
to invest so much in security on top of the other investments we’re making that it will
significantly impact our profitability going forward.”
Facebook is confronting one of the toughest periods in its 13-year history. This week,
Facebook’s general counsel faced a series of hostile questions from U.S. lawmakers
over its failure to detect the way Russian propagandists used its platform to spread
divisive content through ads, free posts and event listings.
The grilling raises the specter of regulation and added scrutiny, which could slow
Facebook’s growth and ability to rapidly develop new products. The crisis also put
Facebook in the awkward position of playing down the effectiveness of the Russian
ads while touting the strength of its ad targeting and reach to legitimate advertisers.
Advertisers, too, are wary of Facebook’s video ad products after a series of missteps in
calculating advertising performance.
“The underlying issue is whether Facebook can be sufficiently trusted by
stakeholders,” said Pivotal Research analyst Brian Weiser. “There’s always been this
concern that at the top of the company they’re not taking these matters seriously
enough. Lack of trust creates friction, lack of trust creates rules and those rules come
with costs.”
Facebook reported a third-quarter profit of $1.59 a share, up from 90 cents a share a
year ago. The company also generated $10.33 billion in revenue, up from $7.01 billion
in the prior year’s quarter.

wsj.summary_analysis: This Heard on the Street column examines Facebook's fourth-quarter 2017 results through the lens of CEO Mark Zuckerberg's stated 2018 goal of 'fixing' the social network, including an overhaul of the News Feed and video efforts, which he had warned could hurt usage since 'protecting our community is more important than maximizing our profit.' The column finds Zuckerberg 'half right' so far: usage did take a real hit, with daily active users reaching 1.4 billion, up only 2.4% sequentially -- the lowest sequential growth on record for that metric and down sharply from 4.1% growth a year earlier -- and the 33 million net new daily users added in the quarter came in below the 46 million Wall Street analysts had expected. Yet the article stresses that the financial results told the opposite story: revenue jumped 47% year over year to just under $13 billion, operating income surged 61% to $7.4 billion, and Facebook wasn't cutting spending to protect margins either, with 2017 capital expenditures soaring 49% to $6.7 billion. The column adds a comparative data point on profitability, noting that on a trailing twelve-month basis Facebook generates about 50 cents of operating profit per dollar of revenue, roughly twice the margin of megacap peers Microsoft, Apple and Alphabet. The piece's forward-looking conclusion is explicitly cautionary rather than descriptive of the quarter itself: it argues investors should 'get ready for a slightly less profitable Facebook' once the more significant product changes -- and their effects on advertisers -- are fully reflected in future results.
wsj.why_moved: As a Heard on the Street opinion column, the piece does not report an after-hours trading reaction or attribute the stock's actual multi-day move to any specific figure; it instead lays out the tension between a clear engagement miss (33 million new daily users versus the 46 million analysts expected, the slowest sequential DAU growth on record) and record financial strength (47% revenue growth, 61% operating income growth) without stating which side the market weighted more heavily. Given that the stock rose over the following days, it is a reasonable inference that investors leaned toward the financial-strength side of that split described above rather than the engagement slowdown, but the article itself offers no explicit statement connecting its content to the specific positive price reaction -- it stays focused on warning that the true financial cost of Zuckerberg's 'fixing Facebook' agenda has not yet arrived, a caution about the future rather than an explanation of the immediate move.

No Bill Yet for Facebook’s Fixes
The social network’s changes slow user growth but financials stay strong
By Dan Gallagher
Jan. 31, 2018 at 6:12 pm ET
CEO Mark Zuckerberg has made ‘fixing’ Facebook his goal for 2018. MARK SCHIEFELBEIN/ASSOCIATED PRESS
So what will it cost to “fix” Facebook? The company’s fourth-quarter results reported
Wednesday offered an early clue.
CEO Mark Zuckerberg has made “fixing” the social network his top goal for the new
year. He has previously outlined several efforts in this direction—including an
overhaul to the company’s key News Feed tool and video efforts. He also has warned
that the changes could affect the site’s usage, but added that “protecting our
community is more important than maximizing our profit.”

No Bill Yet for Facebook’s Fixes - WSJ 2026-08-28, 4:49 PM
Results reported Wednesday afternoon showed Mr. Zuckerberg was half right, at least
for now. Usage indeed took a hit in the fourth quarter, reflecting some of the changes
the company had put in place. Facebook reported 1.4 billion daily average users for the
period, an increase of only 2.4% from the third quarter. That was the lowest sequential
growth on record for this key engagement metric—and down notably from the 4.1%
growth the company reported at this time last year. The 33 million daily average users
added in the quarter was below the 46 million expected by Wall Street analysts.
But Facebook’s fixes are still invisible in its financial statements. In fact, the fourth
quarter was the company’s strongest on record in many respects. Revenue jumped
47% year over year to just under $13 billion, fueled by a strong mobile-advertising
business. Operating income surged 61% to $7.4 billion. And Facebook isn’t exactly
pinching pennies to goose the bottom line: Capital expenditures soared to $6.7 billion
in 2017—a 49% jump from the previous year.
Facebook’s profits can be deemed the envy of the tech world. On a trailing 12-month
basis, Facebook now generates about 50 cents in operating profit per dollar of
revenue. That is roughly twice as much as its megacap tech peers Microsoft Corp.,
Apple Inc. and Google parent Alphabet Inc.
But investors should still get ready for a slightly less profitable Facebook. Some of the
company’s more significant changes have yet to be fully reflected, and the changes
already in effect may not have hit advertisers’ radar. When both hit, that may be the
truest test of Mr. Zuckerberg’s resolve—and that of his investors.

The results themselves were mixed rather than uniformly weak: earnings per share of $1.74 edged past the $1.72 analyst consensus, but revenue of $13.23 billion missed the $13.36 billion analysts had expected, according to Thomson Reuters -- the company's first revenue miss since the first quarter of 2015, as the article specifically notes. Management layered a pointed deceleration warning on top of that miss: executives said the revenue growth rate had already fallen seven percentage points quarter over quarter and would decrease by 'high single-digit percentages' in the second half of 2018, while guiding operating margins down from the quarter's 44% to the 'mid-30s' over the next several years due to higher product and infrastructure spending. User trends in lucrative markets also softened: daily active users in the U.S. and Canada were flat at 185 million, while European daily users slipped to 279 million from 282 million, a decline executives attributed to the new European GDPR privacy law taking effect during the quarter. Zuckerberg himself called the results 'another solid quarter' on the call, but the article notes those comments were 'quickly overshadowed' when other executives detailed the growth deceleration and margin guidance, with SocialFlow CEO Jim Anderson quoted wondering whether the results signaled 'an early warning sign that the market's assumptions about tech companies' growth failed to account for the fact that each of us only has 24 hours in a day.'
wsj.why_moved: The article ties the record plunge directly to the specific combination established above: a rare revenue miss against consensus -- the first since early 2015 -- landing alongside an explicit management warning that revenue growth would keep decelerating by high single digits through the back half of 2018 and that operating margins would compress from 44% toward the mid-30s for years to come. That the softness showed up specifically in Europe, where daily active users actually declined and where executives linked the drop to new GDPR rules, gave the deceleration warning concrete, near-term evidence rather than leaving it as an abstract caution, which the article suggests amplified the market's reaction. Zuckerberg's own characterization of the quarter as 'another solid quarter,' delivered just before the more cautious guidance from his fellow executives took over the narrative, underscores the article's framing that it was the forward-looking guidance and the rare revenue miss -- not the past quarter's underlying growth of 42% -- that investors reacted to so severely.

wsj.summary_analysis: This Heard on the Street column covers Tesla's first-quarter 2016 results, in which the company reported revenue of $1.15 billion and an adjusted loss of 57 cents a share -- a figure the article says 'narrowly topped consensus expectations.' The column's focus, however, is on CEO Elon Musk's newly accelerated promises: Tesla raised its delivery target to 500,000 vehicles by 2018, two years earlier than the previous goal, and reaffirmed that Model 3 production would begin in late 2017, following preorders that had exceeded even the most optimistic projections. The article treats these more ambitious targets skeptically, noting that meeting production deadlines 'has never been Tesla's strong suit,' pointing specifically to quality issues that plagued the Model X SUV's rollout, which arrived years after originally promised, and to the departure of two senior manufacturing executives around the same time. It also flags a financial reversal: Musk said the new plan 'will likely require additional capital' and guided 2016 capital expenditures 50% higher than the previous $1.5 billion guidance, which the column calls an 'abrupt reversal' since Tesla had said as recently as February that it wouldn't need to raise additional capital. The piece further notes, with some alarm, that Tesla was using refundable Model 3 customer deposits to pay down its asset-backed line of credit, and closes by observing that at more than 50 times projected 2018 earnings, Tesla shares were 'priced for perfection.'
wsj.why_moved: Tesla shares fell sharply over the following days even though the reported results themselves 'narrowly topped consensus,' as the article states, and the column's skeptical framing supplies the likely explanation: rather than reassuring investors, the newly accelerated 500,000-vehicle target seems to have raised the bar Tesla would need to clear against a track record the article calls into question via the Model X's own delayed, quality-plagued launch and the exit of two senior manufacturing executives. The 'abrupt reversal' on capital needs -- guiding capital expenditures 50% higher just months after saying no capital raise would be necessary -- combined with the eyebrow-raising use of Model 3 deposits to pay down a credit line, gave the column concrete reasons to argue that Musk's more ambitious 2018 goals deserved 'thorough scrutiny' rather than celebration, a skeptical framing consistent with the stock's decline despite the narrow quarterly beat.

Tesla Motors CEO Elon Musk has made big promises. PATRICK T. FALLON/REUTERS
Enthusiasm for the Model 3 mass-market car has powered Tesla Motors TSLA -1.71%
to lofty heights. But first-quarter results should remind investors that the future isn’t
too far away.
Tesla reported revenue of $1.15 billion and an adjusted loss per share of 57 cents
Wednesday. That narrowly topped consensus expectations.
But, expectations for the future, rather than current performance, tend to dictate
what eventually happens to stock prices. That is especially true for Tesla.

Tesla Earnings: It’s All About the Dream - WSJ 2026-08-28, 4:55 PM
Chief Executive Elon Musk, as usual, made big promises. Tesla now expects to deliver
500,000 vehicles by 2018, two years earlier than the previous goal. And the company
affirmed that Model 3 production will begin late next year. This comes after Model 3
preorders exceeded even the most optimistic projections.
More ambitious goals should be great news, but the new plan deserves thorough
scrutiny. Meeting production deadlines has never been Tesla’s strong suit. Quality
issues have plagued the rollout of the Model X sport-utility vehicle, which came to
market years after originally promised. Meanwhile, two senior manufacturing
executives are leaving the company.
Mr. Musk also said the new goal “will likely require additional capital.” He added that
2016 capital expenditures will likely be 50% higher than the previous guidance of $1.5
billion. This marks an abrupt reversal, since Tesla said it wouldn’t need to raise
additional capital back in February. Tesla’s use of Model 3 deposits to pay down its
asset-backed line of credit should also raises eyebrows.
And, as always, at more than 50 times projected 2018 earnings, Tesla shares are priced
for perfection.
Hope for a bright future still drives the stock. That hope will be put to the test—and
soon.

The seemingly encouraging detail was on the cash-flow side: Tesla reported operating cash flow of $150 million against $295 million in capital spending, producing a free cash outflow of just $145 million -- the company's best quarterly cash-flow performance in more than two years. But the column's central argument, reflected in its headline, is that this improvement is a 'mirage.' It notes that refundable customer deposits for the Model 3 were included in operating cash flow, which could reverse sharply if orders are later refunded, and separately flags that Tesla went silent on updating its Model 3 order count -- more than two months had passed since the company last disclosed roughly 373,000 orders. The article also stresses that capital spending is set to rise significantly: Tesla had guided in May to about $2.25 billion in 2016 capital expenditures related to Model 3 readiness, yet had spent just over $500 million so far that year, implying a steep ramp still ahead. While Tesla had raised $1.7 billion in a May equity sale and held $3.2 billion on its balance sheet as a cushion, the column argues that spending on the company's 'huge automotive ambitions' is not optional, and notes the pending SolarCity acquisition -- which the article describes as burning 'prodigious amounts of cash' -- would add further strain rather than relief.
wsj.why_moved: The stock's reaction over the following days was close to flat, a pattern the article does not directly explain, since its own report is that the quarterly loss 'fell short of analysts' estimates' -- a miss that might on its own suggest a more negative reaction than the muted move that occurred. The column's skeptical thesis, that the improved free-cash-flow figure benefited from including reversible Model 3 deposits and masked a looming capital-spending ramp alongside the cash-hungry SolarCity deal, offers a plausible reason for cautious rather than enthusiastic investor sentiment, but the article does not state that these specific concerns drove the observed price action; it stops at arguing 'shareholders shouldn't put away their wallets just yet' as a forward-looking caution rather than an explanation tied to the quarter's actual stock move, which should be treated as unclear based on what the article itself says.

wsj.summary_analysis: Tesla's fourth-quarter 2016 results, covered by both a news article and a skeptical Heard on the Street column, showed revenue jumping 88% to $2.28 billion -- described as 'ahead of analysts' expectations' -- alongside a narrowed loss of $121.3 million, a reversion to red ink following the prior quarter's surprise profit. The news piece details Tesla's aggressive production plan for the Model 3, targeting a July production start and a ramp to 5,000 vehicles a week by the fourth quarter of 2017, with Musk telling analysts that while the plan itself doesn't require additional funds, the company's cash pile would drop 'close to the edge' and that 'it probably makes sense to raise capital to reduce risk.' Notably, Tesla had spent only about half its projected $1 billion in fourth-quarter capital expenditures by deferring payments to equipment suppliers in exchange for better terms, ending the quarter with $3.39 billion in cash. The Heard on the Street column takes a more pointed view of the balance sheet, noting that total liabilities had ballooned to nearly $17 billion from $7 billion a year earlier following the SolarCity acquisition, against cash of just $3.4 billion, and that free cash outflow widened to nearly $1 billion for the quarter -- a figure the column notes was artificially reduced by the deferred vendor payments described above. The column also flags the same-week resignation of Tesla's chief financial officer, who was replaced by a previous CFO who had left the company in 2015, and highlights that Tesla shares had surged roughly 50% since December 1 even as the stock traded at more than 200 times expected 2018 earnings.
wsj.why_moved: The two articles present a split picture that is not explicitly reconciled with the stock's sharply negative multi-day move: the reported revenue beat expectations and the Heard on the Street column even notes shares were initially 'higher in late trading' following the release. What the column does supply as concrete concerns -- the SolarCity-driven surge in total liabilities to nearly $17 billion, free cash outflow nearing $1 billion for the quarter (aided by the deferred vendor payments noted above), Musk's own acknowledgment that the cash pile would run 'close to the edge' and that raising capital 'probably makes sense,' and the same-week departure of the sitting CFO -- collectively support the column's overall warning that investors should 'prepare for the day when the market loses faith in Mr. Musk.' However, neither article explicitly states that these specific factors, rather than the underlying beat, are what caused the several-day decline that followed, so the connection between the articles' cautionary content and the observed negative return should be read as suggestive context rather than a stated explanation.
