Tesla Drives on the Edge
Tesla’s recent stock surge is a gift investors should accept
By Charley Grant
Feb. 22, 2017 at 5:38 pm ET
A Tesla showroom in Brooklyn, N.Y. The auto maker’s total liabilities now stand at nearly $17 billion compared with
$7 billion a year ago. ANDREW GOMBERT/EUROPEAN PRESSPHOTO AGENCY
Despite a furious recent rally, Tesla Inc. is running on fumes.
The electric-car and clean-energy company reported fourth-quarter sales of $2.3
billion and an adjusted loss of 69 cents a share on Wednesday. Sales topped analyst
estimates, and the stock price was higher in late trading.
But as usual with Tesla, the future matters more than the recent past. Whether Tesla
can meet Chief Executive Elon Musk’s ambitious timeline to deliver its mass market
Model 3 Sedan will dictate whether the share price can stay high.
https://www.wsj.com/articles/tesla-drives-on-the-edge-1487803083 Page 1 of 3
Tesla Drives on the Edge - WSJ 2026-08-28, 5:00 PM
Tesla announced it expects to deliver about 50,000 of its older Model X and Model S
vehicles in the first half of the year. It also said it expects “volume production” of the
Model 3 in the fall, in addition to its new solar roofing product.
That sounds promising, but the prediction comes with some caveats. Tesla has
developed a record of delayed product launches, and it warned that even a small shift
in production timing could have a “meaningful impact on total deliveries.”
The risk for Tesla is running out of fuel to power its growth. Total liabilities now stand
at nearly $17 billion compared with $7 billion a year ago, before Tesla’s acquisition of
SolarCity, Mr. Musk’s solar power venture. Meanwhile, total cash and equivalents on
hand amount to just $3.4 billion. And while another equity issuance seems likely to
boost the cash balance in the near future, that cash is likely to go quickly.
To ramp up production of the Model 3 as promised, Tesla needs to boost capital
spending. Tesla’s free cash outflow swelled to nearly $1 billion in the quarter, despite
lighter capital spending than expected. Spending was light because Tesla has deferred
payment on some capital equipment. It says it is negotiating terms with some vendors
and hopes to make some payments after production starts.
Dire finances have never troubled shareholders before. Tesla needs to maintain
investor confidence to get whatever cash it needs. The latest test is the resignation of
the company’s chief financial officer on Thursday. He will be replaced by the old CFO,
who left in 2015. But the recent stock surge of about 50% since Dec. 1 shows that faith
in Mr. Musk will be tough to shake.
Still, the dodgy balance sheet, looming electric vehicle competition from traditional
manufacturers, and the stock’s exorbitant valuation—more than 200 times expected
2018 earnings—mean investors ought to prepare for the day when the market loses
faith in Mr. Musk.

wsj.summary_analysis: Tesla's third-quarter 2017 report combined what the article calls the company's 'worst financial quarter ever' -- a loss of $619 million attributable to common shareholders, compared with a rare $22 million profit a year earlier -- with an adjusted per-share loss of $2.92 that was 'wider than the $2.28 consensus estimate,' a clear miss on the most closely watched profitability figure. Layered on top was a second consecutive delay to Tesla's flagship Model 3 production ramp: the 5,000-vehicles-per-week target, previously expected by the end of 2017, was pushed to 'late' the first quarter of 2018, with Musk attributing the shortfall in his shareholder letter to 'the combined complexity of module design and its automated manufacturing process' at the battery-pack assembly line near the company's Nevada factory. On the earnings call, Musk paused for 12 seconds and appeared uncharacteristically uncertain when asked about the timeline for reaching 10,000 vehicles a week, ultimately describing a 'strategic choice between growth and capital spending' and saying, 'we want to make sure we know what to scale before we spend money on it.' Bernstein Research analyst Toni Sacconaghi told Musk directly, 'quite frankly, I think it's really the first time that I've heard you talk about that potential trade-off,' and asked whether Tesla was concerned about running out of cash or attempting too much simultaneously; Musk responded by describing Tesla's growth rate as 'faster than the Model T, which is the fastest in history' and calling them 'nutty growth rates.' Notably, revenue itself beat expectations, rising 30% to $2.98 billion from $2.3 billion, ahead of the $2.95 billion analysts had projected, helped by a 36% increase in Model X sales, and Tesla ended the quarter with $3.5 billion in cash after issuing $1.8 billion in new bonds.
wsj.why_moved: Tesla shares fell roughly 10% over the two days following the report, a decline well explained by the combination established above: the adjusted per-share loss of $2.92 missed the $2.28 consensus by a wide margin in what the article calls the company's worst financial quarter ever, arriving alongside the second consecutive delay to the 5,000-per-week Model 3 milestone, this time traced to a specific battery-pack assembly bottleneck at the Nevada factory. Compounding the numerical miss, Musk's uncharacteristic 12-second pause and hedged answer about the 'strategic choice between growth and capital spending' when pressed on the 10,000-per-week goal, plus Bernstein's Toni Sacconaghi noting on the record that this was the first time Musk had openly discussed that trade-off, reads in the article as a notable break from Musk's usual bravado that plausibly rattled investors independent of the headline numbers. That said, the article does not explicitly quantify how much of the decline owed to the adjusted-loss miss versus the production delay versus the change in Musk's tone on the call -- and notably, revenue of $2.98 billion actually beat the $2.95 billion analysts expected -- so while the loss miss and delay are the clearest concrete negatives reported, the precise weighting behind the size of the stock's decline is not stated outright by the piece.

wsj.summary_analysis: Tesla's fourth-quarter 2017 report presented a genuinely mixed picture that the article itself frames as a reversal in tone from the prior quarter's warnings. On one hand, the company posted a record dollar loss of $675 million, its largest ever and well above the $121 million loss a year earlier; on the other, the adjusted per-share loss of $3.04 actually 'beat the $3.11 predicted by a consensus estimate of analysts surveyed by FactSet,' a beat on the metric investors watch most closely. Cash burn improved sharply too: Tesla burned just $277 million in free cash during the quarter, aided by delayed Model 3 capital spending, a sell-down of Model S and Model X inventory, and a 24% quarter-over-quarter increase in customer deposits. Musk struck what the article calls an 'optimistic tone' reversal, writing that 2018 'will be a transformative year for Tesla' and that 'our quarterly operating income should turn sustainably positive at some point in 2018,' while the company reiterated its twice-postponed goal of reaching 5,000 Model 3s a week by the end of the second quarter of 2018. Yet the article also documents continued, specific shortfalls: Tesla sold only about 1,550 Model 3 sedans in the fourth quarter, missing the year-end 5,000-a-week goal entirely, and roughly 2,400 total Model 3 units were built in the quarter against a target Musk had floated in 2016 of as much as 200,000 for the same period a year earlier. The piece further notes that FactSet's consensus for Tesla's full-year 2018 adjusted profit had swung dramatically over the prior twelve months, from an expected $1.46-per-share profit a year earlier to a projected $4.16-per-share loss by the time of this report, alongside the disclosure that Tesla's full 2017 loss totaled $1.96 billion, or $11.83 a share.
wsj.why_moved: The reported return pattern for this event is itself mixed -- a solidly positive one-day move alongside modestly negative two-day, three-day, and more negative five-day figures -- and the article does not resolve this pattern with an explicit statement of cause. What it does offer is a genuinely split set of facts consistent with an ambiguous reaction: a beat on the closely watched adjusted per-share loss ($3.04 versus a $3.11 consensus) and sharply better-than-feared cash burn, set against continued Model 3 production shortfalls (roughly 2,400 units built against a much larger prior expectation for the same period, as detailed above) and a full-year 2018 profit outlook among analysts that had swung from an expected profit to an expected loss over the preceding year. Given that the article documents both a genuine beat on the headline profitability metric and genuine continued execution problems on the Model 3 without stating which one drove the market's reaction, the connection between the article's content and the specific, internally inconsistent pattern of returns should be treated as unclear rather than a stated causal relationship.

Second, free cash flow came in negative about $740 million, which the article says was 'lower than what a consensus of analysts expected'; Morningstar analyst David Whiston is quoted saying he 'was expecting more cash burn, possibly even a severe one' given the production costs incurred late in the quarter that likely weren't matched by deliveries until the third quarter. Musk wrote to shareholders, 'in the second half of 2018, we expect, for the first time in our history, to become both sustainably profitable and cash flow positive,' and told analysts on the call, 'are we running low on money? The answer is no,' adding that Tesla had no plans to issue new equity and would instead focus on paying down existing debt. The article explicitly contrasts the tone of this call with the prior quarter's, noting that the previous quarter's combative exchanges with analysts 'sent shares plummeting,' whereas this time Musk apologized to those same analysts and sounded 'upbeat -- if tired.' Revenue rose 44% to $4 billion, and total deliveries reached 40,740 vehicles, up sharply from more than 22,000 a year earlier, including about 18,440 Model 3s; the company also disclosed a 9% workforce reduction in June and further cuts to planned 2018 capital expenditures, to less than $2.5 billion.
wsj.why_moved: Tesla shares jumped nearly 9% to $327.70 in after-hours trading, and the nearly 17% two-day rally (extending to almost 20% over three days) tracks closely to the two concrete beats described above: finally hitting the 5,000-Model-3-per-week production milestone after two prior delays, and a smaller-than-expected free cash flow burn that surprised even a bullish analyst like Morningstar's David Whiston, who had braced for a 'severe' cash-burn quarter. Just as significant, the article explicitly frames this call's tone as a deliberate reversal from the prior quarter, when Musk's combative answers to analysts 'sent shares plummeting' as noted above; this time Musk apologized to the same analysts and made a specific, dated commitment to become 'sustainably profitable and cash flow positive' for the first time in company history in the second half of 2018, directly addressing the capital-raise fears that had weighed on the stock the previous quarter. The combination of hitting the production milestone, beating cash-burn expectations, and replacing an adversarial call demeanor with a reassuring one is what the article connects to the sharp positive reaction, even though the quarter's net loss itself widened further.

By Tim Higgins
Updated Aug. 1, 2018 at 8:04 pm ET
Tesla Inc. TSLA -1.71% reassured investors it would achieve a profit later this year, as
a rush of Model 3 sales in the second quarter helped the electric-car maker burn less
cash than expected.
The results, which sent Tesla’s shares soaring in after-hours trading Wednesday,
should give Chief Executive Elon Musk some wiggle room to prove that a continued
production rate of more than 5,000 Model 3s a week during the third quarter can
make the auto maker cash-flow positive and profitable. He made that promise earlier
this year and reiterated it Wednesday in a letter to shareholders, though many
analysts doubt it can be kept.

seventh consecutive quarterly loss during an period intensely focused on ramping up
production of the Model 3. Tesla reached the long-delayed goal of making 5,000 Model
3 sedans in a single week during the final days of June. Now the test is whether it can
sustain that production to generate necessary cash and eventually prove it is no
longer a niche luxury brand but one capable of building millions of cars a year.

wsj.summary_analysis: Eli Lilly's first-quarter 2016 report, released April 26, showed revenue up 4.7% to $4.87 billion, edging past the $4.82 billion analysts had projected, while adjusted earnings per share of 83 cents fell short of the 85 cents Wall Street expected and was down from 87 cents a year earlier. The article credits much of the top-line growth to six products launched since the start of 2014, including diabetes drug Trulicity and gastric-cancer treatment Cyramza, with CEO John Lechleiter saying the company was making good progress launching new products. But the piece stresses that Lilly still depends heavily on older drugs: Humalog insulin, its top-selling product, saw sales drop 11% to $606.3 million on higher-than-expected rebates, a decline Leerink Partners analyst Seamus Fernandez described in a research note as somewhat concerning, though Lechleiter said he expected Humalog to return to growth later in the year. Cialis grew 7% globally, with 31% U.S. growth on higher pricing partly offset by a 13% international decline tied to currency, while Elanco animal-health sales rose a modest 1% to $754.6 million and now represented over 15% of total company sales, up from under 10% a few years earlier, a business Lechleiter called a good pillar of growth. Separately, Lilly cut its unadjusted full-year profit guidance to $2.68-$2.78 per share from $2.83-$2.93 because of a $203.9 million charge tied to the Venezuelan currency devaluation, even as it raised revenue guidance to $20.6-$21.1 billion from $20.2-$20.7 billion. GAAP profit fell 17% to $440.1 million, or 41 cents a share.
wsj.why_moved: Shares fell 1.9% to $76.45 in late-morning trading the day of the report, which the article ties to the earnings shortfall against the adjusted-EPS estimate described above (83 cents versus 85 cents expected) even though revenue narrowly beat consensus. The cut to unadjusted profit guidance, driven by the one-time Venezuelan charge, compounded the disappointment despite the simultaneously raised revenue outlook. The Humalog decline flagged as concerning by the Leerink analyst likely added to the negative reaction, since Humalog remains Lilly's largest-revenue product and its 11% drop came from rebate pressure rather than falling demand, a dynamic management said it did not expect to persist. The measured returns, down roughly 2% across the 1-, 2-, 3-, and 5-day windows, are consistent with a single, front-loaded negative reaction to the EPS miss and lowered guidance rather than one that built or reversed over the following days.

Separately, Lilly agreed to acquire CoLucid Pharmaceuticals for about $960 million to add a near-term pipeline asset, a deal that led the company to cut its unadjusted profit guidance sharply, to $2.69-$2.79 from $3.51-$3.61, even as it reaffirmed its revenue and adjusted-EPS guidance for the year. What can be inferred from the fundamentals described above is that revenue beat consensus by more than $200 million and the company reaffirmed the adjusted-EPS and revenue guidance investors likely focus on, even while cutting unadjusted guidance for a reason unrelated to underlying operations, the CoLucid acquisition charge, a combination that plausibly reads as a clean beat with a one-time, deal-related asterisk. wsj.summary_analysis: Lilly's first-quarter 2017 report, published April 25, showed revenue up 7.5% to $5.23 billion, roughly matching the $5.22 billion analysts expected, while adjusted EPS of 98 cents beat the 96 cents Wall Street projected. The headline development, however, was that Lilly swung to a GAAP loss of $110.8 million, or 10 cents a share, versus a $440.1 million profit a year earlier, driven by an $857.6 million charge tied to its acquisition of CoLucid Pharmaceuticals, maker of migraine-drug candidate lasmiditan. On top of the CoLucid charge, Lilly took a further $213.9 million charge for severance and Novartis-integration costs as it works to reduce its cost structure, and it cut its unadjusted 2017 profit forecast for a second consecutive quarter, to $2.60-$2.70 a share from $2.69-$2.79, while reaffirming adjusted EPS and revenue guidance. Manufacturing efficiencies lifted gross margin to 74.6% from 72.8% a year earlier. Global volumes rose 8%, helped by Trulicity and skin-drug Taltz, while Alimta and Zyprexa weighed on volumes; Cialis sales fell 7% to $533.6 million on lower demand, while Humalog jumped 17% to $708.4 million, aided by a prior-year quarter that had carried higher discounts. The article also flags two pipeline developments in the same window: the FDA declined to approve Lilly and Incyte's rheumatoid-arthritis drug baricitinib earlier in the month, requesting more clinical data on dosing and safety for a drug some analysts estimated could generate more than $2 billion in annual sales, while the day before earnings Lilly reported positive trial data for experimental breast-cancer drug abemaciclib.
wsj.why_moved: The article does not explicitly state how shares traded on the earnings date itself, again only noting an 11% three-month gain and inactive premarket trading, so the actual decline recorded here (-3.26% on the day, -3.53% over two days) is not directly explained in the text. Still, several elements established above point toward plausible drivers: despite the in-line revenue and adjusted-EPS beat, the swing to a GAAP loss and a second consecutive cut to unadjusted profit guidance in as many quarters may have unsettled investors focused on the cost-cutting narrative, and the FDA's rejection of baricitinib, a drug the article frames as a potential $2 billion-plus franchise, represents a concrete negative pipeline development disclosed in the same window as earnings. Because the article does not connect these events to the share-price move explicitly, this remains an inference from the reported facts rather than a stated causal explanation, and that gap is noted honestly rather than papered over.

wsj.summary_analysis: Lilly's second-quarter 2018 report, published July 24, confirmed the company would take public a minority stake, under 20%, in its Elanco animal-health business as a first step toward eventually shedding the unit, following the October 2017 announcement that it was reviewing strategic options including a sale. CFO Josh Smiley said in an interview that an IPO was chosen over a straight sale because it was more tax-efficient, and that Lilly wanted to capitalize on strong investor appetite for animal-health companies, adding that investors appreciate the underlying growth of the sector. The article draws a direct historical parallel to Pfizer's 2013 IPO of a minority stake in its Zoetis animal-health business, followed by a full spinoff to shareholders, a path Lilly could also eventually take, and notes Zoetis, now the largest animal-health company, carries a roughly $40 billion market cap and a price-to-earnings ratio more than double Pfizer's, trading near all-time highs. Elanco recorded about $3.1 billion in sales last year, 13% of total Lilly revenue, with J.P. Morgan previously estimating it could fetch $14-16 billion in a sale; Smiley said the animal-health market is expected to grow about 5% annually, benefiting from less pricing pressure and generic competition and shorter development cycles than human pharmaceuticals. On the underlying quarter, Elanco revenue grew just 0.9% to $792.1 million, while total company revenue rose 9.1% to $6.36 billion, boosted by higher sales of Humalog, Trulicity and Basaglar. GAAP results showed a $259.9 million loss, or 25 cents a share, versus a $1 billion profit a year earlier, but adjusted EPS of $1.50 beat the average analyst estimate of $1.30 on Thomson Reuters, with the GAAP loss tied to charges related to two acquisitions.
wsj.why_moved: Shares rose 2.9% to $91.49 in early afternoon trading the day of the report, and the article's numbers explain why directly: adjusted EPS of $1.50 beat the $1.30 analysts had modeled by a wide margin, and total revenue growth of 9.1% was driven by the core human-pharmaceutical products, Humalog, Trulicity and Basaglar, rather than by the smaller, slower-growing Elanco unit. The confirmation of the Elanco IPO plan discussed above likely reinforced the positive reaction by giving investors a concrete timeline and structure, a sub-20% stake, filing expected within weeks, process complete in the second half of the year, after nine months of uncertainty since the October 2017 review was first announced. The Zoetis comparison cited in the article, a business trading near all-time highs at a rich multiple, offers a benchmark for what a public Elanco could be valued at, which may have added to enthusiasm beyond the quarter's core results alone.

The world’s biggest retailer has spent to make its U.S. stores more efficient and pleasant. GETTY IMAGES
Wal-Mart Stores Inc. is reaping the benefits of spending heavily to improve stores and
draw shoppers, a sign that retailers need to work hard to lure customers in an era of
fast-changing shopping behavior.
Wal-Mart, previously the poster child of staid retailers, reported strong second-
quarter results on Thursday, with sales at established stores up for the eighth
consecutive quarter and more shoppers visiting for the seventh period in a row.
The report followed weak sales from rival Target Corp. TGT -1.66% and mixed results
from other U.S. chains. Analysts said Americans are willing to shop, but favor stores

This week home-improvement chain Home Depot Inc. reported a 4.7% jump in sales at
established stores for its latest quarter, while TJX Cos., the parent of T.J. Maxx,
HomeGoods and other off-price chains, posted a 4% increase. However, many apparel
retailers and department stores have reported lower foot traffic and falling sales.
Target Chief Executive Brian Cornell said patchy consumer spending was to blame.
Macy’s Inc.’s M -2.22% executives pointed to encroaching competition from online

year.
A strong job market, wage gains and low gasoline prices are boosting household
budgets. But retailers touting clothes, electronics and household staples from physical
stores are struggling to adjust to other changes in consumer behavior.
Americans are being asked to spend more on health care as costs rise, and are
choosing to spend more on services such as travel and entertainment. And online
retailers, mainly Amazon.com Inc., are gobbling up more spending. In the first seven
months of the year, sales at nonstore retailers—a category that includes Amazon—
rose 10% from the year-earlier period, according to the U.S. Commerce Department,
while department stores and electronics outlets posted declines.
Wal-Mart has poured billions recently into making its U.S. stores more efficient and
pleasant, boosting employee wages and improving e-commerce operations as it tries
to fend off Amazon and keep shoppers happy to roam its 3,500 giant U.S. Supercenters
for paper towels or milk.
“With transitions like this you tend to gain first with existing customers,” said Wal-
Mart U.S. CEO Greg Foran, on a conference call to discuss earnings Thursday. Those
customers are visiting more often and “I think they are putting an extra item in the

previous quarter. Sales were hurt by deflationary food prices, executives said.

Consumers are still “a little more cautious than the numbers might indicate,” said

By Sarah Nassauer
Updated Feb. 21, 2017 at 9:48 am ET
Wal-Mart Stores Inc. reported strong sales over the winter holiday season, a marked
contrast with the weak numbers posted by many brick-and-mortar competitors
including Target Corp. TGT -1.66% and Macy’s Inc. M -2.22%
Wal-Mart said Tuesday that sales in stores open at least 12 months rose 1.8% in the
quarter ended Jan. 31, the 10th consecutive quarter of gains. More shoppers came to
its stores and spent more when they did. But the strength of the company’s U.S. store
business continues to come at the expense of profits, which fell 18% in the quarter.
The retail behemoth is investing billions to raise U.S. store worker wages, lower prices
and expand e-commerce sales to better compete with Amazon.com Inc. AMZN 3.97%
“Rapid advances in technology mean we need to become more of a digital enterprise—
and that’s what we’re doing,” Chief Executive Doug McMillon said in a prerecorded
call to discuss the results.
Still, Wal-Mart’s global e-commerce sales growth decelerated compared with the
previous quarter. Online sales rose 16% including the first full quarter of sales from
Jet.com Inc., which Wal-Mart purchased in September. In the previous quarter e-
commerce sales rose 21%.

The Moody's analyst's comment that margins held steady despite heavy investment spending speaks directly to a recurring investor concern about Walmart in this period, that its growth was coming at the cost of profitability, suggesting this quarter's results specifically addressed that worry, which likely reinforced the positive reaction beyond the traffic and e-commerce numbers alone. Wal-Mart Stores Inc. said sales rose in its latest quarter. PATRICK T. FALLON/BLOOMBERG NEWS
Wal-Mart Stores Inc.’s sales rose in the latest quarter, boosted by an e-commerce
surge and strong grocery sales, as the world’s largest retailer continues to brush off
the malaise afflicting some competitors.
But as has become typical for brick-and-mortar stores, the growth came at a cost. The
company invested in lowering prices, improving stores and driving online sales, and
in the quarter its expenses rose and margins fell.

“Our customers are responding to the improvements in stores and online,” Wal-Mart

The article frames this as bucking a broader wave of downbeat retail results that week, including Target and TJX, with Home Depot the other notable exception, aided by hurricane-recovery spending. Grocery, roughly half of Walmart's U.S. revenue, posted its strongest same-store-sales growth in more than five years, an effort the article ties to Amazon's Whole Foods acquisition earlier in the year and the expansion of online grocery pickup to 1,100 stores. U.S. e-commerce sales rose 50% year over year, decelerating slightly from 60% the prior quarter; Walmart projected full-year global e-commerce sales of $17.5 billion against nearly half a trillion dollars in total annual revenue. Morgan Stanley analyst Simeon Gutman said any way you slice it Walmart seems expensive given margin pressure, but also credited investors for embracing a new narrative that positions Walmart to compete with Amazon, adding that some of the share gain likely reflected money rotating out of consumer-staples and other retail stocks; GlobalData's Neil Saunders called the growth impressive and evidence Walmart is trying to extend its lead, not just defend it. The company also disclosed it was close to settling a multiyear foreign-bribery probe tied to Mexico and other countries, booking a $283 million charge on top of $870 million already spent on the investigation and compliance upgrades. The acknowledgment that some gains reflected capital rotating away from other retail and staples stocks suggests the move reflected both company-specific results and a broader sector reallocation described in the piece, rather than the same-store-sales beat alone.

Adjusted EPS came in at $1.33, below the $1.37 analysts polled by Thomson Reuters had expected; full-year EPS guidance of $4.75-$5.00 was described as lower than some had anticipated, driven mainly by a smaller-than-expected benefit from the new U.S. tax law, which added $207 million to the quarter versus a figure still being finalized, plus 60 cents of dilution from closing 63 Sam's Clubs and other discontinued items. The article situates this within a broader industry response to Amazon and Walmart, noting Albertsons' planned purchase of the remainder of Rite Aid and Target's December purchase of same-day delivery service Shipt, both explicitly framed by executives as competitive responses.
wsj.why_moved: The article is explicit and detailed about the cause of the roughly 10% one-day decline: the e-commerce growth deceleration to 23% from over 50% in each of the prior three quarters, tied directly to the inventory misjudgment described above that left online warehouses short of basic goods, combined with adjusted EPS missing the Thomson Reuters consensus by four cents. Because Walmart shares had, per the article, skyrocketed earlier in the year on high expectations for online growth specifically, the deceleration in that one metric was enough to erase confidence built on a narrower thesis, which is why a quarter with continued same-store-sales growth, a 14th straight increase, and still-strong holiday spending nonetheless produced the stock's worst day since 1988. The lower-than-expected full-year EPS guidance, driven partly by a smaller tax-law benefit than hoped and partly by one-time Sam's Club closure costs, added a forward-looking disappointment on top of the backward-looking e-commerce miss, consistent with the decline holding steady across the 1-, 2-, 3-, and 5-day windows, all in the -9.5% to -11.7% range, rather than reversing.

By Sarah Nassauer
Updated Feb. 20, 2018 at 5:11 pm ET
Walmart posted a profit of $2.18 billion, or 73 cents a share, compared with a profit of $3.76 billion a year ago. ELISE
AMENDOLA/ASSOCIATED PRESS
Walmart Inc., which had improved its e-commerce operations over the past year in its
fierce battle with Amazon.com Inc., stumbled in the fourth quarter after misjudging
its online inventory for the holiday season, sending its stock tumbling and slicing
more than $31 billion from its market capitalization.
Walmart shares fell more than 10% Tuesday, with the downdraft pulling many retail

stocks along. It was the biggest one-day drop in stock price since 1988 for the world’s
largest retailer.
Walmart Chief Executive Doug McMillon said that as holiday goods like TVs and toys
flooded Walmart’s e-commerce warehouses, they squeezed the room for everyday
items such as toilet paper. That meant the retailer ran out of some items, hurting
online sales. “Our in-stock for basic items suffered as a result,” Mr. McMillon said.
Walmart also said its U.S. profit margins were hit by lower prices and by more sales
shifting to the web. Online sales are generally less profitable than those in stores.
The retailer’s shares had skyrocketed this year, boosted by high expectations for its
online growth. On Tuesday, Walmart reported a 2.6% gain in overall sales for the
quarter ended Jan. 31, for its 14th consecutive quarter of growth. But its U.S. online
sales grew only 23% in the quarter, in contrast with three previous quarters of more
than 50% growth.
That wasn’t enough for investors. “This quarter did not live up to those high
expectations,” said Simeon Gutman, a retail analyst for Morgan Stanley.
Still, Mr. McMillon on Tuesday expressed confidence. “Looking ahead, we expect e-
commerce growth to increase from the fourth-quarter level as we enter the new year,”
he told analysts.
E-commerce accounts for less than 4% of Walmart’s over-$500 billion in annual
revenue. Walmart expects online sales to grow 40% for the current fiscal year, which
ends next Jan. 31.
Walmart has been working quickly to build its e-commerce business in recent years
and head off Amazon.com’s dominance online. It has shifted spending to invest in its
web operations, including faster home delivery and e-commerce acquisitions. It also
has spent to improve existing stores, while it cut jobs and tightened expense controls.

The company closed 10% of U.S. Sam’s Club locations earlier this year and has slowed

The retail industry more broadly is struggling to meet the e-commerce challenge. On
Tuesday, grocer Albertsons Cos. said it plans to buy the rest of Rite Aid Corp. that isn’t
already being sold to Walgreens Boots Alliance Inc. The chief executives of the
companies said in interviews Monday the merger is the best way for them to compete
against the increasing threaten from Amazon and an emboldened Walmart. Target
Corp. bought same-day delivery service Shipt in December.
Walmart’s acquisition of online store Jet in September 2016 was a big part of the
retailer’s e-commerce strategy, and new features like free two-day shipping on more
items and an expanded online selection helped boost online sales quickly.
Walmart has added hundreds of online grocery pickup locations at stores, which are
counted in the e-commerce sales figures.
On Tuesday, Walmart signaled a shift in its online strategy, saying it would put more
focus on acquiring new customers for its main Walmart website, which has national
brand recognition, and would slow marketing spending for Jet, which caters to
higher-income, urban shoppers.
That will lead to slowing sales for Jet temporarily, Mr. McMillon said.
“E-commerce growth, it ebbs and flows,” at all retailers, said Brendan Witcher,
principal analyst at Forrester Research. The latest quarter indicated e-commerce
growth at Walmart remained healthy, he added.
Walmart said Tuesday earnings per share would come in between $4.75 and $5.00 for
the fiscal year, lower than some had been anticipating, mainly due to a smaller-than-
expected benefit from recent tax-code changes. The company said the new U.S. tax law
added $207 million to earnings in its latest quarter, but that amount could shift in
future quarters as the company completes its analysis.

Penney, Nordstrom and Home Depot in the context of a strong U.S. economy, low unemployment and rising wages, helping traditional chains recapture business from online rivals, while cautioning that not every retailer benefited, with J.C. Adjusted EPS of $1.29 beat the $1.22 analysts had estimated, and revenue of $128 billion topped the $126 billion consensus estimate; same-store sales rose 4.5% against an analyst estimate of just 2.4%, which the column identifies as the specific figure that sent the stock up 10% in morning trading. The column frames the central analytical question as whether the improvement reflects genuine gains in Walmart's online operations or simply a strong consumer economy, arguing that investors underestimated the economy's contribution, something the column says appears obvious only in hindsight, while still crediting Walmart's e-commerce execution. E-commerce head Marc Lore said a redesigned website improved navigation, which the column says has drawn in more brand partners and driven more consumer traffic; Walmart said it expects 40% e-commerce growth for the full year, and the company raised its full-year EPS guidance to $4.90-$5.05 from $4.75-$5, excluding any impact from the pending Flipkart acquisition. The column contrasts Walmart's reaction with peers reporting the same week: Macy's also posted good numbers but had its third-worst day on record, while J.C. Penney, which reported weak results, suffered its worst decline since at least 1972, a divergence the column attributes to Walmart having been down for the year heading into the report while Macy's had already rallied significantly, meaning investors were chasing what they saw as the next big growth story in Walmart specifically.

Because Walmart shares had been down for the year heading into this report, the column's explicit contrast with Macy's, which was already up significantly and fell despite similarly good numbers, the positive surprise had more room to move the stock than it might have for a stock already priced for good news. The column does flag risks going forward, including rising prices potentially cutting into profits and Flipkart-related expenses, echoing the dilution guidance disclosed in the prior quarter's report, but explicitly treats those as worries for another day rather than factors relevant to this quarter's reaction, consistent with the sustained gain across the 1-, 2-, 3-, and 5-day windows, 8.53%, 7.24%, 7.47%, and 4.89%, rather than an immediate reversal.

Company boosts sales, profit forecast for the year as demand grows for construction and
mining equipment
By Bob Tita and Andrew Tangel
Updated Oct. 24, 2017 at 4:46 pm ET
Caterpillar’s fortunes have improved over the past year after a long slump caused by a downturn in the global
commodities markets and a slowdown in construction. MIKE BLAKE/REUTERS
Caterpillar Inc. CAT -2.05% raised its sales and profit forecast for the year amid
growing demand for construction and mining equipment and the company’s new
emphasis on boosting profit margins.
The world’s largest producer of bulldozers, excavators, and other earth-moving
machinery experienced widespread improvement in sales during the third quarter.
Caterpillar’s fortunes have improved over the past year after a yearslong slump

caused by a downturn in the global commodities markets and a slowdown in

months, gaining 5% Tuesday to close at a record $138.24.
Slow-growing economies around the world, a still-fragile mining sector and the
absence of a significant infrastructure-spending plan in the U.S., however, still
threaten to undermine the prolonged upturn in machinery demand that company
executives and investors have been expecting.
The manufacturer based in Deerfield, Ill., said Tuesday that its dealers stepped up
their purchases of equipment to restock inventories in response to rising customer
demand, especially from an improving oil and natural-gas industry in North America
and for large excavators in China. Construction-equipment sales in North America
rose 31% from a year earlier and mining-equipment sales increased 28%.
Chief Executive Jim Umpleby, who took over as CEO on Jan. 1, has said a prime focus
under his watch would be profitable growth, rather than only increasing revenue and
market share, with an eye toward parts and services. The third-quarter operating
margin on machinery and engines was 14%, up from 7.8% a year earlier, reflecting the
company’s emphasis on profit expansion. Caterpillar said it intends to maintain the
lower cost structure from years of reducing employee rolls and closing plants during
the slump to improve profit as its markets recover.
“We believe our margins going forward will be higher than they’ve historically been,”
said Chief Financial Officer Brad Halverson in an interview Tuesday.
Mr. Halverson said several rounds of layoffs, while difficult, have put the company on a
better long-term footing.
“They were very hard—hard for us to figure out how to do it but, more importantly
probably, hard on our employees,” he said. “But now we’re seeing the benefit of that in
terms of the efficiency of our operations.”

wsj.summary_analysis: Caterpillar reported that annual revenue jumped 18% to $45.5 billion in 2017, breaking a four-year streak of declining sales, with the largest gains coming from North America and, in Asia-Pacific, from China amid increased building construction and infrastructure investment. CFO Brad Halverson told analysts "The global economy is the strongest it has been in several years, with nearly every region of the world expected to grow in 2018," though the company did not offer a formal 2018 revenue forecast. Caterpillar reported a fourth-quarter loss of $1.3 billion, or $2.18 a share, versus a year-earlier loss of $1.17 billion, or $2 a share, driven by a one-time charge tied to the new U.S. tax law, largely from a mandatory tax on stockpiled overseas profit; on an adjusted basis excluding the tax charge, the company earned $2.16 a share, above analyst expectations, on quarterly revenue that rose 35% to $12.9 billion versus an expected $11.98 billion. Caterpillar said it expects an effective tax rate of 24% this year, down from 28% in 2017, and CEO Jim Umpleby, asked whether the new law might help resolve an ongoing federal tax dispute involving the company's Swiss subsidiary, said, "It's an ongoing discussion with the government. We're cooperating, and we hope to get to a resolution in an expeditious manner." The company reported a 15% operating margin for 2017, up from 5% the prior year, reflecting Umpleby's continued focus on profitable growth, and added 4,800 U.S. jobs during the year, reversing several years of domestic cuts, bringing its U.S. headcount to 50,500.

It isn’t alone in navigating rough waters. Rival Honeywell International Inc. startled

Boston-based GE, which makes a range of industrial equipment from jet engines to MRI
machines, is under increasing pressure to show that the company’s 2015 pivot away from

That task may be more complicated thanks to Trian Fund Management LP, the activist

that sell equipment for pumping and drilling.

to standardize product offerings to reduce expenses. Chief Financial Officer Jeffrey

boss’s strategy for boosting results.

at the helm. The bad news from investors’ point of view was that GE tempered profit
expectations for the current year and said investors would have to wait until mid-
November for CEO-designate John Flannery to discuss the outlook for 2018.
It is unusual for a big company, especially one such as GE that is being pressured by an

“This is a strange situation,” said Nicholas Heymann, an analyst with William Blair &

2017 is set and that he is “not worried that we’re going to be, you know, dead in the
water in the meantime.”
Mr. Immelt will step down at the end of this month after 16 years as CEO.
GE is under increasing pressure to show that its pivot away from financial services,
big bets on the oil industry and a renewed focus on making jet engines and power
turbines would be good for investors.
Shares fell 2.9% to $25.91 each in Friday trading.
Mr. Flannery, who formerly ran GE’s health-care unit, is meeting with small groups of
investors and visiting the business units of the roughly 300,000-person company.
Jeffrey Bornstein, GE’s chief financial officer, defended the timeline in an interview
and said the company would have to “play through” any uncertainty created by a
review that includes “testing everything we believe.”

Industrial segment cash flow swung to a positive $1.5 billion after a $1.6 billion shortfall in the first quarter, and the company cut $593 million in industrial costs during the quarter, bringing year-to-date cuts to $670 million and keeping it on pace for its $1 billion annual savings target; GE backed its full-year guidance of $12 billion to $14 billion in cash flow and $1.60 to $1.70 in earnings per share. The piece quotes Citigroup analyst Andrew Kaplowitz saying the results 'may not be enough to significantly alleviate negative investor sentiment,' and notes Immelt's imminent replacement by John Flannery, who was expected to conduct a comprehensive business review and deliver updated 2018 guidance in mid-November.

Flannery told investors "Our results are unacceptable to say the least," said he was reviewing whether GE could sustain its current dividend, and announced a plan to sell more than $20 billion of assets over one to two years plus cut an additional $1 billion in expenses next year, bringing total planned two-year cost reductions to $3 billion. Third-quarter profit fell to $1.8 billion from $2 billion a year earlier as the company absorbed hefty restructuring charges; adjusted per-share earnings fell to 29 cents from 32 cents, well below Wall Street's roughly 49-cent expectation, even as revenue rose 14% to $33.5 billion, beating a $32.56 billion estimate, boosted by the Baker Hughes oil-and-gas merger. Flannery, in an interview, said he was surprised by the weak results from the power business — GE's largest by revenue — blaming prior management for overestimating demand and carrying too much inventory: "I'm disappointed in the power business. Deeply... We have not run the business well of late." Analyst Scott Davis of Melius Research said "Expected bad. Got bad," adding that "Pressure to break this up just went through the roof." Separately, incoming CFO Jamie Miller promised a "back to basics" overhaul of GE's financial reporting — including scrapping the adjusted-earnings metric and revising how cash flow is presented — after Wall Street analysts had long described GE's accounting as "aggressive"; the company also disclosed a $500 million correction to cash flow reported earlier in the year, tied to misclassified derivative hedge settlements, and said it would restate 2016 and 2017 results under new revenue-recognition rules for long-term service contracts.

GE’s Other Problem: Complex Financial Reporting
GE’s next finance chief promises to get ‘back to basics’ with the company’s financial
reporting
By Charley Grant
Oct. 20, 2017 at 10:01 pm ET
A GE logo sits on a panel inside the General Electric power plant in Veresegyhaz, Hungary, on June 13. Wall Street
analysts have long expressed frustration with GE’s presentation of financial results, typically describing the
accounting as ‘aggressive.’ AKOS STILLER/BLOOMBERG NEWS
General Electric Co.’s next finance chief promised Friday to get “back to basics” with
the conglomerate’s financial reporting, after the latest quarterly results highlighted
the complexity of the company’s bookkeeping.
Sharp revisions to the company’s forecasts for the current year, just three months
after the company had backed them, raised fresh concerns among investors and
analysts about the way the company measures its performance.
https://www.wsj.com/articles/ges-other-problem-complex-financial-reporting-1508551271 Page 1 of 4
GE’s Other Problem: Complex Financial Reporting - WSJ 2026-08-29, 5:26 PM
The financial reports will likely be a focus of new CEO John Flannery and incoming
Chief Financial Officer Jamie Miller. In meeting with investors in recent months, the
new boss was told that the muddy reporting needed to change. In his letter to
employees on his first day, Mr. Flannery said he heard investors “loud and clear.”
GE GE -0.04% presents its financials to investors in unusual ways. Besides reporting
traditional earnings per share under generally accepted accounting principles, GE
also reports that figure on an adjusted basis that excludes results of businesses that
might be sold in the future.
The Boston-based company also reports a key cash-flow metric differently from most
public companies. The company adjusts the figure to exclude taxes on the company’s
deals, as well as costs to fund its employee pension plan.
Wall Street analysts have long expressed frustration with GE’s presentation of
financial results, typically describing the accounting as “aggressive.” In a recent note
to clients, William Blair analyst Nicholas Heymann expressed hope that Mr. Flannery’s
review would include “replacing aspirational with tangible pragmatic operating
targets and simplifying GE’s accounting.”
Ms. Miller promised changes on a conference call with Wall Street analysts on Friday,
including scrapping its adjusted earnings figure and reporting cash flow in line with
industry standards.
“We’re really looking at, how can we report in a much cleaner way, just a much
simpler presentation of what you see? I’d kind of call it a back-to-the-basics
approach,” she said.
Ms. Miller, who previously ran the company’s transportation unit, will take over from
Finance Chief Jeff Bornstein on Nov. 1. She joined GE in 2008 as chief accounting
officer and previously was a finance executive at insurer Anthem Inc. and a partner at
PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP.
https://www.wsj.com/articles/ges-other-problem-complex-financial-reporting-1508551271 Page 2 of 4

Mr. Bornstein told investors Friday he was leaving because of the company’s poor
performance. “We are not living up to our own standards or those of investors, and
the buck stops with me,” he said.
On Friday, GE cut its profit targets for the year by a third and sliced its forecast for
cash flow by half. The company’s ability to generate cash has been a question among
investors, nervous about its ability to support its $8 billion annual dividend. Those
fears have been heightened since the first quarter of the year, when GE surprised
investors with a negative cash flow.
One focus of investors has been the ability of the company to use its GE Capital
business to smooth earnings of the more-cyclical industrial business. As GE has sold
down its financial operations, its overall financial performance has declined.
GE executives told investors the company’s GE Capital business didn’t pay a dividend
to the parent company—and would halt any such payments until the company
completes an actuarial analysis of claims reserves in the company’s long-term-care
reinsurance business.
Mr. Bornstein also disclosed the company had made a $500 million correction to the
cash flow reported in the first half of the year. He said it had been underreported
because derivative hedge settlements had been incorrectly classified.
The company has made other changes to its reporting in recent history. In May GE
changed the way it calculates the rate that profits convert into free cash flow, a closely
watched metric for industrial companies.
The effects of the change resulted in more-impressive figures. GE reported a
conversion rate of 91% for 2016 under the new method, instead of 76% under the old
method.

We have a long way to go but the mission is clear." HEARD ON THE STREET Follow
GE Looks Ugly in Its Underwear
GE’s new transparency is welcome, but a focus on cash shows the company is probably
no bargain even after its swoon
By Spencer Jakab
Updated Jan. 24, 2018 at 4:11 pm ET
Investors, who have grown numb to bad news at GE, actually celebrated the company’s weak earnings on
Wednesday. THIBAULT CAMUS/ASSOCIATED PRESS
Sunlight may be the best disinfectant, but General Electric is learning that it can leave
some nasty burns—particularly for those who have spent too much time in the shade.
Investors, who have grown numb to bad news at GE, actually celebrated the
company’s weak earnings on Wednesday and only sold off shares after the disclosure
of a Securities and Exchange Commission probe into GE’s accounting. What has
become increasingly clear as the bad news mounts at GE is that the company’s
business is pretty weak.
https://www.wsj.com/articles/ge-looks-ugly-in-its-underwear-1516816477 Page 1 of 3
GE Looks Ugly in Its Underwear - WSJ 2026-08-29, 5:28 PM
The SEC review concerns not only the recent bombshell about the company’s $7.5
billion charge for a legacy insurance business but also revenue recognition in its
industrial business. That latter item, including so-called contract assets, may lead to
restatements of past financials.
While GE is a serial tweaker of financial disclosure, the company is doing the right
thing by shifting its focus to more transparent free cash flow. Unfortunately, it paints
an unflattering picture. Even after its shares fell 44% in the past year, and even using
2016 financial figures, before the recent collapse in earnings in its power unit, a
comparison with industrial competitors hardly suggests a screaming bargain. GE’s
ratio of enterprise value to free cash flow is 31% dearer than the median of eight peers.
And, even as GE posted its best return on invested capital in a decade that year, it was
the second-weakest of that group in 2016. Today’s numbers, of course, look worse, and
there doesn’t appear to be anything in the near future to turn things around.
GE ended the year with net cash of a little more than $11 billion in its industrial units.
Cutting its dividend in half will preserve a little more than $4 billion this year, but
suspending dividends from its GE Capital unit for the foreseeable future as it plugs its
insurance hole will offset those savings. And while GE sees its cash balance excluding
62.5% owned Baker Hughes climbing to about $15 billion by the end of 2018, that
includes an anticipated $4 billion to $5 billion in proceeds from disposals. In other
words, the actual business of selling and servicing stuff probably won’t generate any
net cash this year.
In addition to the uncertainty about how much contract assets flattered past earnings,
even cash flow may have been boosted. GE Capital often buys receivables from its
industrial units so cash is received more promptly. As the finance business conserves
cash to make statutory insurance contributions, that could create a short-term hiccup.
GE Capital also may be less willing to underwrite riskier deals for industrial
equipment, sapping revenue.
It says something about GE that horrific earnings and an SEC probe knocked only 3%
https://www.wsj.com/articles/ge-looks-ugly-in-its-underwear-1516816477 Page 2 of 3
GE Looks Ugly in Its Underwear - WSJ 2026-08-29, 5:28 PM
off the share price. Wednesday’s news could have been worse. It also speaks volumes
that bargain hunters have avoided this wounded blue chip. There clearly was a lot less
there than met the eye.

wsj.summary_analysis: GE reported a first-quarter net loss of $1.18 billion, driven by a $1.5 billion charge tied to a potential settlement of a Justice Department probe into WMC Mortgage, a subprime-lending business once housed in GE Capital — a risk the Journal had flagged the previous month. Excluding the charge, the company said profits were ahead of plan; GE cut $805 million of industrial costs in the quarter and reaffirmed its 2018 financial targets, including per-share earnings of $1.00 to $1.07. CEO John Flannery, nine months into a strategic review, said he was "encouraged by the progress" and aimed to "earn back investor trust in 2018," while promising more detail on a possible company breakup by the end of June; he also declined to firmly recommit to the dividend, saying his view "continues to evolve." Adjusted earnings of 16 cents a share beat the 11-cent analyst estimate, and revenue rose 7% to $28.66 billion, beating a $27.45 billion estimate, aided by the prior year's Baker Hughes oil-and-gas merger. The power division continued to struggle: revenue fell 9%, profit fell 38%, and orders dropped 29%, with the company reporting no customers yet for its new H-class turbine and CFO Jamie Miller saying "The pace of the market decline is greater than the near-term benefit of those [cost-cutting] actions." Profits and sales rose in the aviation and health-care units, with aviation profit up 26%. The companion Heard on the Street column called the quarter "the first time in months" GE news wasn't dismal, noting there was no fresh bad news about GE Capital or new accounting-probe disclosures, but cautioned that the rally merely returned shares to where they traded in mid-March and that GE remained "a long way from health," with the power business and GE Capital still "unfixed."

Both pieces attribute the initial pop to relief that the quarter held no fresh negative surprises — the dividend was untouched, full-year guidance was reaffirmed, and the mortgage charge had already been previewed by prior reporting — rather than to any actual improvement in the still-struggling power division, which the Heard column notes showed no concrete sign of turning around.

HEARD ON THE STREET Follow
No Bad News Counts as Good News at GE
Conglomerate’s recovery will hinge on concrete signs of improvement in cash flow at its
power unit
By Spencer Jakab
April 20, 2018 at 11:13 am ET
General Electric Co. on Friday beat analysts’ consensus estimate for quarterly earnings and reaffirmed its full-year
guidance. BRENDAN MCDERMID/REUTERS
For the first time in months, an announcement from General Electric wasn’t dismal.
Yet the bounce in the troubled conglomerate’s share price Friday morning merely
returned it to where it was in the middle of last month. Recall that just three years ago
investors cheered the company’s radical downsizing of GE Capital and its plan to
return $90 billion in cash by the end of 2018. The sad reality is the cash return was just
$50 billion and GE’s loss in market value has been twice as much.
https://www.wsj.com/articles/no-bad-news-counts-as-good-news-at-ge-1524237214 Page 1 of 4
No Bad News Counts as Good News at GE - WSJ 2026-08-29, 5:29 PM
But that was then and this is now. The fact that GE didn’t eliminate its remaining
dividend, beat analyst’s consensus estimate for first-quarter earnings per share and
even reaffirmed its full-year guidance of $1.00 to $1.07 a share on Friday counts as
great news relative to the market’s radically recalibrated expectations.

The other big positive was there was no fresh bad news about GE Capital, no new
details about investigations of the company’s accounting and the company didn’t
make any desperate moves to shore up cash. With $20 billion in asset sales under way
and the company projecting adjusted industrial free cash flow of $6 billion to $7
billion, a cash crisis now looks less likely.
Investors were almost euphoric, bidding up GE shares more than 7%, though they
https://www.wsj.com/articles/no-bad-news-counts-as-good-news-at-ge-1524237214 Page 2 of 4
No Bad News Counts as Good News at GE - WSJ 2026-08-29, 5:29 PM
quickly sobered up and the gains ebbed from there.
The reality is GE is a long way from health. GE Capital and GE Power are still unfixed
and the company’s record of selling assets isn’t impressive. Aside from successful
asset sales, the best evidence that new chief John Flannery’s turnaround plan is
working would be an improvement in how efficiently the Power division, the
company’s biggest by revenue, converts so-called contract assets—long-term
equipment and service contracts—into cash. There was scant sign of that in Friday’s
announcement and the company noted that the power market “continues to be
challenging and hard to predict.”
Without any sign of if or when that unit will turn around, the safest assumption is to
gauge GE’s fair value on current levels of profitability. Applying industry multiples of
earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization to GE’s five main
industrial businesses plus the market price of its 62.5% owned oil services unit, there
isn’t much reason to chase GE’s stock above $15. This assumes that GE Capital’s value
is zero, which, while that sounds harsh, is better than some fear.
As invigorating as Friday’s results were, GE cleared a low bar. Now comes the hard
part, and it is likely to be a long, treacherous slog.

The order softness hits GE’s cash flow because payments from customers while the

wsj.summary_analysis: U.S. shoppers continued cutting back spending on household staples, and P&G said it could not explain why. The company reported fiscal first-quarter organic sales growth of just 1%, driven almost entirely by emerging markets, with CFO Jon Moeller telling investors "We've been unable to put our finger on why this has been," and adding "I've heard theories but nothing to explain the broad slowdown." P&G estimated global consumer-staples industry growth at about 2.3% for the quarter, down from 2.5% the prior period, with U.S. growth essentially flat; rival Unilever also reported weaker-than-expected sales that same week. Moeller explicitly discounted several theories floated for the U.S. slowdown, including private-label gains, trading down to cheaper brands, reduced spending by Hispanic shoppers amid immigration-policy concerns, and a shift of spending toward services, saying of the latter: "the idea that, 'I want a cellphone so I'm not going to wash my hair,' doesn't make sense to me." He suggested retailer-driven price cuts amid competitive and online pressure might partly explain the decline. Profit rose 5%, helped by a turnaround in China — where organic sales rose 8% and Moeller hosted the analyst call from P&G's Guangzhou office to highlight the progress, two years after CEO David Taylor had publicly acknowledged the company lost its footing there. Profit rose to $2.85 billion, or $1.06 a share, from $2.71 billion, or 96 cents a share; total sales rose to $16.65 billion from $16.52 billion. The results came as activist investor Nelson Peltz narrowly missed winning a board seat in a preliminary vote tally, after a proxy fight that cost at least $60 million, the most expensive in U.S. history.

Netflix reports quarterly earnings Monday. ASSOCIATED PRESS
Slowing growth, rising costs and increasing competition: That is usually a recipe for
trouble on Wall Street.
Then there is Netflix Inc.
The video-streaming service’s meteoric stock rise has defied logic, thanks to its
growing popularity and original programming. That has overshadowed the steep rise
in the cost of doing business and slowing U.S. subscriber growth. More channels are
going direct-to-consumer through the Internet and rivals such as Hulu and

Netflix’s stock has surged more than 300% in three years, repeatedly proving
naysayers wrong on the ride higher. But with shares waffling in volatile fashion in
recent months, doubts about the rally’s sustainability continue to grow. Ahead
of Monday’s earnings report, the skepticism might be warranted.
Analysts expect earnings of 3 cents a share, down from 5 cents a year earlier. Revenue
is estimated to have increased 25% to $1.97 billion. Over the past five years, Netflix has
consistently exceeded expectations, yet shares have moved up or down by at least 10%

Much of the attention is now focused on Netflix’s overseas opportunities. In January,

Still, investors shouldn’t lose sight of Netflix’s slowing domestic subscriber growth.
Netflix expects a net 1.75 million new U.S. subscribers in the first quarter, lower than

analysts project higher churn rates, particularly as grandfathered pricing comes to an
end. Slower growth and higher U.S. churn matter as domestic subscribers may remain
more profitable than international ones.

third consecutive quarter these costs exceeded $10 billion. They were lower by about
one-third two years ago. And Netflix’s net operating cash flow turned negative last
year for the first time since 2000.
Fetching more than 200 times projected earnings for the next 12 months, the stock
trades more on faith than fundamentals.
The product is great, but this stock isn’t worth bingeing on.

Shares fall as video service reports lowest number of new additions in two years
By Shalini Ramachandran and Maria Armental
WSJ PRO Updated July 18, 2016 at 10:33 pm ET
Netflix Inc. NFLX 2.47% on Monday reported its weakest subscriber expansion in
three years, as the streaming-video company suffered a sharp slowdown in net
customer additions in the U.S. and abroad.
Shares of Netflix, down 14% this year, fell 13% in after-hours trading.
During the second quarter, Netflix added 160,000 subscribers in the U.S. and 1.52
million in international markets, below expectations of 500,000 in the U.S. and 2
million abroad. It ended the quarter with 83.18 million subscribers.
The Los Gatos, Calif.-based company said price increases for existing subscribers led
to higher service cancellations and contributed to its weaker-than-expected results.
In the U.S., more than half its customers had been “grandfathered” under lower prices
but will be phased into higher rates this year.
“Whatever the price is for something, people don’t like it to go up,” Chief Executive
Reed Hastings said on a videoconference call with analysts. “We apologize for the
volatility; I know it’s not easy on everyone,” he said. “The big picture is very much
intact.”

For the third quarter, Netflix projected a modest increase of 300,000 U.S. customers,

Netflix Jump in New Users Fuels After-Hours Stock
Surge
The better-than-expected results boosts stock price, eases concerns about user growth
By Shalini Ramachandran and Maria Armental
Updated Oct. 17, 2016 at 7:25 pm ET
Netflix Inc. NFLX 2.35% blew through its forecast for subscriber additions in the
September quarter, reassuring investors who were skittish about the streaming
giant’s growth trajectory and sending its shares soaring 20% in after-hours trading.
The better-than-expected performance came mainly in international markets, where
the company has completed a massive, near-global expansion this year. Netflix is
making a big bet that the same mix of edgy original content and library programming
that has taken the U.S. media world by storm will translate overseas.
The company added 3.2 million international subscribers in the quarter, compared
with its guidance of 2 million.
In the U.S., Netflix added 370,000 subscribers in the period. That is more than 20%
ahead of its forecast of 300,000, though sharply below the year-ago quarter’s 880,000
additions, reflecting how the U.S. streaming market is maturing as more consumers
sign up for Netflix, Amazon.com, Hulu and other services.
Wall Street’s reaction shows that the company’s global rollout across many territories
at once is creating a foggy business outlook—for itself and investors—and leading to a
volatile expectations game.

Last quarter, when Netflix missed its internal estimates for subscriber growth, Netflix
Chief Executive Reed Hastings apologized on the call to investors for the volatility of
Netflix’s stock, which sank 13% after the results. On Monday, as Netflix shares soared,
Mr. Hastings smiled and said: “We can all see it’s time for me to apologize for the
volatility again.”
Shares surged nearly 20% to $119.35 in after-hours trading. Before that, the stock had
fallen 13% this year as the streaming video giant has struggled to keep up with
investors’ growth expectations.
“This is a weird year,” said MoffettNathanson analyst Michael Nathanson. “In some
ways, we’re being swung around by our inability to forecast what’s a brand new
market, which is the rest of the world.”
Despite the subscriber beat this quarter, he said “we’re in the camp that we think

international is not all it’s cracked up to be,” due to the uneven nature of internet

Longtime Netflix investor Zevenbergen Capital Investments takes the opposite view.
It has taken advantage of recent dips in Netflix’s shares to buy, and says it’s in the
stock for the “long term.”
“We realize this is a long process,” said Joe Dennison, Zevenbergen portfolio manager,
referring to the global expansion. “If you look at the bigger picture, this is the
direction the world is moving and they are really the only global player.”
Netflix’s report of 3.57 million new streaming subscribers globally, which brings its
total customer base to about 83 million paid users, comes a quarter after it reported
its weakest subscriber expansion in three years. Growing the customer base is crucial
for the company to offset its growing content costs, as it seeks to offer evermore
shows and movies to appeal to customers all over the world.
In a letter to shareholders, Netflix said the impact of its original show premieres was
“greater than anticipated” in international markets, propelling strong subscriber
numbers. The company called out “Narcos,” the Latin American drug drama, as a
show that had “positive impact” on subscriber acquisition across all of its markets.
“We’re having broad success around international,” Mr. Hastings said on a video call
with analysts. “We’re continuing to make those investments” but “we’ve got a lot of
room to go to improve the service.”
Turning a profit off the global expansion is the next challenge. Netflix said it expects to
lose more money from its international operations next quarter as it continues to
invest in original content, targeting more than 1,000 hours of original programming
next year, a roughly two-thirds increase.
The company expects content spending in 2017 to increase to $6 billion from $5 billion
this year, and it plans to take on more debt in the coming weeks.

Netflix reiterated that it expects to start delivering material global profit next year.
In the letter to shareholders, Netflix said it is going to explore opportunities to license
its shows to other online players in China, a way to build Netflix’s brand. Mr. Hastings

The video company said the revenue contribution from China licensing will be

Netflix has also been customizing its user interface in markets such as Poland and
Turkey, accepting payments in local currencies and offering local-language options

Netflix Inc.’s subscriber additions surged in the fourth quarter, fueled by an
aggressive international expansion, as the streaming giant continues to stock up on

The company added 5.12 million subscribers abroad in the period and 1.93 million in
the U.S., beating both internal and Wall Street targets and delivering the biggest
quarterly subscription growth in its history. Netflix ended the year with 93.8 million
total subscribers, including 49.4 million in the U.S.

is to keep “spreading and evangelizing this vision of internet TV.”
The streaming video giant has prioritized growth over profit as it pursues its
international rollout—it is now available in almost every country and territory—and
ramps up investments in original programming, with plans to spend $6 billion in 2017
up from $5 billion last year.
Those bets have weighed on financial results. Netflix said in a letter Wednesday to
shareholders it expects to increase profit margins gradually—with improvements
expected in the international unit this year.

wsj.summary_analysis: Netflix blew through its subscriber-growth estimate for the second quarter, ending with nearly 104 million subscribers globally after adding 5.2 million total users, far more than the 3.2 million it had projected or the 3.5 million Wall Street had expected. Revenue jumped 32% to $2.79 billion, while global operating margin was 4.6%, down from 9.7% in the first quarter. The article notes the unpredictability of Netflix's quarterly results, raising the open question of whether the surge reflected specific show releases or broader underlying momentum; in its shareholder letter, Netflix said it had underestimated the popularity of its growing programming slate, which drove subscriber growth across its major markets, citing 91 Emmy nominations this year, up from 54 in 2016, including best-drama nods for "Stranger Things," "The Crown" and "House of Cards." CEO Reed Hastings said, "When we produce an amazing show like 'Stranger Things,' that's a lot of capital upfront, and then you get a payout over many years... seeing the positive returns on that for the business as a whole is what makes us comfortable that we should continue to invest." International subscriber additions of 4.14 million beat a 2.6 million guidance figure, and U.S. additions of 1.07 million beat a 600,000 target. The sequential increase to 5.2 million adds from 5 million in the first quarter ran against normal seasonal patterns, and Netflix projected 4.4 million third-quarter additions while cautioning it had over-forecast in the past and that some growth may have been pulled forward. Second-quarter profit was $66 million, or 15 cents a share, versus $41 million, or 9 cents a share, a year earlier.

Home Depot Inc. expects a substantial drop in its effective tax rate and continued

Financial Officer Carol Tomé.
The federal tax overhaul lowered the U.S. corporate tax rate to 21%, from 35%
previously, and set the country on the path to a territorial tax system.
The world’s largest home-improvement chain forecasts its effective tax rate will fall to
26% in 2018, from 39.6% in the fiscal fourth quarter of 2017. The anticipated decline is
“a direct result of the tax law that was passed in December,” Ms. Tomé said Tuesday in
an interview with CFO Journal.
“Our projection for 26% includes the fact that we operate in 50 states,” Ms. Tomé said.
“We have state tax in that number, we have foreign tax in that number because we’re
moving to a territorial system, so when you add it all up we get 26%.”
Home Depot reported earnings of $1.8 billion for the fiscal fourth quarter of 2017, up
from $1.7 billion in the same period of 2016. Sales rose 7.5% to $23.9 billion from the
same period a year earlier. The company also reported record sales of $100.9 billion
for 2017, up 6.7% from fiscal 2016.

The column also notes that at least three of the analysts who downgraded the stock the following Wednesday cited Cisco Systems as a growing competitive threat, given Cisco's ability to bundle security technology with its broader array of networking products and services. The column's own view is that Palo Alto's struggles are partly explained by cybersecurity spending moderating from its panic-driven 2014 peak, but that the deceleration is still painful for a company that scaled from a $255 million business to a $1.4 billion one in just four years.

There was a time—not long ago—that good cybersecurity was thought to practically
sell itself.
Not so much anymore, at least if you consider the recent travails of Palo Alto
Networks. The one-time star of a new class of cybersecurity companies has seen its
once whirlwind growth rates decelerate sharply over the past year. That continued for
the fiscal second quarter reported late Tuesday, where sales grew 26% year over year
—the slowest on record. The company also forecast a growth range of 17%-20% for the

were taking longer to make their purchasing decisions. On Tuesday, the company also
called out problems with the structure of is sales force, which it promises to remedy.
Palo Alto’s share price still plunged 20% following the report.
Given that cybersecurity spending has moderated from its panic-induced levels from
2014, some of these struggles make sense. But they are still painful for a company that
scaled a $255 million business into a $1.4 billion one in just four years. And it is worth

Texas Instruments Reports Slightly Higher Profit
Chip maker’s sales fell in personal-electronics segment
By Maria Armental
April 27, 2016 at 5:44 pm ET
Texas Instruments Inc. TXN -2.96% on Wednesday reported slightly higher profit for
the first three months of the year, even as sales fell in its personal-electronics
segment.
The Dallas-based chip maker had already warned first-quarter revenue would decline
on weakness in the personal-electronics market, which includes mobile phones and
so-called wearables that integrate technology into jewelry and clothes.
Shares, up 8% over the past 12 months, rose 1.5%, to $60.80, in after-hours trading.
Founded in 1930 as Geophysical Service Inc., the company initially focused on
reflection seismography, which is used to search for oil. It now counts itself among
suppliers for Apple Inc.
TI, which makes chips used in everything from cellphones to industrial equipment,
focuses on analog chips, which have a high profit margin, and embedded processors,
the “brains” of many electronic devices from electric toothbrushes to driver-
assistance systems that help drivers, for example, to maintain adequate distance
between cars and park.
In the latest period, sales of analog chips fell 8%, to $1.88 billion, while sales of
embedded processors improved 8%, to $729 million.

wsj.summary_analysis: The article reports that Applied Materials said orders hit a 15-year high in the fiscal second quarter, prompting the semiconductor-equipment maker to project a major business rebound later in the year as those orders convert to revenue. Second-quarter results topped expectations, as did the projection for the fiscal third quarter. The company attributed the gains primarily to spending on new tools to produce memory chips using 3-D NAND -- a manufacturing approach that stacks layers of circuitry rather than shrinking individual transistors -- and to displays using organic light-emitting diode, or OLED, technology rather than liquid-crystal displays, along with strong demand from customers in China building new manufacturing capacity. CEO Gary Dickerson is quoted calling these "big inflections, big waves that we think are sustainable over the next few years." Net income declined 12% to $320 million from $364 million, though per-share earnings were flat at 29 cents because of a lower share count, on revenue essentially flat at $2.45 billion versus $2.44 billion. Orders surged 37% year over year and 52% sequentially to $3.5 billion. Excluding restructuring charges and other items, adjusted per-share profit was 34 cents versus an analyst estimate of 32 cents on $2.43 billion in revenue. For the current quarter, the company guided to 46 to 50 cents in adjusted earnings, well above the 36 cents analysts had anticipated, and to $2.84 billion in sales, above the $2.51 billion analysts had predicted.
wsj.why_moved: The article states that shares rose nearly 8% in after-hours trading. It attributes this to the 15-year-high order level -- up 37% year over year and 52% sequentially -- and to guidance for the coming quarter that came in far above what analysts had been expecting on both earnings and revenue, driven by the 3-D NAND memory tooling shift, growing OLED display demand, and Chinese capacity expansion.

Spending cycle by chip makers expected to stay strong into next year
By Dan Gallagher
Nov. 16, 2017 at 5:50 pm ET
Even Applied Materials AMAT -4.29% knows the party can’t last forever. But the
company doesn’t see the bash ending anytime soon.
In its fiscal fourth quarter earnings report Thursday, the maker of semiconductor
manufacturing gear showed revenue jumping 20% year over year to $3.97 billion. That
makes for the company’s sixth straight quarter of double-digit sales growth, helped
by strong prices for memory chips as well as growing demand for display production
equipment. Operating income hit a record of $1.1 billion, up 41% year over year.
Applied Materials gave an early peek into fiscal 2018. CEO Gary Dickerson said the
company is “confident” in delivering “strong double-digit growth” for the year. The
first quarter, ending in January, is expected to see revenue grow about 25% at the
midpoint of the company’s forecast, exceeding the 21% growth expected by analysts.
Chip equipment is a highly cyclical business that depends on a handful of large
customers who tend to curtail their spending quickly when demand shifts. That
dynamic hasn’t gone away, but the largest chip makers are still working to catch up
with soaring demand as well as update their manufacturing lines with the latest
processes. Last month, Samsung Electronics boosted its planned capital expenditures
to more than $26 billion in semiconductor and display for this year. That compares
with about $11.4 billion spent in these areas last year, estimates Wes Twigg of

Profit reached $508.3 million, or 76 cents a share, up from $474.6 million, or 69 cents, a year earlier, and comfortably ahead of the company's own prior projection of 68 to 70 cents. Separately, Colorado-based Newmont, the world’s No. 2 gold miner by production,
said it was updating its gold price-linked dividend policy to take advantage of rising
prices and said that Nancy K. Buese, most recently chief financial officer at MPLX LP,
will take over as CFO on Oct. 31.
The company’s next quarterly payout, under its old policy, will be on Dec. 29, when
shareholders will receive 5 cents a share, double its previous payout.
Under the new policy, the company would pay at least 10 cents a share at gold prices
below $1,150 an ounce beginning in the first quarter.

dividends.
“We have got our debt down,” so now “we’ll look at modifying our gold-price-linked
dividend policy,” Mr. Goldberg told The Wall Street Journal in an interview.

Revenue rose 15% to $1.79 billion.

profit on $1.9 billion in revenue.
