wsj.summary_analysis: Lockheed Martin lifted its full-year earnings forecast as the company benefited from sales of its F-35 jet fighter and its recently acquired Sikorsky helicopter unit, part of a broader reshaping of the business that also included plans announced earlier in the year to carve out its government information-technology unit. Aeronautics sales rose 21% to $3.80 billion, which the company attributed to F-35 program sales plus increased C-130 cargo plane deliveries, while mission-systems revenue surged 52% thanks to Sikorsky; those gains offset declines in the information-systems and space-systems segments. The company had also launched a voluntary layoff program in its aeronautics business the prior month, aiming to cut about 1,000 U.S. jobs, or roughly 0.8% of its workforce. CFO Bruce Tanner said Lockheed expected to end the year with a backlog of $90 billion to $95 billion, down from almost $100 billion after the planned IT-unit sale to Leidos, and flagged that the Pentagon isn't expected to decide on two large missile-defense and long-range-missile contracts until 2018. First-quarter profit was $794 million, or $2.58 a share, down from $878 million, or $2.74, a year earlier, with job-cut charges reducing earnings by 21 cents a share; revenue climbed 16% to $11.70 billion versus an expected $2.59 adjusted EPS on $11.34 billion in sales, according to Thomson Reuters. Lockheed raised full-year guidance to $11.50-$11.80 a share (from $11.45-$11.75) on sales of $49.6 billion to $51.1 billion.

Lockheed confirmed the next group of F-35s would cost less than $100 million each, matching a pre-existing Pentagon target, and said it was close to a deal to sell 90 more planes at that price; Hewson said on the investor call, "It's not about slashing our profit." The company expects F-35 profit margins to rise almost a percentage point in 2017, catching up with margins on older jets like the F-16, as the Pentagon pushes toward an $85 million inflation-adjusted price target by 2019. Analyst Robert Stallard of Vertical Research was quoted skeptically noting that Lockheed conceding nothing new in the talks "may not be 'The Deal' that President Trump is hoping to advertise." Lockheed reported forecast-beating fourth-quarter earnings of $988 million, or $3.35 a share, up from $933 million, or $3.01, a year earlier, on revenue up 19% to $13.75 billion. However, its initial 2017 guidance of $12.25 to $12.55 a share fell short of the $12.87 consensus among analysts surveyed by Thomson Reuters, reflecting a lower-than-expected pension tailwind and a flagged potential accounting issue at Sikorsky; revenue guidance was set at $49.4 billion to $50.6 billion.

wsj.summary_analysis: Starbucks said profit rose 16% in its fiscal second quarter as the company drew in more mobile users in the U.S., but it missed comparable-sales expectations, with same-store sales up 6% against the 6.7% rise analysts had anticipated. Domestic sales drove the increase, with U.S. same-store sales up 7%, offsetting slower growth in Europe, where the business was hurt by the terror attacks in Paris and Brussels and by a strong dollar that made drinks and snacks more expensive in local currency; same-store sales in the Europe, Middle East and Africa division rose a smaller-than-expected 1%. COO Kevin Johnson explained that because 72% of Starbucks stores in that region are now licensed to other operators, the same-store-sales figure — which covers only company-operated stores — doesn't capture the full picture: systemwide EMEA sales, including licensed stores, actually grew 4%, ahead of the 3.4% analysts had expected, and Johnson said, "We need the investment community to think about system sales in EMEA." The company continued its international expansion, opening its first South Africa store and growing its Asia store base 18% in the quarter; CEO Howard Schultz highlighted 5% transaction growth in China and previewed a planned Starbucks at the entrance to Shanghai Disneyland that he expects to become the chain's highest-grossing location. Mobile order-and-pay usage doubled year over year to 8 million transactions a month, and active U.S. rewards members reached 12 million, up 16% from a year earlier. Starbucks reported profit of $575.1 million, or 39 cents a share, up from $494.9 million, or 33 cents, with revenue up 9.4% to $4.99 billion.

Johnson told investors, "I am personally committed to acting on several fronts to make sure it never happens again," and the company said it would close about 8,000 company-owned stores the following month for a day of anti-bias training, while stating, "We're not seeing an impact on comparable sales as a result of Philadelphia." Global same-store sales rose 2%, ahead of the 1.8% analysts had expected, with China, the company's fastest-growing market, posting 4% growth. Excluding one-time items, Starbucks earned 53 cents a share; revenue jumped 14% to $6.03 billion, beating the $5.93 billion estimate, and the company reported a second-quarter profit of $660.1 million, or 47 cents a share, up from $652.8 million, or 45 cents, a year earlier. The company reiterated its full-year outlook for 3%-5% global comparable-sales growth, though it noted that figure excludes the impact of the store closures for training.

Revenue rose 18% to $43.73 billion. Favor of Copies

By Joseph Walker and Paul Ziobro
Aug. 2, 2016 at 6:17 pm ET
CVS, best known as a retail pharmacy chain, is also a major player in the pharmacy benefit management industry.
REUTERS
CVS Health Corp. CVS 0.15% is embracing new, cheaper copies of biotech medicines
in an attempt to combat rising prescription drug costs.
CVS, whose Caremark unit administers drug-benefit plans for employers and insurers,
said Tuesday it would drop coverage of two higher-priced medicines used in diabetes
and cancer treatments. It will instead cover their replica versions, sometimes called
biosimilars, for many of its drug-plan members.
https://www.wsj.com/articles/cvs-drops-coverage-of-2-branded-biotech-drugs-in-favor-of-copies-1470176277 Page 1 of 4
CVS Drops Coverage of 2 Branded Biotech Drugs in Favor of Copies - WSJ 2026-08-29, 11:43 PM
The changes, which go into effect Jan. 1, are a blow to Sanofi SA’s SAN -0.04% Lantus,
a popular brand-name insulin treatment for diabetes, and Amgen Inc.’s AMGN -1.05%
Neupogen, which helps to prevent infections related to cancer treatment. A vial of
Lantus retails for about $260 while a single dose of Neupogen costs about $350,
according to GoodRx.
Cheaper copies of biotech drugs have only recently begun to enter the U.S. market and
haven’t yet made much of a dent in the nation’s drug spending, in part because they
have been priced at relatively small discounts to their branded rivals.
But the move by CVS is the latest indication that U.S. health insurers and pharmacy
benefit managers are eager to reap savings from the new drugs. CVS Chief Medical
Officer Troyen A. Brennan said biosimilars are typically priced 10% to 15% cheaper but
that CVS has negotiated additional discounts.
“We want to signal that this biosimilar movement is real,” Dr. Brennan said in an
interview. “We have big hopes for [biosimilars] to reduce drug costs over all.”
An Amgen spokeswoman said Neupogen “is competitively priced,” and that patients
and doctors should be able to choose which product they want to use. A Sanofi
spokesman said CVS’s decision to exclude Lantus and another of the company’s
insulins would make “it difficult for patients to benefit from the gold standard of basal
insulin treatment.”
CVS, best known as a retail pharmacy chain, is also a major player in the pharmacy
benefit management industry, overseeing drug spending for U.S. employers, health
insurers and labor unions. CVS and other PBMs pool their customers’ purchasing
power to negotiate better prices from drugmakers. In exchange, PBMs often steer
their clients to products for which they receive the best prices. Last year, CVS dropped
coverage for Pfizer Inc.’s anti-impotence pill Viagra in favor of Eli Lilly & Co.’s Cialis.
However, the exclusions aren’t ironclad. Some PBM clients customize their own

The changes that CVS announced on Tuesday, for instance, will apply mainly to its
commercial employer and labor union clients who subscribe to its standard
formulary, or list of covered drugs.
CVS said it would exclude an additional 35 products in 2017, including Novartis AG’s

djnw.summary_analysis: Coverage of this quarter comes from three separate MarketWatch/Dow Jones Newswires "Market Snapshot" roundups on the broader U.S. equity session of August 8, 2017, rather than a dedicated CVS earnings story, so the CVS-specific content is limited to how the stock traded around its release rather than a detailed breakdown of results. All three pieces agree on the same core fact: CVS Health reported earnings and revenue that beat analyst estimates ahead of the opening bell, yet the stock declined anyway. None of the roundups provides specific revenue or EPS figures for CVS, or any guidance or management commentary from the company itself; instead they use CVS as an example within a broader discussion of that day's market, quoting analyst James Meyer of Tower Bridge Advisors on why beats were common that earnings season: "If expectations get low enough, you can beat them."
djnw.why_moved: The roundups report that CVS shares fell over the course of the session despite the earnings and revenue beat, with the three updates citing declines of 1.6% (in an early snapshot, "Ahead of the open, drugstore operator CVS (CVS) posted earnings and revenue that beat estimates. Shares fell 1.6%"), 1.4%, and 1.9% at different points in the day's coverage. The articles do not fully explain the disconnect between the beat and the decline beyond the general observation, via the Meyer quote, that with depressed expectations across the sector a beat did not necessarily translate into a higher share price. No other specific driver of the decline is identified in the source material.

djnw.summary_analysis: This Dow Jones Newswires company story, published November 6, 2017 ("CVS's Revenue Rises as It Pursues Aetna"), covers CVS Health's third-quarter results. Revenue rose 3.5% to $46.2 billion, matching analyst expectations, while net income was $1.3 billion, or $1.26 per share, down from $1.43 per share a year earlier; adjusted earnings of $1.50 per share beat the $1.48 analyst estimate. The pharmacy-services division grew sales 8.1% to $32.9 billion on expanded network claims and specialty-pharmacy volume, while the retail segment declined 2.7% to $19.6 billion amid falling same-store sales and $55 million of hurricane-related costs, mostly in retail. CVS narrowed its full-year adjusted EPS guidance to $5.87–$5.91 from a prior $5.83–$5.93 range. The report landed amid CVS's pursuit of a $66 billion acquisition of health insurer Aetna, which the article frames as an effort to strengthen CVS's negotiating leverage with drugmakers and bolster its prescription business.
djnw.why_moved: The article states that CVS shares, which were already down 12% year-to-date, rose marginally — less than 1% — in premarket trading on minimal volume following the release. It attributes this muted move to a quarter that beat on adjusted EPS and matched revenue expectations, without describing any stronger reaction; the piece offers no further explanation for why the move was so limited beyond noting the light premarket volume.

CVS to Raise Starting Pay to $11 an Hour
Retailer also reports higher-than-expected earnings
By Sharon Terlep
Updated Feb. 8, 2018 at 8:26 am ET
CVS plans to raise its starting pay and wages for lower-wage retail workers. RICHARD B. LEVINE/NEWSCOM/ZUMA
PRESS
CVS Health Corp. CVS 0.15% said it will use some of the extra cash from the U.S. tax
overhaul to raise its starting hourly pay to $11 for U.S. workers, the latest company to
announce employee perks in the wake of the legislation.
The company, with 240,000 U.S. workers, currently pays a starting wage of $9 an hour,
though many employees make more. It said that in addition to raising the minimum, it
will increase pay for lower-wage retail workers at its nearly 10,000 U.S. stores. CVS
didn’t provide an average increase.

CVS to Raise Starting Pay to $11 an Hour - WSJ 2026-08-29, 11:47 PM
A tight labor market has driven up competition for unskilled hourly workers. Walmart
Inc., the country’s biggest private employer, said last month it would lift its starting
pay to $11 an hour. Several states and municipalities already have a minimum wage at
or above $11 an hour.
CVS also will offer all full-time employees four weeks of paid parental leave and will
freeze employee health premiums for the coming year. About 100,000 workers are
enrolled in CVS’s employee health plan.
The moves are expected to cost $425 million a year. The company said last month it
expects the tax changes will boost cash flow in 2018 by about $1.2 billion.
“We said that we would invest our tax savings back into our business, and that’s
exactly what we’re doing,” CVS Chief Executive Larry Merlo said in a statement.
CVS said paying a more competitive wage to retail workers, from pharmacy
technicians to cashiers, will bolster efforts to make its stores into health-care hubs.
Reinventing its stores is a key cog in CVS’s plan to create a vertical health-care system
with insurance giant Aetna Inc., which CVS last year agreed to acquire for $69 billion.
Other money from the tax plan will go toward items such as data analytics and pilot
programs aimed at improving health outcomes.
CVS also reported higher-than-expected fourth-quarter earnings on Thursday, as
rising sales from its pharmacy-services segment offset sluggish retail growth.
The company said same-store sales excluding pharmacy sales rose 0.1% in the most
recent quarter. The figure came in ahead of expectations from analysts polled by
Consensus Metrix, who had predicted a 2% decline in same-store sales.
Overall for the period, the company reported a profit of $3.29 billion, or $3.22 a share,
up from $1.71 billion, or $1.59 a share, a year earlier. Excluding the impact of the tax
benefit per-share earnings grew to $1.92 from $1.71.

them happy to pay rebates and that PBMs are retaining these rebates. And this is
simply not true,” Mr. Merlo said on a conference call Wednesday. “Our data showed

The Adobe Systems logo on one of the software maker’s products. LUCY NICHOLSON/REUTERS
Speeding up means speed bumps hurt a bit more. Just ask Adobe Systems
ADBE 0.82% .
Among the older software companies once reliant on plastic compact discs, Adobe
stands out for its relatively rapid transition to the cloud. Five years ago, digital
subscriptions accounted for just 15% of Adobe’s annual revenue. That number now
stands at 84% for the nine-month period ended Sept. 1.

Can Adobe Keep the Clouds Away?
Software maker’s solid performance should help as rising peer valuations will make
investors pickier
By Dan Gallagher
Dec. 15, 2017 at 11:55 am ET
Investors have embraced Adobe’s transition to a cloud-based, subscription business model. LUCY NICHOLSON/
REUTERS
When it comes to software, investors sometimes get what they are willing to pay for.
Adobe Systems has never been a cheap stock to own. It has averaged about 32 times
forward earnings over the past five years, compared with an average of 18 times for
the S&P 500 Software & Services group. The stock trades around that level now, after
having gained about 70% this year as investors embraced the company’s transition to
a cloud-based, subscription business model, which has boosted both revenue and
operating earnings.
https://www.wsj.com/articles/can-adobe-keep-the-clouds-away-1513356909 Page 1 of 3
Can Adobe Keep the Clouds Away? - WSJ 2026-08-30, 1:17 AM
Adobe’s fiscal fourth-quarter results posted Thursday suggests the steam hasn’t yet
run out on that shift. Revenue jumped 25% year over year and exceeded the $2 billion
mark for the first time. Operating margins of 32% were the highest in at least seven
years, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence. Adobe also projected revenue
growth of 21% year over year for the current quarter, which ends in February, and
maintained a previous forecast for full-year growth of 20%.
That should also cool some of the fears that arose over Adobe following its last report,
when the company warned that some larger deals were taking longer to close. With
84% of its revenue now coming from subscriptions, Adobe is showing that strong
growth is still possible at what might seem the tail end of its transition, as demand for
the company’s content and marketing services continues to grow from big and small
businesses.
But Adobe and its peers may still face a higher bar heading into the new year.
Software stocks have been on a tear this year, especially those selling cloud-based and
subscription-based services. The 10 largest cloud software stocks on the market are
up 68% this year—more than double the Nasdaq Composite’s gain. J.P. Morgan’s
software analysts downgraded 19 stocks, including Adobe, earlier this week, citing the
belief that a repeat performance for the sector will be difficult for the coming year.
That will keep the pressure on Adobe to keep up its pace. The company’s solid
performance to date has rightfully made it one of the brightest spots in the cloud
sector. That should give some protection when the rains come.

Chinese e-commerce leader Alibaba, based in Hangzhou, is expanding beyond

wsj.summary_analysis: Ford's first-quarter 2016 results, reported April 28, 2016, showed net income more than doubling to $2.5 billion (61 cents a share) from $1.2 billion (29 cents) a year earlier, when the prior-year quarter had been hurt by short supplies of the newly redesigned aluminum-bodied F-150. Results handily beat the 48 cents a share analysts had expected. On an operating basis, Ford earned $3.8 billion, or 68 cents a share, with global automotive margin near 10%. North American operating margin hit a record 12.9% for the quarter, outpacing GM's 8.7% and Fiat Chrysler's 7.2% for the same period, with North American operating profit nearly doubling to a record $3.1 billion as U.S. sales grew 8.4%. The article details regional performance: Ford's best European quarter since 2008, swinging to a $434 million pretax profit from a $42 million loss a year earlier; Asia Pacific profit doubling to $220 million on China strength (equity income from Chinese joint ventures up 23% to $443 million); and a widened South American operating loss of $256 million. CFO Bob Shanks said, 'You're starting to see a better balance of profitability,' and pushed back on concerns that Ford's profitability had peaked or that the U.S. economy faced recession, saying, 'we're proving that to be a misconception.' Revenue rose 11% to $37.7 billion. Ford flagged an upcoming Super Duty truck launch in the third quarter -- its first major overhaul in 19 years -- as a further earnings driver for the back half of the year.
wsj.why_moved: The article states Ford shares rose 3.4% to $14.12 in morning trading, which it directly ties to results that 'handily beat' the 48-cent consensus EPS estimate, alongside record North American margins and strength in China and Europe that it says 'could cheer investors' who had worried Ford's profitability had peaked. The article frames the gain around the magnitude of the beat and the regional profit improvements described above rather than any single metric.

Truck Sales Drive Soaring Profit at Ford
Profit jumps 63% and outlook brightens, as auto maker commands an average price of
$45,400 for its pickups
By Mike Colias and John D. Stoll
Updated Oct. 26, 2017 at 9:56 am ET
A Ford F-250 truck is displayed at a dealership in Florida. New versions of Ford’s Super Duty lineup of work trucks
have fueled sales. ALAN DIAZ/ASSOCIATED PRESS
Ford Motor Co. F -0.50% delivered a fresh reminder that—amid all the talk about
driverless cars and electric vehicles—Detroit is a truck town.
The No. 2 U.S. auto maker on Thursday reported a 63% third-quarter profit increase, a
positive sign following a summer marked by management reshuffling, a renewed cost-
cutting drive and continued malaise for the share price. Those results were fueled by
sales of F-Series trucks, hulking vehicles that likely made up more than half of the $2
billion in operating profits Ford fetched over the period.
https://www.wsj.com/articles/ford-posts-63-profit-jump-1509017675 Page 1 of 5
Truck Sales Drive Soaring Profit at Ford - WSJ 2026-08-30, 1:35 AM
The average Ford pickup sold for $45,400 even with incentives factored in during the
July through September period. That price firmly outpaces the $31,200 J.D. Power
estimates is the average transaction price on vehicles sold in the U.S., and was also
$2,800 higher than F-Series prices during the same period a year ago.
General Motors Co., which reported earnings Tuesday, also saw truck pricing
increases, raking in $43,220 per Chevy Silverado or GMC Sierra sold in the third
quarter, or nearly $1,300 more than the same period a year ago.
Ford’s results highlight a persistent reality for car executives eager to showcase
investments in future technology. The billions of dollars being spent on autonomous-
vehicle research and making more affordable electric cars wouldn’t be available if it
weren’t for brisk truck sales.
The truck momentum has been sparked by the redesign of Ford’s so-called Super Duty
lineup, a series of bulky work trucks that can cost more than $100,000. The auto
maker put new versions on sale last fall, including the F-250, as U.S. buyers soured on
bread-and-butter sedans and compact cars. It marked the first major redesign of the
Super Duty in several years.
Ford also sells the F-150 truck for lighter-duty needs. The F-Series has been the best-
selling vehicle in America since 1977.
Competitors, convinced that low gasoline prices and favorable economic conditions
will remain, are angling to cut in on Ford’s truck dominance. GM and Fiat Chrysler
Automobiles NV are prepping redesigned models for introduction late next year, and
those projects require billions of dollars and thousands of engineers.
Pickup trucks are a vital source of profit for the Detroit companies. While the Asian
auto makers are formidable rivals in cars and crossover SUVs, none offer any serious
challenge in the market for big pickups. Profit margins on those trucks—used to haul
recreational boats and on construction sites across America—are typically far above

10% and can outpace luxury cars.
Ford needs to protect its turf. North America continues to fuel Ford’s bottom line,
contributing nearly all of its automotive operating profit as other regions net out at
about break-even. Ford’s operating margin rose to 8.1% in the third quarter, short of
the 10% margins that Detroit executives expect to squeeze from core operations but
substantially better than the same period a year ago.
The auto maker’s redesigned Super Duty lineup of bulky work trucks has carried the bottom line. LM OTERO/
ASSOCIATED PRESS
Ford’s overall profit increase during the quarter was also attributed to a lower tax rate
and belt-tightening measures. The No. 2 U.S. auto maker by sales reported net income
of $1.6 billion for the July through September period, and it raised its full-year
earnings guidance.
The brighter outlook is a sign the company is optimistic about measures it is taking to
improve its business, Chief Financial Officer Bob Shanks said during a round table
with reporters. Ford posted adjusted earnings per share of 43 cents, better than the
average analysts’ forecast of 33 cents.
Revenue grew 1% to $36.5 billion, surpassing Wall Street expectations of $32.8 billion.

Ford cited early progress on new Chief ExecutiveJim Hackett’s goal of slashing

as it pivots to longer-term bets on electric cars and autonomous vehicles. Costs
improved by about $700 million in the quarter.
“I would look at this as a first down payment (on) good strong cost management,” Mr.
Shanks said.
The company, however, posted a surprise loss in Europe related to continued fallout
from Brexit in the U.K. market, and slimmer margins in China due to pricing pressure.
Pretax profit in the Asia-Pacific region more than doubled to $289 million, as cost-
cutting lifted the company’s profit margin there to 7.9%, from 4.3%. Ford also got a lift
from its finance arm, where pretax profit edged up 6% to $600 million, despite

Ford Motor Co. is planning to boost profit margins faster than initially forecast, saying

that are unprofitable in an effort to keep pace with Detroit rivals.

aggressive action on costs. For example, Ford said it is pulling a number of
unprofitable small cars it offers in U.S. dealerships, planning eventually to have trucks

and sport-utility vehicles make up 90% of sales volume.
The commitment comes as the company’s first-quarter net profit rose 9% to $1.7
billion because of a lower corporate tax rate. Operating profit for the first-quarter fell
13% to $2.2 billion as weaker results in North America and losses in Asia Pacific offset
improved results from Ford Credit, the company’s in-house financing arm.
The U.S. auto market is slumping after nearly a decade of growth, pressuring Ford and
others to find additional ways to earn money at the same time big investments are
needed for electric cars and driverless-vehicle research. Ford is committed to rolling
out battery-powered cars that could compete with Tesla Inc. in 2020 and offering
hybrid versions of its most popular sports cars, trucks and SUVs.
Ford is projecting lower profit in 2018, its third consecutive year of earnings declines.
It cited progress on identifying areas to cut costs and now expects to slash expenses
by $25.5 billion by 2022, up from the $14 billion in cost cuts previously planned.
Executives are also targeting a 10% margin in North America by 2020, a goal that, if
achieved, would put it closer to its chief rival General Motors Co. in regional operating
profitability.
Ford Chief Financial Officer Bob Shanks said the savings will in part be derived from a
$5 billion reduction in capital spending in coming years. He declined to give details on
other areas the company plans to make savings but indicated it could include exiting
unprofitable businesses and pulling capital away from underperforming areas.
“Everything will be on the table,” he said. “We can make different investments, we can
partner, we can exit products and markets, and we will do that.”
Ford was able to keep costs, excluding commodities, flat in the first quarter, a sign that
its efficiency efforts are starting to bear fruit, Mr. Shanks said. But the bulk of the
savings won’t come until 2019 and 2020, he said.

Mr. Hackett, who is approaching his first anniversary at Ford’s helm, outlined last fall
a corporate “fitness” plan that, among other measures, would shift $7 billion in
spending away from small cars and sedans and redeploy it to developing more higher-

Ford said Wednesday it will only sell the Mustang and a crossover version of the
compact Focus in the U.S. in the near future. That means the Fusion and Taurus family
sedans and the small Fiesta will be eliminated.
Wall Street, however, has shown little enthusiasm for Mr. Hackett’s plans so far.
Shares closed at $11.11 on Wednesday, little changed from when he took over last May
after the firing of former CEO Mark Fields.
Operating profit in North America slipped to $1.9 billion in the first quarter, compared
with $2.1 billion in the same period a year earlier. Ford said its North American
operating margin was 7.8%.
The company’s Ford Smart Mobility division, which includes new transportation
ventures, such as its van-shuttle service Chariot, incurred a $102 million loss in the

In China, Ford’s profit from its joint ventures amounted to $138 million, down from

wsj.summary_analysis: Ford's second-quarter 2018 results, reported July 25, 2018, showed net income dropping 48% and the company lowering its 2018 profit outlook, citing tariff-related commodity cost pressures and weakness in Asia and Europe; it also outlined a broad multiyear restructuring that could bring $11 billion in charges. Net income of $1.1 billion was hurt by about $300 million in higher year-over-year commodity costs, nearly half tied to U.S. steel and aluminum tariffs, which CFO Bob Shanks said could shave up to $600 million off full-year profit; Shanks called it 'obviously a very tough quarter for us.' China sales sank 26% in the first half of the year, and the China business swung to a $483 million operating loss from a $23 million profit a year earlier, which Shanks attributed to a stale product lineup hurting both volumes and pricing. Adjusted EPS of 27 cents missed the 31-cent analyst consensus; revenue fell 2% to $38.9 billion. Results were also hurt by nearly $600 million from a truck-production disruption after a parts-supplier outage idled Ford's truck plants for more than a week in May. CEO Jim Hackett's restructuring plan, separate from the existing $25.5 billion cost-cutting program, aims to redirect capital toward the most profitable segments, especially the North American truck lineup; Shanks said, 'As we allocate capital to the places we think we can be bigger, better and stronger and away from the areas where we don't think we can get a return, there will be consequences.' The article notes rival GM also cited rising steel costs from the tariffs that took effect June 1 that same day.

Ford Lowers Full-Year Outlook
Earnings fell 48% in second quarter; higher commodity costs hurt auto maker’s results
By Mike Colias
July 25, 2018 at 4:49 pm ET
Ford vehicles on display at a dealership in Shanghai. The auto maker’s struggles deepened in China, where the
company’s sales sank 26% in the year’s first six months. QILAI SHEN/BLOOMBERG NEWS
Ford Motor Co. on Wednesday reported a 48% drop in second-quarter net income and
lowered its 2018 profit outlook, citing tariff-related commodity cost pressures and
trouble in Asia and Europe. It also outlined plans for a broad, multiyear restructuring
that could result in $11 billion in charges.
Ford’s net income of $1.1 billion was hampered by about $300 million in higher
commodity costs compared with a year earlier, nearly half of which stemmed from
U.S. tariffs on steel and aluminum, Chief Financial Officer Bob Shanks said during a
roundtable discussion with reporters. The company expects the effect of the tariffs to
https://www.wsj.com/articles/ford-lowers-full-year-outlook-1532551742 Page 1 of 3
Ford Lowers Full-Year Outlook - WSJ 2026-08-30, 1:36 AM
shave as much as $600 million from the bottom line this year, Mr. Shanks said.
Ford’s struggles deepened in China, where sales sank 26% in the first six months of the
year. Ford’s China business swung to an operating loss of $483 million, from a $23
million profit a year earlier. Mr. Shanks said Ford’s product portfolio has grown stale
in the world’s largest car market, which has hurt both sales volumes and pricing.
The No. 2 U.S. auto maker by sales posted adjusted earnings per share of 27 cents,
short of analysts’ average forecast of 31 cents. Revenue fell 2% to $38.9 billion.
Ford also was hurt by a nearly $600 million hit from a drop in truck production
stemming from a disruption at a parts supplier, which idled Ford’s truck plants for
more than a week in May.
“Obviously a very tough quarter for us,” Mr. Shanks told reporters at Ford’s
headquarters Wednesday.
Ford Chief Executive Jim Hackett was appointed more than a year ago to set a long-
term plan for the auto maker as innovations such as driverless and electric cars, and
ride-sharing, threaten to transform the industry’s century-old business model. He
also has emphasized improving Ford’s financial “fitness” by boosting profitability, in
part through a plan to slash $25.5 billion in cumulative expenses by 2022.
The restructuring effort would be separate from those cost cuts, Mr. Shanks said. He
declined to give specifics but said the restructuring will be aimed at directing
resources toward the most profitable and highest-potential parts of the business, such
as the company’s truck lineup in North America, which generates the bulk of Ford’s
bottom line.
“As we allocate capital to the places we think we can be bigger, better and stronger
and away from the areas where we don’t think we can get a return, there will be
consequences,” he said.
